This means that having realized equality—which is without beginning, middle, or end—the three bodies of all Buddhas, within that Buddha-ground and Buddha-pure land, possess no spatial limitations whatsoever.

"Reaching the limit of the dharma-realm" demonstrates that the Blessed One, throughout the very bounds of saṃsāra, constantly manifests the sublime qualities of bringing about the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings.

This means that because this dharmadhātu is perfectly pure, it constantly gives rise to the outflow of teachings such as the sūtras until the very end of saṃsāra; for the sake of sentient beings to be converted in future ages, it perpetually manifests and brings about their benefit and happiness, according to what is appropriate and at the proper time.

The phrase "extending throughout the nature of space and to the furthest limits of the future" reveals the Bhagavat’s inexhaustible and ultimate, preeminent qualities. This means that just as space is eternally without end, so too are the qualities arising from the Buddha-dharmadhātu; they are likewise inexhaustible.
Furthermore, just as there is no point at which the future limit ends, so too his application (*prayoga*) for the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings never ceases.
Are the merits of all Buddhas by nature eternal, inexhaustible, and ultimate?
Or are they by nature impermanent, yet continuous and uninterrupted?
It cannot be definitively stated that they are inexhaustible and ultimate.

Because the nature of the merit of the Buddha’s Dharma-body—the pure dharma-realm and the essence of its rational nature—is eternal, the merits of the two bodies, the enjoyment body and the transformation body, although their nature is impermanent, are inexhaustible and ultimate because they are never severed or exhausted.

All Tathāgatas originally made great vows to seek great enlightenment for the sake of sentient beings; if all sentient beings were to attain extinction, at that time, would not the conditioned merits of the Buddhas come to an end?
Since there is no time when the realm of all sentient beings is entirely extinguished and passed into nirvāṇa, the merit of the Buddha is never severed or extinguished.
Why is this? It is because it is the very nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
Since beginningless time, all sentient beings possess five types of spiritual dispositions:
first, the śrāvaka disposition; second, the pratyekabuddha disposition; [and so forth].
3. the lineage of the Tathāgatas;
4. the indeterminate lineage;
5. the lineage lacking supramundane qualities.

As explained in detail in other sūtras and śāstras, the first four types of lineage are established through analysis; although there is no fixed time limit, they nonetheless possess the certainty of eventually attaining nirvāṇa, owing to the compassionate skillful means of all Buddhas.
Regarding the fifth lineage, because they lack the causes for supramundane merit, they will ultimately never have the opportunity to attain nirvāṇa.

Although the Buddhas may employ skillful means to manifest supernatural powers for them and teach the dharmas for leaving the evil realms and being born in the good realms, even if they diligently cultivate wholesome causes according to these instructions and succeed in being born among humans or even as high as the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, they will inevitably fall back down and descend into the various evil realms.

The Buddhas, through their skillful means, further manifest supernatural powers and preach the Dharma to transform them; yet they again practice wholesome deeds and attain birth in the happy realms, only to later fall back once more and undergo various sufferings and afflictions.

The Buddhas employ further skillful means to rescue them, continuing in this manner through the succession of kalpas until the end of the future, yet they cannot cause them to attain ultimate parinirvāṇa.

Although other sūtras proclaim that all classes of sentient beings possess buddha-nature and shall all become Buddhas, these statements are made either with reference to the buddha-nature of the *tathatā-dharmakāya*, or as a skillful means directed toward a limited portion of all sentient beings, for the purpose of ensuring that those of indeterminate lineage will definitely and swiftly proceed toward the fruit of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.

By this principle, the merit of the Buddhas in bringing benefit and happiness to sentient beings is never exhausted; this virtue of benefiting others remains uninterrupted precisely because it depends upon the virtue of self-benefit. Therefore, although the conditioned merits of the Tathāgata arise from causes and perish moment by moment, they are nonetheless without end or exhaustion.
Because the Buddha’s virtues are inexhaustible and ultimate, he thus achieves the most pure awakening.
All subsequent phrases should be applied in this same manner, one by one.
Why is it that the pure lands of all Buddhas are mentioned first, followed by such merits of the World-Honored One?

It is to demonstrate that such merits of the Buddhas depend upon their pure lands; and it is to demonstrate that the World-Honored One, relying upon a pure Buddha-field and possessing such virtues, has preached this sutra.

Next, the perfection of the Blessed One’s retinue is revealed, namely the great śrāvakas and great bodhisattvas. Other sūtras state that his retinue consists of those who are well-tamed and those who are liberated; this is called the perfection of the Tathāgata’s retinue.

This describes an assembly of immeasurable great śrāvakas together with immeasurable bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; all are disciplined and compliant, equal to the sons of the Buddha, all dwelling in the Mahāyāna and traversing the Mahāyāna, thus fulfilling the retinues of śrāvakas and bodhisattvas in their respective order.
Why are the śrāvakas mentioned first and the bodhisattvas mentioned later here?

It is for the sake of removing the doubts of those who harbor uncertainty regarding the Mahāyāna; for the sake of inducing firm faith in bodhisattvas of indeterminate lineage; for the sake of causing the great śrāvakas who have already attained purification to relinquish their pride of self-importance—since they were personally transformed by the World-Honored One in the presence of the assembly, being close to him and receiving his direct instruction; furthermore, because the śrāvakas constantly follow the Buddha, resemble the Buddha in form, and constitute his inner retinue; and finally, so that bodhisattvas may develop reverence toward the śrāvaka community.

As stated in the Sūtra, a bodhisattva should not fail to show respect toward the assembly of śrāvakas; for this reason, he praises the virtues of the śrāvakas, so as to inspire pure faith in them among others as well.
Within this assembly, there were also other groups who compiled the Dharma; however, for brevity, only two groups are mentioned because they are preeminent.

As stated later in the sutra: "The entire great assembly—the world with its gods, humans, asuras, and others—having heard what the Buddha taught, all rejoiced greatly, believed, accepted, and practiced it."

It was previously stated that the Pure Land has the most supremely sovereign pure consciousness as its characteristic. How is it that the presence of śrāvakas and others within the assembly does not contradict this?
What contradiction exists?
Since the various śrāvakas perceive [the assembly] in the same manner as the bodhisattvas, a contradiction arises;
such a statement could only be made if the śrāvakas also perceived it in this way.
Although the various śrāvakas are present in this assembly, they are obstructed from seeing its purity and excellence because they are hindered by their karma.

It is like one born blind who cannot see such pure and wondrous realms; it would be improper to object that because they cannot see them, they should not be among the assembly. For although they do not see such pure wonders, they do see the impure land and the emanation body (nirmāṇakāya) preaching the Dharma.

Although they are in the same assembly, what each perceives differs due to the power of their own karma; it is like seeing genuine gold and taking it to be fire, or like the four types of sentient beings each perceiving a single place differently.

Alternatively, through the empowerment of the Tathāgata’s supernormal power (*ṛddhi*), they may temporarily obtain the sight and hearing of the preaching of the sublime Dharma; this is the inconceivable power of the Tathāgata, which cannot be challenged on account of faculties, stages, or spiritual levels. Such a transformation is without fault, as it serves to adorn the assembly where the Dharma is preached; it may be a creation by the Buddha himself, or a creation brought about by various Bodhisattvas.

The Sūtra says: Together with an immeasurable assembly of great śrāvakas, all of whom were well-disciplined and true sons of the Buddha; their minds were well-liberated, their wisdom was well-liberated, and their precepts were perfectly pure. They sought the joy of the Dharma; they had heard much and retained what they had heard, so that their learning was accumulated. They were skilled in what they contemplated, skilled in what they spoke, and skilled in what they did. They possessed swift wisdom, rapid wisdom, sharp wisdom, emergent wisdom, superior discerning wisdom, great wisdom, vast wisdom, and peerless wisdom—having achieved the treasure of wisdom.

He was endowed with the three types of clear knowledge (trividyā), had attained the foremost dwelling in happiness in the present life (dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra), possessed great purity as a field of merit (puṇyakṣetra) and tranquil deportment (īryāpatha), was perfected in great patience and gentleness without decline, and had properly practiced the noble teachings of the Tathāgata.
The Treatise says:
Regarding the "immeasurable great assembly of śrāvakas," their number is so vast as to be difficult to calculate; hence they are called "immeasurable.
Because they hear the Buddha’s voice and enter the Noble Path, they are called "śrāvakas" (hearers).
Furthermore, because they include the ordained monastics, it is called a "community" (saṃgha).
Since all of them are śrāvakas of the most acute faculties belonging to the lineage of the pāramitās, it is called "great."
One interpretation holds that they are called "great" because they all abide in the stage of the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).
According to the true meaning, however, they are all śrāvakas of indeterminate lineage who, having attained the small fruits, have set out for great enlightenment; therefore, they are called "great."
Alternatively, it is called "great" because the number of members is large, as in the case of the present great assembly.

Regarding "all being well-tamed": according to one interpretation, those in training (śaikṣa) have abandoned the one hundred and twelve kinds of coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) consisting of conceptual afflictions that are severed by the path of seeing; because they are no longer stubborn or unruly, they are like fine horses and are thus termed "well-tamed."

There is an interpretation that because the one beyond training (aśaikṣa) is free from the one hundred and twenty-eight kinds of afflictions abandoned through seeing and cultivation, and is thus not rigid or stubborn, he is like pure gold and is therefore called "well-tamed" (dānta).

In its true sense, all these belong to the lineage of dedication to bodhi; they are all capable of setting out toward the great fruit, following the Buddha’s will like a wise elephant, and are therefore called "tamed and compliant."
Because the Noble Path arises through the power of the Buddha, they are called "sons of the Buddha.
As it is said, they are all born from the mouth of the World-Honored One because they are born from the True Dharma.

According to another interpretation, they are all Mahāśrāvakas who proceed toward [enlightenment] and are able to succeed to the lineage of the Buddha so that it remains unbroken; therefore, they are called "sons of the Buddha."
One whose mind is well-liberated is so because of being free from craving for the three realms; as it is said, "The mind attains liberation through freedom from craving.
One who is well-liberated through wisdom is so because of having already abandoned all defiled ignorance; as it is said, "Wisdom attains liberation through freedom from ignorance."

Regarding "morality that is well-purified," as stated in the sūtras, one is said to possess morality that is well-purified by being endowed with six factors: namely, abiding in pure ethical discipline (*śīla*) while skillfully guarding oneself; being fully complete in the rules and conduct of the Pratimokṣa vows; perceiving great dread even in minor transgressions; training in the precepts (*śikṣāpada*); and furthermore, having attained untainted (*anāsrava*) morality. For these reasons, it is called "well-purified."

Regarding the meaning according to reality: one who dwells in the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) and dedicates themselves to the Mahāyāna purifies their own foundational morality by cultivating the bodhisattva precepts;

therefore, it is called "thoroughly pure. As for "seeking the joy of the Dharma": when seeking the true Dharma, one desires to proceed toward great bliss—that is, the awakening of a Buddha—and seeks nothing else. Alternatively, when seeking the Dharma, one acts for the sake of bringing happiness to others, having no intention of seeking faults, and remaining free from improper conduct.

According to the true meaning, these great śrāvakas exclusively seek the joy of the Dharma, not seeking fame, profit, or honor; they are able to hear and receive immeasurable sūtras in their beginning, middle, and end, and are thus called "learned" (bahuśruta).
They are able to remember and maintain all meanings as they have heard them so that they are never lost, and are thus called "retainers of what is heard" (śrutadhara).
By repeatedly practicing the words and meanings, they cause them to remain firmly established; for this reason, it is said that "their learning is accumulated."
Worldly fools contemplate what is ill-considered, speak what is ill-spoken, and perform what is ill-done;

the supramundane noble ones transcend those qualities and act in their opposite. Therefore, they are said to contemplate what is well-considered, speak what is well-spoken, and perform what is well-done; their three karmas are pure and follow the course of wisdom.
Because one swiftly enters into the meaning of the Dharma and Vinaya taught by the Buddha, it is called "swift wisdom" (*javana-paññā*).
Because one enters extensively into the meaning within that very [teaching], it is called "quick wisdom" (*tara-paññā*), for one who is able to practice extensively is said to be "quick."
Because it penetrates subtle meanings, it is called "sharp wisdom" (*tīkṣṇa-prajñā*).
Because it attains the sublime wisdom capable of transcending birth and death, it is called "wisdom of transcendence" (*niḥsaraṇa-prajñā*).
This wisdom serves as the cause of illumination for *nirvāṇa*; therefore, it is termed "supreme wisdom of discernment" (*pravicaya-prajñā*).

It is called "supreme discernment" (*viniścaya*) because it is supreme discernment; that is, *nirvāṇa*. Since this wisdom serves as the revealing cause (*vijñapti-hetu*) for that [nirvāṇa], it is named in reliance upon it.
Because its resolution through question and answer is inexhaustible, it is called "Great Wisdom."
Because it is profoundly deep, vast, perfect, and thoroughly mastered, it is called "Vast Wisdom" (Pṛthu-mati).
According to another version of the text, it is also called "Profound and Sublime Wisdom," meaning that others cannot fathom its depths.
Because this wisdom is superior to that of the śrāvaka assemblies of dull faculties and so forth, it is called "unequaled wisdom.
Because this wisdom can bring about the supreme goal, it is called the "jewel of wisdom."
These śrāvakas possess this jewel of wisdom; therefore, they are said to be "accomplished in the jewel of wisdom.
Regarding those who are "endowed with the three types of clear knowledge" (trividyā), it means they have attained the three kinds of clear knowledge of one beyond training (aśaikṣa).
What are called the three knowledges of one beyond training?
First, the supernormal knowledge of the realization of the recollection of past abodes;
second, the supernormal knowledge of the realization of death and rebirth.
Third, the supernormal knowledge of the realization of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣayajñānasākṣātkriyābhijñā*).

The three supernormal knowledges attained by those of sharp faculties who are beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) are called the "three clear knowledges" (*tisro vidyāḥ*), because they eliminate ignorance regarding the three time periods, whether defiled or undefiled.
One interpretation holds that "clarity" (*āloka*) has wisdom (*prajñā*) as its nature; because wisdom can dispel darkness, it is called clarity.

Another interpretation holds that it has the wholesome root of non-delusion (*amoha-kuśalamūla*) as its nature, as it is the opposite of ignorance (*avidyā*). Regarding the phrase "attaining the foremost dwelling in happiness in the present life," this refers to realizing and attaining the supreme meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) of non-retrogression.
The "greatly pure field of merit" is so called because it is eternally free from afflictions like a worldly fertile field, being able to swiftly produce vast and expansive fruits.
"Tranquil in deportment" means that all modes of conduct are maintained with correct awareness (*saṃprajanya*).
"Having achieved great patience and gentleness without diminution" means that one is capable of enduring suffering and is easy to dwell with.
"Having already properly practiced the holy teaching of the Tathāgata" means that all that was to be done has been brought to fulfillment.

The holy teaching of the Tathāgata is fundamentally intended for sentient beings to emerge from the suffering of birth and death; since all these śrāvakas have attained the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa) and have thus emerged from birth and death, they have well practiced the holy teaching of the Tathāgata.
If this is so, for what purpose does he further preach the Dharma for them?
It is in order to cause them to dedicate [their merit] toward Great Enlightenment (*mahābodhi*).

These Śrāvakas all abide in the state of No-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*); having exhausted this single retribution, they will certainly enter the eternal extinction of Nirvana without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*), where their tranquility and bliss are no different from those of a Buddha, as stated in other treatises.
Why lead them toward great enlightenment only to cause them to suffer for a long time?
There is no fault in this, as there are no sensations of suffering within the stage of transformation (*pariṇāma*).
However, because the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*) exists, this constitutes a great fault.
Although one undergoes this suffering, it brings about the great joy and great bliss of the merits of the Tathāgata’s three bodies;
therefore, there is no fault. No great bliss whatsoever surpasses nirvāṇa.
Since he has already realized this, what more could he lack that he would further seek as bodhi or nirvāṇa?

Although there is the bliss of quiescence, there is no experience of pleasure; since the bliss of the three types of awakening involves the cessation of the experience of pleasure and so forth, what use is there for the conditioned pleasure of the suffering of practice (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*) when there are immeasurable merits [to be attained]?

Conditioned uncontaminated phenomena (*anāsrava-saṃskṛta*) are like *nirvāṇa*; because they are uncontaminated, they are not subsumed under the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).

Furthermore, if one becomes a Buddha, one is able to transform immeasurable sentient beings who are to be converted so that they emerge from birth and death; would those who have already become Buddhas lack this capacity?

Since beginningless time, it is the natural law (*dharmatā*) of sentient beings that the transformer and the transformed are linked by their spiritual lineage (*gotra*); those who lack such a connection possess no capacity for transformation. Therefore, through various skillful means (*upāya*), the Tathāgata transforms all sentient beings, causing them to attain the fruit of Buddhahood, thereby transforming those who are to be transformed.

If that is so, then for a śrāvaka, either seven births are eliminated, or one birth is eliminated, or one birth in each respective realm of the upper spheres is eliminated; all remaining births attain non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), or all births indeed attain non-analytical cessation.
How is it that one further passes through three incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*) to cultivate the causes of enlightenment and thereby attain Buddhahood?

Although the *pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha* (cessation not through deliberation) has been attained regarding the birth-and-death (*bhava*) moistened by the various afflictions (*kleśa*), one undergoes transformational birth (*pariṇāmi-janman*) by the power of vows; thus, there is no fault in cultivating the causes of enlightenment for three incalculable eons.

As for non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), it refers to that which absolutely does not arise during a certain period due to the incompleteness of necessary conditions; it is not, however, a state of never arising again.

Although such a person may dwell for a long time within saṃsāra, through the power of their meditative concentration and vows, they support and influence the causes of birth so that their functional capacity produces effects over a prolonged duration. Thus, this very single body successively increases in excellence until the attainment of Buddhahood, just as one who employs the method of prolonging life does not undergo further rebirth.
Therefore, the treatise states:
Question:
Do Śrāvakas who have dedicated themselves toward Bodhi do so while abiding in the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder, or while abiding in the realm of nirvāṇa with remainder?
Answer:
This can only occur while abiding in the realm of nirvana with remainder. Why is this so?
In the realm of nirvana without remainder, all undertaking of activities is distanced and all functional efforts have entirely ceased.
Question:

If one who sets out for unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment dwells solely within the realm of nirvana with remainder, how is it that they are able to realize unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment through only a single lifetime?
Why is this? For even Arhats and others shall have no further existence beyond a single birth, let alone the continuity of many births.
Answer:

Since it must be accomplished by increasing the life-force (*āyus-saṃskāra*), the Blessed One, for the most part with reference to those śrāvakas who have dedicated themselves toward enlightenment, spoke with intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*):
"If one has well cultivated the four bases of power (*ṛddhi-pāda*), one can remain for an eon or even longer than an eon."
"Remaining for one kalpa" here means that more than one kalpa has passed.
Although they thus increase their life-span and set out toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, the practice they cultivate becomes extremely sluggish because they delight in nirvana.

This is not equal to a bodhisattva who has newly resolved upon the path and begun their practice; for once such a one has thus increased their lifespan, they leave behind the body with its faculties (*sendriya-kāya*) and manifest a separate transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), demonstrating before those of like dharma that they have entered parinirvāṇa within the realm of nirvana without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇadhātu*).
For this reason, they all thought:

"The Venerable One named [so-and-so] has already attained parinirvāṇa within the realm of nirvana without remainder; yet, by means of his remaining physical body of faculties, he dwells in seclusion wherever he pleases within this Jambudvīpa. Even all the gods cannot behold him, let alone other sentient beings."

Because they take great delight in dwelling in nirvāṇa, whenever they are negligent—whether while traveling through various worlds to attend upon and make offerings to Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, or while practicing the noble paths that constitute the provisions for enlightenment—the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas repeatedly awaken them.
Having awakened to this, they are able to practice without negligence.

Furthermore, regarding the śrāvaka who dedicates [their practice] toward bodhi: some are able to abandon the aspiration for the state of a śrāvaka while still in the stage of training (śaikṣa), while others are only able to abandon it upon reaching the stage beyond training (aśaikṣa). This is because there are differences in their spiritual faculties (indriya) and differences in the various conditions (pratyaya) they depend upon.

Likewise, if one within the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) redirects [the roots of merit] toward enlightenment, through the power of meditative concentration and vows, one repeatedly nourishes the causes that previously brought about the present body, causing the continuity of the resulting fruits to persist for a long duration; these gradually increase in excellence until their functional capacity is finally exhausted upon the attainment of Buddhahood.

Although this retribution is produced by causes that are tainted (*sāsrava*), it is nevertheless assisted by untainted meditative concentration (*anāsrava-samādhi*) and vows; therefore, it is called "inconceivable transformation-death" (*acintya-nairmāṇika-vaiparītya-maraṇa*), because the untainted concentration and vows are themselves inconceivable.

If those on the stage of training (śaikṣa) dedicate their roots of virtue toward enlightenment, or through the force of the rebirth-inducing power of secondary afflictions (upakleśa), they experience that birth; having experienced it, they subdue all afflictions in their final birth and, by generating the power of meditative vows, they provide the causal support for their subsequent existence, proceeding according to the aforementioned principle until the attainment of Buddhahood.

Alternatively, once they have turned their minds [toward awakening], they immediately subdue their afflictions and give rise to the power of meditative concentration and vows to support the causes for their present bodies, proceeding according to the principles previously explained until they attain Buddhahood.
All instances where the power of untainted meditative concentration and vows assists that which is not an affliction are subsumed under the inconceivable transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*).

If it is comprised within the segmented body (vibhajya-kāya) that is the maturation (vipāka) induced by the power of afflictions, then if one says that a śrāvaka is a transformation-body (nirmāṇa-kāya), there is no need for such questioning and analytical distinction.

The Sūtra says: Furthermore, there were immeasurable bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who came together from various buddha-fields and assembled; all of them dwelt in the Mahāyāna and roamed within the Mahāyāna teachings. Their minds were impartial toward all sentient beings, free from all conceptualization, non-conceptualization, and various forms of discrimination. They had subdued all Māras and adversaries, remained far removed from all the mental preoccupation and discrimination of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and were sustained by the joy and delight of the vast flavor of the Dharma. Having transcended the five fears, they were single-mindedly entering the stage of non-retrogression. They appeared before us, having brought to rest the ground where all sentient beings are oppressed by every form of suffering and affliction, with the Bodhisattva Wondrous Birth (Ghoṣadatta) as their leader.
The treatise says:
Regarding the term "bodhisattva-mahāsattva," it refers to those *sattvas* who seek *bodhi*.
This term applies generally to all three vehicles; however, in order to specifically select those of the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*), the word "mahāsattva" must be further stated.

Furthermore, because they take the bodhisattva as their object, they are called "bodhisattvas"; they are endowed with the great vows for self-benefit and the benefit of others, seeking great enlightenment for the sake of benefiting sentient beings.
Furthermore, "sattva" carries the meaning of "valiant. Because one seeks great enlightenment with diligence and valor, one is called a "bodhisattva.
This term applies to all stages; however, here it refers specifically to the great bodhisattvas on the bhūmis. For this reason, the word "mahāsattva" (great being) is further added.
For what reason are the merits of bodhisattvas praised?
It is in order to cause sentient beings to abandon their conceited and disdainful minds. Some say:
"One should pay homage to the assembly of bodhisattvas, who have long cultivated pure conduct (*brahmacarya*), just as one honors the assembly of śrāvakas."
Furthermore, in order to inspire pure faith in sentient beings, [it is said that] if even a bodhisattva possesses such merit, how much more so the Tathāgata!
Within this praise of the bodhisattva’s virtues, it is revealed that bodhisattvas are called *mahāsattvas* (Great Beings) due to three great matters:
first, greatness of number, because they are immeasurable;...
Second is greatness of virtue, meaning dwelling in the Great Vehicle, traversing the Great Vehicle, and so forth;

third is greatness of activity, meaning that because it pacifies the various sufferings and afflictions of sentient beings, bringing benefit and happiness to sentient beings is the activity of a bodhisattva.

"Those who have come together from various Buddha-fields" means that they have gathered together from the diverse Buddha-fields of the ten directions for the purpose of hearing the Dharma; it should also be understood that Bodhisattvas from this Sahā world have likewise come to gather here.

However, the compilers of the canon spoke only of bodhisattvas from other directions gathering there, intending to counteract the indolence and arrogance that prevent others from attending assemblies to seek out the hearing of the Dharma.

Thus, these bodhisattvas come from those directions, seeking to hear the Dharma of their own accord rather than being led by others; they all possess great majestic spiritual power and yet come even from the most distant realms of other worlds—how much more so would the rest not gather here?
Previously, the assembly of śrāvakas was not mentioned as having gathered because they were already present here;
now, it is stated that those from other directions have all assembled together, which makes it known that there are also bodhisattvas from this direction, though they were omitted for brevity.
Regarding the greatness of qualities (*guṇa-mahattva*), one should know that, in brief, there are nine kinds of greatness of qualities:

first, the greatness of diligence (*vīrya-mahattva*). This refers to all [bodhisattvas] abiding in the Great Vehicle through the power of diligence; they dwell securely in the Great Vehicle to rescue sentient beings and cause them to leave behind birth and death, as well as personally setting out toward unsurpassed enlightenment.

2. Greatness of cause (*hetu-mahattva*): This refers to traversing the Mahāyāna teachings, namely the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) and so forth, traversing them gradually through hearing, reflection, and cultivation.

3. Greatness of object (*ālambana-mahattva*): This refers to having an impartial mind toward all sentient beings; that is, attaining equality between self and others regarding all sentient beings by means of the equalizing expedients of great compassion and so forth.

Fourth, the greatness of time: this means being free from all conceptualization, non-conceptualization, and various forms of discrimination, such that at all times it proceeds with equanimity, as if in a single thought-moment.

The kalpa is named "Discrimination," because it involves the discrimination and severance of all kalpas and non-kalpas; and because one does not discriminate between kalpas and non-kalpas, one is able to practice for a long duration without weariness.

Fifth, the greatness of non-attachment (*asaṃkliṣṭa-mahattva*): this refers to the subduing of all demonic adversaries by relinquishing everything that is grasped. One is able to overcome demonic adversaries because, as it is said: "If a bodhisattva, regarding all things that are grasped, knows them to be unsubstantial and their mind does not crave them, they are then able to crush and subdue all demonic adversaries."

Sixth, the greatness of mental attention (*manasikāra-mahattva*): this refers to being far removed from all conceptualizations associated with the mental attention of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas; that is, it is the thorough severance of all mental attentions pertaining to the two vehicles.

7. Greatness of Sustenance (*dhṛti-mahattva*): This refers to being sustained by the joy and bliss of the flavor of the vast Dharma; that is, taking the flavor and joy of the Mahāyāna Dharma as one's food.

8. Greatness of Purity (*viśuddhi-mahattva*): This refers to transcending the five fears; that is, through the purity of the three types of action (*trikarma*), one emerges from all fears, because there are no causes for fear such as falling into evil destinies due to transgressing the precepts.

The five fears are: first, the fear of not being able to subsist; second, the fear of ill repute; third, the fear of death; fourth, the fear of the miserable realms; and fifth, the fear of timidness before an assembly. These five fears are all completely abandoned upon realizing the stage of pure intention (*śuddhāśaya-bhūmi*).

9. Greatness of Realization (*prāpti-mahattva*): This refers to the state of entering exclusively into the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika-bhūmi*). That is to say, when one attains the stage of the prediction of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-vyākaraṇa*), one never again regresses. While in the first seven stages, there is still movement through applied effort (*prayoga-sābhoga-pravṛtti*), and the effortless path of non-retrogression (*anābhoga-avaivartika-mārga*) has not yet been attained; however, in the remaining stages, one attains movement without applied effort and enters exclusively into the stage of non-retrogression. Because one enters exclusively into the stage of non-retrogression by means of the effortless path, it is called "entering exclusively into the stage of non-retrogression."

Regarding "the greatness of activity (*karmamahattva*), which manifests as the state that pacifies all sentient beings from being oppressed by every form of suffering and affliction": this refers to the stage where bodhisattvas are able to manifest the level that pacifies all internal and external sufferings and afflictions of sentient beings. Within this stage, there is great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) and great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*); by means of these two, they are able to pacify the oppression of all internal sufferings such as illness and external afflictions such as poverty. Because these two primarily bring about the benefit and happiness of sentient beings, one who attains this is said to possess the greatness of activity.

Furthermore, regarding "all dwelling in the Great Vehicle": this refers to when one dwells in the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*) and realizes the all-pervading true dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*); because one has for the first time attained the true Great Vehicle, it is called "dwelling in the Great Vehicle."

"Practicing the Mahāyāna Dharma" refers to the Bodhisattva practicing the threefold aggregate of pure precepts (*tri-śikṣā-saṃvara*) in the second stage; thus, the practice of the Mahāyāna is precisely these three aggregates of pure precepts.

"Having a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings" refers to attaining various superior meditative concentrations in the third stage, thereby giving rise to the four immeasurables (*catur-apramāṇa*) to equally benefit and bring happiness to all sentient beings.

"Free from all conceptual constructions," etc., means that in the fourth stage one attains the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma), thereby becoming free from all conceptual constructions, non-conceptualizations, and various types of discursive thought.
The various conceptualizations refer to the conceptually acquired view of self (*parikalpita-ātma-dṛṣṭi*), which is abandoned upon the first stage (*bhūmi*).
The non-conceptualizations refer to the innate view of self (*sahaja-ātma-dṛṣṭi*) abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), which is abandoned within this stage.

These two types of associated dharmas are termed "various conceptualizations" (*vicitra-vikalpa*), because their modes of activity and understanding differ. Although they are separated sequentially, they are collectively described in terms of their ultimate cessation; this is like the Fourth Dhyāna being said to be "free from pleasure and pain," or like the Third Fruit being said to be "free from the five lower fetters."
One interpretation holds that on this stage, all innate afflictions within the seventh consciousness are completely abandoned.

Another interpretation holds that on this stage, all innate self-view within the sixth consciousness is completely abandoned, but not that of the seventh consciousness, because subtle afflictions still manifest from the seventh stage onward.
If the seventh consciousness did not exist, there would be no basis for defilement, and it would not resemble the [other] five [consciousnesses].

If the subtle afflictions of the seventh consciousness were already abandoned, then the coarse afflictions of the six consciousnesses across the five, six, or seven stages would not manifest; this would contradict the explanations in the *Yogācārabhūmi* and the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*.

Furthermore, just as in the *vajropama-samādhi* of the two vehicles, the afflictions of the seventh consciousness and the most subtle afflictions among those of the six consciousnesses are severed simultaneously; how is it that in this [context] one first abandons the subtle afflictions of the seventh consciousness and subsequently abandons the coarse afflictions of the six consciousnesses?

Therefore, upon attaining the wisdom of non-self in the fourth stage, one eliminates the innate view of self within the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), yet has not yet abandoned the subtle afflictions of the seventh consciousness nor the remaining afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation within the six consciousnesses.

This teaching refers to subduing and departing from [afflictions], not their permanent extinction; it is only upon reaching the diamond-like mind (*vajra-citta*) of the tenth stage that they are suddenly severed and extinguished, because these are the seeds to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

Regarding "crushing all demonic adversaries": this means that in the fifth stage, one contemplates the four noble truths as being of an equal nature, thereby crushing and subduing the demonic adversaries who cling to the distinction between saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.

"Being far removed from all conceptualizations associated with the mental fixations of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas" means that in the sixth stage, one contemplates the equality of the twelve links of dependent origination in both their defiled and purified aspects, thereby remaining free from the conceptualizations associated with the mental fixations of the two vehicles that involve aversion toward defilement and longing for purity.

"Supported by the joy and bliss of the vast flavor of the Dharma" means that in the seventh stage, one realizes the principle of signlessness and, within the wisdom of emptiness, gives rise to superior practices, thereby experiencing the great joy of the Dharma.

"Transcending the five fears" means that in the eighth stage (*bhūmi*), all afflictions (*kleśa*) no longer manifest; because one is free from the causes of the five fears, it is called "transcending the five fears. The results of the five fears were already abandoned starting from the first stage (*bhūmi*).

"One who invariably enters the stage of non-retrogression" refers to one who, in the ninth stage, definitely enters the tenth stage—the stage of non-retrogression in which the bodhisattva's manifold practices are perfected.

Regarding "pacifying all sentient beings" and so forth: this refers to attaining the Great Dharma-body in the tenth stage, from which one raises clouds of great compassion and rains down the great rain of Dharma, thereby pacifying and eliminating all instances of sentient beings being oppressed by suffering and affliction.

Furthermore, these ten phrases of the sūtra—such as the ten *pāramitās* and the ten great vows—should likewise be correlated and explained, because within each and every stage above the first, all practices of the various stages are universally subsumed.
Regarding "with Bodhisattva Wondrous Birth as the leader": this refers to one who is able to give rise to various samādhis of perfected merit; thus he is named Wondrous Birth.
Because the Bodhisattva has attained these samādhis, he is given the title Wondrous Birth, for the names of Bodhisattvas are generally based on their dharmas, as in the case of Maitreya and others.

Because among this assembly the Bodhisattva Subhūti is the foremost, he is called the "Leader"; therefore, immediately below [the opening salutation], the Buddha addresses Subhūti alone to initiate what is to be taught. Because this sutra is concise, only one name is listed; as for the rest of the assembly, only their number is mentioned, for the intention of the compiler was to be brief.
*The Treatise on the Buddha-bhūmi Sūtra*, Scroll Two;
*The Treatise on the Buddha-bhūmi Sūtra*, Scroll Three.
Composed by Bodhisattva Bandhuprabha and others.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang, by Imperial Decree,
the Sutra says:
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Maitreya:
“Wondrous Birth, you should know that there are five dharmas that encompass the stage of Great Enlightenment.
What are these five? They are:
the pure dharma-realm, the great perfect mirror wisdom, the wisdom of equality, the wisdom of wondrous observation, and the wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done.”
The Commentary says:
Having thus explained the section on the causes and conditions for the arising of the teaching, we shall next demonstrate the section on what is taught in the Noble Doctrine.
The reason for addressing only the Bodhisattva Wonderful Birth (Sujāta) is that he is the most excellent recipient of this teaching.
Why was this not told to the assembly of śrāvakas?

It is because bodhisattvas single-mindedly aspire for all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*); upon hearing such a Dharma, they give rise to superior resolve; having given rise to superior resolve, they are able to enter it; having entered it, they are able to practice correctly; and having practiced correctly, they quickly achieve accomplishment. Śrāvakas, however, are unable to seek all-knowledge.

Although there may be those capable of seeking to hear such a Dharma, they do not give rise to resolute conviction; although they may give rise to resolute conviction, they are unable to practice correctly; and although they may be able to practice correctly, they do not quickly achieve accomplishment. For these reasons, it is not taught to them.
If that is so, for what reason?

When this sutra was being preached, he was already present in the assembly; however, in order to manifest the supreme greatness of the gathering at that time, he manifested in such a form. Furthermore, it was to cause those śrāvakas who were directed toward enlightenment to set out upon the Great Vehicle and to lead them into the assembly. Alternatively, it is not contradictory because various bodhisattvas may manifest under this name.
Briefly, the Buddha-ground is established by way of four aspects:
first, by way of number;
second, by way of inclusion.
Third, by way of names;
fourth, by way of the distinctions of the meanings determined [therein].
Now, within this context, I shall first explain the enumeration and the distinctions of the names.
First, regarding the enumeration: there are five kinds of phenomena (*dharma*), whose specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) will be explained later, so their number is self-evident.
Why is the number stated?

It is for the sake of determination; there are only five phenomena, neither more nor less. "Phenomenon" (*dharma*) here carries the meaning of "that which maintains its own characteristic," rather than the meaning of "maturation (*vipāka*) as a desirable fruit."
Second, by way of inclusion, it refers to the inclusion of the *Mahābodhibhūmi*.
"Great Awakening" (*mahābodhi*) is the Buddha, who possesses three bodies:
first, the *svābhāvika-kāya* (essential body); second, the *sambhogika-kāya* (enjoyment body); and third, the *nairmāṇika-kāya* (emanation body).

This shall be explained in detail later. "Ground" (*bhūmi*) refers to that which is the support, the inclusion, and the objective sphere of Great Awakening; it establishes the distinctions of its own characteristics and its objects of cognition (*ālambana*), because it takes all phenomena as its objective sphere.
It establishes the objects of cognition by stating they include everything;
it establishes its own characteristics by subsuming only its own essence into a single unity.
Within the stage of Great Enlightenment, there are boundless merits, which briefly comprise two kinds:
first, the conditioned; second, the unconditioned.
Unconditioned merit is subsumed within the pure Dharma-realm.

The pure dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is precisely suchness (*tathatā*), which consists of unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) merits; these are all distinctions within the essence and characteristics of suchness.

As for conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) merits, they are subsumed under the four wisdoms (*catur-jñāna*); because the functional power of wisdom is predominant within the untainted state (*anāsrava-avasthā*), they are designated by the name "wisdom" to manifest them.

Regarding all types of mind and mental factors, as well as their various categories, if one considers them according to their ultimate reality, each category of wisdom fully encompasses every dharma-gate of merit.

If considered according to their coarse characteristics, the wisdom of wondrous observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*) subsumes the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), because it observes all phenomena such as the body and so forth.

The wisdom of equality (*samatā-jñāna*) subsumes the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*) and the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*); for although the four right efforts take diligence (*vīrya*) as their intrinsic nature, they are embraced by the Tathāgata’s wisdom of equality, and thus lack any characteristic of high or low.
The four immeasurables, because they consist of impartial conduct, are subsumed under this wisdom.
The four bases of psychic power, because their intrinsic nature is samādhi, are subsumed under the wisdom of observation.
It upholds all *dhāraṇī* gates and *samādhi* gates, as explained in the subsequent sutra.

Likewise, the remaining dhyānas, liberations (*vimokṣa*), meditative concentrations (*samāpatti*), attainments (*samāpatti*), *dhāraṇī* gates, *samādhi* gates, the knowledge of non-contention (*araṇā-jñāna*), the knowledge resulting from prayer (*praṇidhijñāna*), the superknowledges (*abhijñā*), the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), the eighteen unique qualities of a Tathāgata (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*), the powers (*bala*), the fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), and so forth, are for the most part subsumed within the wisdom of wondrous observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*);
the superknowledge of the movement of miraculous power (*ṛddhividhi-abhijñā*) is for the most part subsumed within the wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*).

Regarding the supernormal knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-jñānābhijñā*) and the power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-bala*): if one speaks of them as being comprised within four types of wisdom within the continuum of the exhaustion of outflows, or if one speaks of them as having the exhaustion of outflows—nirvāṇa—as their object, they are for the most part subsumed within the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*) and the Wisdom of Equality (*samatā-jñāna*).

Regarding the seventh power, the knowledge of the pervasive operation of mental states (*sarvatraga-dharmajñāna-bala*), it is subsumed under four wisdoms. The faculties such as wisdom and the powers such as wisdom are for the most part subsumed within the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*) and the Wisdom of Equality (*samatā-jñāna*). The factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) and the factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*) are for the most part subsumed within the Wisdom of Equality.

The ten knowledges, such as the knowledge of suffering and so forth, that are truly untainted (*anāsrava*), are for the most part subsumed within the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) and the Wisdom of Equality (*samatājñāna*).
The quality of non-forgetfulness (*asaṃpramoṣadharma*) is for the most part subsumed within the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom.

The permanent severance of all continuities of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) is for the most part subsumed within the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) of the pure dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
As for the *pāramitās*, whether they are untainted (*anāsrava*) or resemble the tainted (*sāsrava*), they are for the most part subsumed within the latter two wisdoms.
The primary marks and secondary signs are for the most part subsumed within the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is to Be Done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*).
As for the remaining qualities of a Buddha, they are subsumed under their respective corresponding wisdoms as appropriate.

Thus, these four wisdoms fully encompass all uncontaminated minds and mental factors of the Buddha-bhūmi, whether they be co-existent phenomena or the various categories of manifested transformations.
The pure dharma-realm subsumes the various marks and merits of the true thusness; therefore, these five dharmas fully encompass all the merits of the Buddha-bhūmi.
Third, by way of names, they are called the pure dharma-realm, and so forth, up to the wisdom of accomplishment.
The pure dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) refers to that which is free from all adventitious stains of the afflictive and cognitive obstructions;
it is the non-erroneous, true nature of all conditioned and unconditioned phenomena; it is the causal basis for the growth and development of all noble dharmas;
it is the true essence of all Tathāgatas; and it is primordially pure by nature since beginningless time. It is endowed with...
It is endowed with various kinds of qualities of nature and characteristics, as numerous as the atoms in the worlds of the ten directions;

it is without birth and without cessation, like space, pervading all phenomena. It is equally shared by all sentient beings, neither identical to nor different from all phenomena, neither existent nor non-existent, and free from all marks—thus it is in every respect.
It cannot be apprehended by any conceptualization or verbal designation; it is realized solely by the pure noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*).
Its intrinsic nature is *tathatā* (suchness) as manifested by the two kinds of emptiness and selflessness. It is partially realized by the various noble ones and perfectly realized by the Buddhas;
this is what is called the "pure dharma-dhātu."

The Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) refers to that which is free from all attachment to self and what belongs to the self, and free from all conceptualization of the grasped object and the grasping subject; its objective referent and mode of activity cannot be discerned; it is neither deluded nor forgetful regarding any sphere of experience, yet does not conceptually differentiate between the characteristics of objects; it is uninterrupted and unceasing across all times and directions; it is forever free from the stains of all afflictive obstructions and the seeds of outflows (*sāsrava*); it is perfected with the seeds of all pure, untainted (*anāsrava*) merits; it can manifest and generate the images of all wisdoms regarding all spheres of experience; it is the basis for the images of all bodies and lands; it sustains all the merits of the Buddha-stages (*buddhabhūmi*), remaining inexhaustible until the end of the future—this is called the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom.

The wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*) refers to the observation that all things—self and other—are equal; it is constantly and uninterruptedly associated with great loving-kindness and great compassion, establishes the Buddha-ground of non-abiding nirvāṇa, and manifests various images of enjoyment bodies and lands according to the inclinations of sentient beings. It is the unique support for the wisdom of wondrous observation (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*); this is called the wisdom of equality.

The wisdom of wondrous observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*) refers to that which constantly observes all distinctions among objects without obstruction; it encompasses and stores all *dhāraṇī* gates, *samādhi* gates, and various sublime meditative concentrations; it is able to manifest all sovereign functions within great assemblies; and it severs all doubts while raining down the great rain of Dharma—this is called the wisdom of wondrous observation.

The wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done refers to the ability to manifest throughout all worlds various, immeasurable, innumerable, and inconceivable Buddha-transformations, according to the needs of sentient beings who are to be converted and matured; through these skillful means, it constantly and uninterruptedly benefits and brings happiness to all sentient beings—this is called the wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done.
Furthermore, these five dharmas are established by way of cause, effect, and the differentiation of effects.
The "cause" is the pure dharma-dhātu, for it is the cause capable of producing the noble dharmas.
The "fruit" refers to the noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*) because it arises by taking that [dharmadhātu] as its object and because it relies upon it.

There are four distinct varieties of this fruit of noble wisdom, established according to their respective functions: namely, because it sustains all things by taking the dharmadhātu as its object; because it realizes the equality of self and others in accordance with the Dharma as heard; because it reveals the supreme skillful means of the true Dharma; and because it is the cause for benefiting others.
Furthermore, these five dharmas are established as the Buddha’s own essence (*svabhāva*), as his cause, and as his fruit.
Regarding the Buddha’s own essence: its essential characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) is pure *tathatā*, and its essential characteristic is also non-conceptual wisdom that takes this [purity] as its object.
The cause refers to the wisdom of equality toward all sentient beings, which is immeasurable, constant, and uninterrupted.
The fruit refers to the benefitting of all sentient beings.
These two superior wisdoms observe who is transformable and who is not, thereby accomplishing what is to be done according to what is appropriate for each.

Furthermore, these five dharmas are established as follows: regarding the distinctions within the resultant stage of Buddhahood, the fruits of wisdom and abandonment constitute the essence of the Buddha-ground.
The fruit of abandonment is the pure dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), because all obscurations have been eternally severed therein.

Wisdom is of four kinds, beginning with the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom. Among all the various merits manifested within the states of the mind and mental factors at the stage of Buddhahood, wisdom is the most preeminent; it is designated by the name "wisdom" because it comprehensively subsumes all conditioned virtues.

Furthermore, this Dharma-gate thus taught establishes five dharmas that comprehensively encompass all Buddha-dharmas of the Buddha-ground (*buddhabhūmi*), because they collectively subsume all unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) merits; because they mature the hearing-perfumation (*śrutavāsanā*) and sustain all merits comprised within the Buddha-ground; because they constantly manifest for all sentient beings the equal activities of the Buddha’s benefit and happiness; because they are accompanied by the gateways of *dhāraṇī* and *samādhi*, as well as the adornments of boundless and immeasurable merit and wisdom; and because they are able to accomplish all transformative activities for the benefit and happiness of sentient beings.
Furthermore, regarding these four wisdoms thus described, by transforming which phenomena are they attained?
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states that they are attained by transforming the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).
Why is it that by transforming the mind one attains the mental factors (*caitta*), rather than attaining the mind itself?
Because it is associated with the mind of the four untainted knowledges (*anāsrava-jñāna*) and is designated as "knowledge" by way of metaphorical designation, the treatise states: "Question:
Regarding right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*), should it be said to exist substantially (*dravyasat*) or should it be said to exist nominally (*prajñaptisat*)?"
Answer: It should be said that they both exist.
Herein, wisdom (*jñāna*) is substantially existent;
however, the various minds and mental factors that are the attendants of wisdom are also called "wisdom," which is spoken of as being conventional (*prajñapti*). Thus, there are two kinds.
In this context, because the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) mind, mental factors, and so forth take wisdom as their primary factor, they are all designated as "wisdom.

By transforming the basis of the consciousness aggregate (*vijñānaskandha*), one attains minds associated with the four uncontaminated wisdoms; that is to say, from the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) up to, in detail, the All-Accomplishing Wisdom (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna*).

By transforming the eighth consciousness, one attains the mind associated with the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom; it is able to sustain all seeds of merit and is able to manifest and give rise to the images of all bodies, lands, and wisdoms.

By transforming the seventh consciousness, one attains a mind associated with the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*), because one is far removed from the two types of grasping and the distinction between self and other, and realizes the nature of universal equality.
By transforming the sixth consciousness, one attains the mind associated with the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation, for it is able to observe all things without obstruction.

By transforming the five manifest consciousnesses, one attains the mind associated with the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is to Be Done, for it is able to manifest and bring to completion external activities.

Furthermore, there is another interpretation which holds that the transformation of the sixth consciousness results in the attainment of the *kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna* (all-accomplishing wisdom), and the transformation of the five manifesting consciousnesses results in the *pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna* (wonderfully observing wisdom). This, however, should not be so, because it does not follow the proper sequence; for preaching the Dharma to eliminate doubts and universal observation are not functions of the five [sensory] consciousnesses.

In this way, as one transmigrates from the state of birth and death, the mind and mental factors associated with the four applications are transformed and attained as the mind and mental factors associated with the four applications of the fruit of Buddhahood; all of these are designated as "wisdom."

Furthermore, regarding the mental states associated with these four wisdoms as described above, what are their objects? As for the mental state associated with the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*), if explained in terms of its single characteristic, it takes only suchness (*tathatā*) as its object;
it is non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) and not subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), because its objective referent and mode of activity (*ālambana-ākāra*) are unknowable.

If explained according to its full characteristics, it takes all phenomena as its object; as the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra* states, the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom is never deluded regarding any object of knowledge.

This sūtra states: Just as various images appear in dependence upon a round mirror, so too do the various images of the sense bases, objects, and consciousnesses appear in dependence upon the mirror of the Tathāgata’s wisdom.
The "bases" (āyatana) refer to the six internal bases;
the "objects" (viṣaya) refer to the six external objects;
and the "consciousnesses" (vijñāna) refer to the six types of consciousness.
Thus, because the images of the eighteen realms appear as reflections upon this wisdom, it is known that this wisdom takes all phenomena as its object.
Since this mirror-like wisdom takes all phenomena as its object at all times, it is said that the Tathāgata possesses all-encompassing knowledge (*sarvajñatā*).

If it were not so, other forms of wisdom would not indubitably know all phenomena, and thus the Tathāgata could not be called "Omniscient. In this same way, the Mirror-like Wisdom internally takes as its object the seeds of its own intrinsic qualities and externally takes as its objects all spheres of knowledge, whether ultimate or conventional, manifesting all images such as the body and the buddha-field.

When it takes the ultimate truth as its object, it is called non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*); when it takes the conventional truth as its object, it is called subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).

Although it takes all things as its objects, its mode of activity (*ākāra*) is so subtle that it cannot be discerned; just as the *ālaya-vijñāna*, although it takes three types of objects, is also said to have objects that cannot be discerned because of its subtlety.

Therefore, one should not use the fact that it cannot be fully comprehended as proof that this mirror-like wisdom (ādarśajñāna) is exclusively non-conceptual wisdom (nirvikalpajñāna) taking only suchness (tathatā) as its object, and is not subsequently attained wisdom (pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna).

Although the substance of all mind and mental factors is one, their functional applications are manifold; thus, there is no fault in dividing them into two types of wisdom according to the differentiation of their functions.

Only by attaining the ultimate truth can one fully comprehend conventional phenomena; therefore, although they are described as sequential for the sake of meaning, that which resembles the subsequent stage is termed "subsequently attained wisdom" (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), and the same applies to the others.
Regarding the mental complex associated with the Wisdom of Equality,
one interpretation holds that it takes only the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom as its object, just as the afflicted manas takes the ālayavijñāna as its objective sphere.
One interpretation holds that it takes only *tathatā* (suchness) and the *bhūtakoṭi* (limit of reality) as its object, because it takes the nature of equality as its cognitive sphere.
According to the true meaning, however, this wisdom also takes all things as its objects, because it universally takes the nature of equality of all things as its object.

The *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra* states that the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*) takes all sentient beings as its object because it regards self and others as equal, and manifests the image of a Buddha in accordance with the various inclinations (*adhimukti*) of sentient beings.

This sutra states that because one realizes the equality of the ten aspects, this equality encompasses both the ultimate and the conventional; therefore, there is no fault in taking all things as objects of cognition.
If it did not take conventional reality as its object, it would be unable to manifest the images of all Buddhas in accordance with the diverse inclinations (*adhimukti*) of all sentient beings.

Furthermore, it is not tenable that the defiled *manas*—which is of the same category as the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*)—should take only the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) as its object; for they differ in being mundane versus supramundane, such a view contradicts the sacred teachings, and the remaining [wisdoms] are not of the same category.

The mental complex associated with the wisdom of wondrous observation universally contemplates all specific and general characteristics without obstruction; therefore, it takes all objects of knowledge as its cognitive domain.
Regarding the mental complex associated with the wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*),

one interpretation holds that it takes only the five kinds of present objects as its domain, because the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra* states that each of the Tathāgata’s five sense organs functions with respect to all five objects.
Regarding the true meaning: the wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*) also takes all things as its object, for it is unobstructed with respect to all objects.

The *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra* states that the wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done manifests various emanations throughout all realms, which are beyond measure and inconceivable, performing every benefit and welfare for all sentient beings.

This sūtra states that the wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done (kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna) initiates the various transformative activities of the three types of karma; it discerns the eighty-four thousand differences in the mental activities of sentient beings, proclaims the remedies by means of the four types of formal responses (vyākaraṇa), and receives and understands the meanings of the past, future, and present.
If it does not universally take all objects as its cognitive range (*ālambana*), it lacks this capacity.

Furthermore, it is said that the Buddha’s mind is unobstructed and sovereign, such that each instance is able to illumine all objects; it merely functions through the power of attention, sometimes taking a single phenomenon as its object and sometimes taking all phenomena. Moreover, while it is stated that the five sense-faculties (*pañcendriya*) operate with respect to their five respective objects, it is not said that they function *only* in that manner; therefore, [the opponent's argument] does not constitute a valid proof.
The *Pramāṇasamuccaya* states that all minds and mental factors realize their own nature; this is termed direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Were it not so, one would be unable to recollect them, just as one cannot recollect what has never been seen. Therefore, each instance of the mental complex associated with the four wisdoms is likewise able to illuminate and know its own nature.
How is it that this does not contradict worldly phenomena?
For a blade cannot cut itself, and a fingertip cannot touch its own tip.
Do you not see that lamps and the like can illuminate themselves?
How is it known that lamps and the like illuminate themselves?
It is because they are clearly perceived in the absence of darkness.
If they did not illuminate themselves, they would be obstructed by darkness and thus would not be clearly perceived; for this reason, it is known that lamps and the like illuminate themselves.
If lamps and the like are not themselves darkness, why do they need to illuminate?

For example, although objects such as vases and garments are not themselves dark, when there is no illumination from lamps and the like, they are obscured by darkness at their peripheries and cannot be perceived. When lamps and the like illuminate, they remove that peripheral darkness and allow for perception; this is what is called "illumination."
It is the same with lamps and the like: when they arise, the darkness that obstructs their own substance is removed, allowing them to be seen; therefore, they are said to "illuminate themselves.

Although various minds and mental factors differ in their degree of excellence, all are capable of externally perceiving objects and internally realizing their own substance, just as light can both illuminate others and illuminate itself. This is not the case for things such as knives and other phenomena, for it is the very nature of dharmas that they cannot be categorized in the same way.

This explanation is given in terms of the coarse characteristics of the various minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), which each possess the two divisions of the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) and the subjective aspect (*darśanabhāga*).

In the *Pramāṇasamuccaya*, it is argued that minds and mental factors all possess three parts: first, the apprehended portion (*grāhyāṃśa*); [second, the apprehending portion (*grāhakāṃśa*); and third, the self-cognizing portion (*svasaṃvittyaṃśa*)].
Second, the apprehending portion (*grāhakabhāga*);
third, the self-verifying portion (*svasaṃvittibhāga*). These three portions are neither identical nor different.

The first is the object of cognition (*prameya*), the second is the means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), and the third is the result of cognition (*pramāṇaphala*). If analyzed in detail, there must be four portions for this meaning to be fully established.
As before, there are three parts, with a fourth, the self-cognizing portion (*svasaṃvittibhāga*), added.
Of these, the first two are external and the latter two are internal; the first is exclusively an object of cognition (*jñeya*), while the others pertain to both categories.

That is to say, the second part cognizes only the first—whether it be valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) or non-valid cognition (*apramāṇa*), whether direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) or inference (*anumāna*).

The third, self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*), can certify the second and certify the fourth; the fourth, self-cognition, can certify the third. Both the third and the fourth are subsumed under direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

By this principle, although it is a single entity, it is composed of many parts; being neither identical nor separate, both the internal and external are known simultaneously, and thus there is no fault of infinite regress.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"The mind of sentient beings has two natures, The internal and all external parts."
"The objects of apprehension and the subject of apprehension entangle, Seeing various kinds of distinctions.

The meaning of this verse is as follows: the nature of the minds of sentient beings is composed of two parts; whether internal or external, both are entwined by the objects of apprehension (*grāhya*) and the subject of apprehension (*grāhaka*). One perceives various distinctions, such as between valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and non-valid cognition (*apramāṇa*), or between direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*). For the most part, these distinctions are manifold.
Although the mental states associated with the four wisdoms comprise many aspects, they are all subsumed under untainted direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
This point is analyzed in detail elsewhere.

They are divided into many according to their functions and meanings, but there is no difference in their essence; just as within a single dharma there are various distinctions in meaning such as suffering and impermanence, yet its essence is one.

Furthermore, regarding these aforementioned mental states associated with the four wisdoms (*caturjñāna-samprayukta-cittapakṣa*), do they possess the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) and the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*), and so forth?

It is certain that there is a seeing-part that illuminates the objects of perception; there is a self-verifying part (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) that universally illuminates both the seeing-part and the verifying-of-self-verifying part (*svasaṃvitti-svasaṃvitti-bhāga*); and because the verifying-of-self-verifying part illuminates the self-verifying part, it is also certainly present.
If these three distinct parts did not exist, there would be no object of cognition, it would not be called "knowledge," and the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) would be indeterminate.

According to one interpretation, because the category of truly pure (*anāsrava*) mind is unobstructed, it directly illumines the preceding object; it does not produce an image resembling the object that evolves in accordance with the mind. Thus, the untainted mind is called "signless" (*animitta*), because it is non-conceptual and because it is said to perceive its object as inconceivable.

There is another interpretation: even the category of truly real, untainted (*anāsrava*) mind possesses an objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*). The fact that all minds and mental factors naturally manifest as resembling objects is what is termed "cognition" (*ālambana*); it is not like a pair of tongs grasping an object through movement, nor is it like a lamp illuminating an object by radiating light. Rather, it is like a clear mirror reflecting an image to illuminate an object; because it manifests resembling the object and clearly cognizes it, it is called "unobstructed. Because it does not grasp or conceptualize, it is said to be "signless" (*animitta*); furthermore, being without discrimination and possessing a wondrous function difficult to fathom, it is called "inconceivable" (*acintya*), yet it is not the case that it does not manifest images.

If one says that there is no aspect (nimitta), then there would be no objective aspect (nimittabhāga); if one says there is no conceptual differentiation (avikalpa), then there should be no subjective aspect (darśanabhāga). If both aspect and vision were entirely absent, it would be like empty space; or else, it should not be called "cognition" (jñāna), because it would lack any grasping or conceptualization.

To say that there are no such characteristics as the grasper (*grāhaka*) and the grasped (*grāhya*) does not mean that there is no functional capacity for the appearance of objects or for the illumination of conditions.

If the uncontaminated mind (*anāsrava-citta*) were entirely devoid of the image-part (*nimittabhāga*), the Buddhas would not manifest various images such as bodies and lands; if this were so, it would contradict the sūtras and śāstras everywhere.

If the transformation of the basis of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) results in the non-attainment of form, then the transformation of the bases of the other four aggregates would likewise entail the absence of consciousness (*vijñāna*) and so forth, which would constitute a great error.

According to another interpretation, the mental complex associated with untainted non-conceptual wisdom (*anāsrava-nirvikalpa-jñāna*), being non-conceptual and because its object—suchness (*tathatā*)—is not distinct from its own essence, does not possess a separate objective part (*nimitta-bhāga*), just as it does not possess a separate aspect when illuminating its own substance.

Because the mental states associated with subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) involve conceptualization (*savikalpa*), and because their objects of perception may be distinct from the [mind's] own substance, they clearly manifest as images resembling the objects and perceive them with clarity, just like a contaminated mind (*sāsrava-citta*).

If an uncontaminated mind (*anāsrava-citta*) were able to take as its object a realm that is distinct from its own substance without possessing a semblance of that [object], then the *Ālambanaparīkṣā* should not have stated that the five consciousnesses do not have atoms as their objects because they lack a semblance of atoms.

In this way, although the objective conditions and aspects are similar, the uncontaminated seeds arise from the uncontaminated mind; even though there are factors that resemble contaminated phenomena, they are not actually contaminated.
This is because, for example, although a contaminated mind may appear to have the characteristics of the uncontaminated, it is not in fact uncontaminated.
Let us cease this extensive discussion of such distinctions; we shall proceed merely according to the principles of conventional discourse, and not according to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

If one proceeds according to the ultimate truth—which is beyond words and transcends thought—since there is neither characteristic nor perception, it cannot be described as mind or mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*); it is free from all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) and is inconceivable.
Furthermore, regarding these aforementioned mental states associated with the four types of wisdom, how many mental factors (caitta) are they associated with?
There are twenty-one.

That is to say: the five omnipresent mental factors (*sarvatraga*), the five object-specific factors (*viniyata*), and the eleven exclusively wholesome factors (*kuśala-mātra*) are present at all times and in all places. Because the Tathāgata always delights in cognizing objects of knowledge, his aspiration (*chanda*) never diminishes; because his resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) in the seal of reality never diminishes; because his mindfulness (*smṛti*) regarding previously experienced objects never diminishes; because the Tathāgata has no unconcentrated mind and is always engaged in discernment (*pravicaya*); because he is constantly associated with the most pure faith and other such qualities; because he is free from affliction; because he is free from sleep (*middha*); because he is free from remorse (*kaukṛtya*); and because he directly realizes all things without applied or sustained thought (*avitarkāvicāra*). In contrast, the categories of tainted (*sāsrava*) minds are characterized by varying degrees of excellence or inferiority; their objects of perception (*ālambana*) impose constraints, resulting in mental factors that may be more or fewer in number according to their association. However, in the categories of untainted (*anāsrava*) minds, there is sovereign freedom and lack of obstruction; the mental factors are equal and do not mutually obstruct one another.
Furthermore, regarding these aforementioned mental states associated with the four wisdoms (*catur-jñāna-saṃprayukta-citta-varga*): at what stage are they first attained?
At what stage do they manifest?

The untainted seed-nature (*anāsrava-bīja-gotra*) has existed inherently from time immemorial, arising and ceasing in a continuous succession dependent upon the ripening consciousness (*vipāka-vijñāna*).
