From the moment the resolve for awakening (*bodhicitta*) is generated, it gradually increases through external perfuming (*bāhya-vāsana*).

When the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) manifests, the mental complex associated with the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*) transforms and eliminates all seeds of the outflowing consciousness (*āsrava-vijñāna*), including the maturation-consciousness (*vipāka-vijñāna*).

At that time, one finally attains the initial manifestation of the complete and dependent attachment of all the untainted seeds of the fruits of Buddhahood, which shall remain constant and uninterrupted throughout the limits of the future.

The mental complex associated with the wisdom of equality first manifests at the time of the initial clear realization (*abhisamaya*) on the first bodhisattva stage (*bhūmi*). From that point onward, throughout the subsequent stages, it is cultivated to increase, become purified, and reach perfection. It manifests constantly whenever untainted contemplation (*anāsrava-darśana*) and the like are present; however, it is interrupted whenever tainted minds (*sāsrava-citta*) manifest.

In this manner, progressing through the stages up to the tenth bhūmi, from the moment of the final mind onwards until the end of the future, it is always uninterrupted. Just as in the state with outflows (sāsrava), the ālayavijñāna constantly arises simultaneously with the manas-vijñāna, so too in the state without outflows (anāsrava), the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (ādarśajñāna) must also always arise at one and the same time as the Wisdom of Equality (samatājñāna); therefore, the Wisdom of Equality is likewise uninterrupted.

The mental complex associated with the wisdom of wondrous observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*) also exists from the first bhūmi; it first manifests at the time of initial clear realization (*abhisamaya*), and from that point onward, it is gradually cultivated and increased.

When a mind with outflows (*sāsrava-citta*) is present, or during states of non-mindfulness (*acittaka*), it is then interrupted; in this manner, it continues through successive stages until the fruit of Buddhahood (*buddhatva*).
Even when entering the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), it does not manifest.

Regarding the mental complex associated with the wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*), there is one interpretation that it manifests in all stages from the first bhūmi upward, because these stages fall within the stream of the Dharma.

According to the correct meaning, however, it arises only at the stage of Buddhahood. This is because, during the ten bhūmis, the five sense faculties transformed by the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) are not untainted (*anāsrava*); since the five consciousnesses that depend upon them are likewise not untainted, and no instance has ever been seen of untainted consciousness being produced by tainted sense faculties, this wisdom does not even constantly manifest at the stage of Buddhahood. Because it arises through intentional application (*manasikāra*), it is repeatedly interrupted.

The mental states associated with these four types of wisdom possess seeds that are inherently present from the beginningless past by the very nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) and do not arise from perfuming; this is called the "seed-nature abiding in its original nature" (*prakṛtistha-gotra*).

After the arousal of the thought of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*), these seeds gradually increase through the stimulation of external conditions; this is called the "seed-nature accomplished through practice" (*samudānīta-gotra*).

From the first bhūmi upward, it arises in manifestation according to what is appropriate; through repeated cultivation, it becomes increasingly enhanced and superior, until one realizes the diamond-like samādhi (vajropama-samādhi).

From this point onward, although these [mental states] may repeatedly manifest, they no longer perfuse the seeds to cause further increase, because their virtues are already perfected and cannot be augmented.

Since the pure consciousness that maintains the seeds (*dhātuvāsanā*) is neither indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) nor susceptible to perfuming, and because it would otherwise entail the fallacy of the merits of preceding and succeeding Buddhas being unequal, the mental factors associated with these four wisdoms are exclusively wholesome, exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*), and subsumed under the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*).

Because all Buddhas lack any seeds of dharmas associated with outflows (*āsrava*), although they manifest through transformation bodies that resemble the truths of suffering and its origin—such as birth-and-death, karma, and afflictions—they are in reality subsumed under the truth of the outflow-free path (*anāsrava-mārga-satya*). While they follow conventional appearances by being designated as the five, twelve, or eighteen aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*), they are in fact not comprised within these aggregates, bases, or elements, for they are free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) and free from all marks (*nimitta*).
These five factors are all applicable to both the provisional and the real; when they do not depend on names and phrases, these other faculties and objects are all substantially existent.
When they do depend on names and phrases, these other faculties and objects are all provisionally existent.

Furthermore, the pure dharma-realm has true suchness (*tathatā*) as its essence, and because it is substantially existent (*dravyasat*), the characteristics of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and so forth are established based upon that suchness, and because they are nominally existent (*prajñaptisat*). Likewise, various mental states and cognitions, as well as colors such as blue and yellow, are substantially existent; whereas qualities such as non-heedlessness (*apramāda*) and physical forms such as length and shortness are nominally existent.
Let us cease this extensive discussion and proceed to explain the main text.
Regarding the fourth section, the determination of the distinctions among the categories, there are briefly three parts:
first, the determination of the distinctions among the five dharmas;
Second, the discernment of the wisdom of the single flavor of unified enjoyment;
third, the summary verse on the characteristics of the pure dharma-dhātu as being endowed with all merits.
Within the distinctions of the three bodies and the five dharmas, each is individually discerned in their respective order.
The Sūtra says:

"O Wondrous Birth, you should know that the pure dharma-realm is like space; although it pervades all various forms and diverse characteristics, it cannot be said to possess those diverse characteristics, for its essence is of a single flavor."

In this way, although the Tathāgata’s pure dharma-realm pervades all various categories of objects of knowledge, it cannot be said to possess various characteristics; its essence is of a single flavor.
The Commentary says:
Next, we shall reveal the characteristics of the pure dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) and resolve difficulties by determining its specific distinctions.
To this end, there is an objection as follows:
"If the dharmadhātu is the nature of all Tathāgatas, then the dharmadhātu has suchness as its essence; and suchness is the common characteristic (sāmānyalakṣaṇa) of all phenomena.
Since phenomena possess various distinctions, and the dharmadhātu conforms to them, how could it be without various distinctions?"
If the dharma-realm were characterized by various distinctions, how could it be pure?
It is not like rock crystal, for since it is in common association with various bases, it lacks any manifold characteristics.
To resolve this objection, the analogy of primordial space (*ākāśa*) is presented.

For example, regarding the phrase "although [space] pervades all various characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) among material forms": just as worldly space, although it pervades all distinct classes of differentiated characteristics—such as material forms possessing resistance, whether similar or dissimilar—is called "various" because of these differences in category; and because its own essence manifests clearly upon the intellect (*buddhi*) and other faculties, it is termed a "characteristic."

Regarding the statement that while it possesses modes of activity (*ākāra*), one cannot say it has various characteristics: this space (*ākāśa*) cannot be described as having various obstructive forms or diverse color-characteristics. Because the nature of this space is inherently such, it is called "ineffable" (*anabhilāpya*) because it should not be spoken of; or, it is called "ineffable" because it cannot be spoken of.

That is to say, the nature of this space is such that it cannot be described as having various manifesting color-forms (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*), nor can it be described as having various manifested color-forms.

To perceive various characteristics in empty space, or to claim that there are various characteristics that can be described, is to see various forms and appearances within emptiness rather than seeing emptiness itself; it is to provisionally designate the existence of various forms and appearances, such as blue or yellow, or long or short. These do not exist in reality; if they did not exist even as provisional designations, then no actual entity would exist at all.

How is it that [space] pervades all forms while lacking various characteristics, its essence being of a single flavor? It is not that this space becomes characterized by variety because it is associated with various forms; rather, it does not abandon its own essential nature, which is uniquely one—a flavor of non-obstruction—because it lacks any distinct characteristics.

Regarding the phrase "the Tathāgata’s pure dharma-realm is thus like this": it is like the space of the world, which, whether considered as having substance or lacking substance, pervades all obstructive material forms yet does not assume their specific differences, nor can it be said to possess any material characteristics.

Although it is also said that [space] exists, this is merely conventional and not real; for this reason, space does not abandon its own characteristic to take on another characteristic. Just as one may conventionally speak of "space" or "emptiness," yet the nature of space is truly ineffable, so too is the pure dharma-realm (dharmadhātu).

Although it is conventionally described as "empty space" and "true emptiness," the nature of true emptiness is in fact ineffable; this is because of the various bases and their mutual associations previously explained as the causes of empty space.
If it were as with crystal—that the dharma-realm should possess various distinct differences—there would be the fallacy of non-exclusivity (*anaikāntika*).
For we observe that although space is associated with various forms and colors, it lacks the various characteristics of those forms, because it is associated with things such as smoke and mist.

At times one perceives space as having various characteristics; this occurs due to the power of one's own false conceptualization, whereby one merely perceives various characteristics such as smoke and the like, rather than perceiving space itself, for the nature of space is invisible.
Thus, by the power of one's own false conceptualization and superimposition, one perceives only various characteristics such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth, rather than the pure *dharmadhātu*.

Although within the pure *dharmadhātu* there are no truly existent various objects, verbal expressions, or scriptural teachings, there nevertheless appear various distinct characteristics of objects, teachings, and their differentiations. It is not because those [objects] possess various characteristics that the *dharmadhātu* itself comes to have various characteristics; for the pure *dharmadhātu* is free from names and words.

All verbal designations take that which arises from conceptual construction as their object; nevertheless, the teachings on all phenomena are not in vain, because they serve as successive causes for realizing the dharmadhātu, just as one understands the meaning expressed by seeing written characters.

Because this Dharma teaching is the outflow of the great compassion of all Tathāgatas, it is able to successively explain the meaning that transcends verbal expression; it is as exceedingly rare as using various colors to paint the void.
To express the ineffable meaning through words exceeds even that rarity.

As it was said, Sāgaramati: for example, suppose there were someone who attempted to paint various colors upon the empty sky—which is colorless, invisible, non-obstructive, and non-manifest—just as one might paint upon a wall or similar surface; this would be exceedingly rare.

The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have realized the profound Dharma that transcends verbal expression; yet, to be able to use verbal expressions to proclaim and reveal this for the sake of sentient beings and individuals is even more difficult than that.
Thus it is explained at length.

Furthermore, because the *dharmadhātu* of crystal has the nature of being pure, it does not serve as a valid example (*dṛṣṭānta*) for the same property; consequently, the meaning of the probans (*hetu*) that is established is either partially unestablished or entirely unestablished.
The Sūtra says:
Furthermore, just as space, although pervasive throughout all forms, is not separated from them and yet is not defiled by their faults;

so too, the Tathāgata’s pure dharma-realm, although pervasive throughout the mental natures of all sentient beings, is not separated from them due to its reality, and yet is not defiled by their faults.
The Commentary says:
Furthermore, there is an objection:

"If the pure dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) is omnipresent throughout all objects of knowledge (jñeya), and since it is also associated with the defilements (kleśa-mala) such as greed and so forth, why is it not—as in the case of other categories of contaminated (sāsrava) mind and mental factors—rendered impure?"
To resolve this difficulty, the second simile of great empty space is taught.
Furthermore, just as empty space pervades all forms yet is not separated from them—because there is no other location [for it] apart from them—it is said to be "not separated."
Because it moves entirely within and is not seen to go outside,
and since it moves within and is not seen to go outside, one cannot definitively say that it is either identical to or different from [the body].
If there were a separate location for it, then space would necessarily possess form and obstruction, and would consequently be impermanent.
As for not being defiled by the faults of form: it is like the great void, which, although it pervades all within the realm of obstructive forms, is not defiled by the defects of those forms.
The defects of form (*rūpa-doṣa*) refer to that which serves as the cause for the arising of greed, hatred, and so forth, rather than the various distinct characteristics such as blue or yellow.

Furthermore, because the forms of clouds, mist, shadows, and the like within space cause the great void to abandon its pure aspect and because they obstruct the arising of pure vision, they are called the defects of form.
Furthermore, the appearance of objects superimposed upon the mind is called the "defect of form" (*rūpa-doṣa*).

This was stated previously in accordance with the intentions of others; it is not that the great void (*mahā-ākāśa*) is defiled by those defects of form, for its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is pure.

Thus, although the Tathāgata’s pure dharma-realm pervades the mental natures of all sentient beings, it is never separated from them because of its reality. Just as the Buddha’s own mind is truly pure—being radiant by nature and pure by nature—all sentient beings’ mental natures are likewise: they are real by nature and pure by nature.
The intrinsic nature of the mind is suchness, the universal equality of the minds of all sentient beings.
As it is said: "By what is the equality of the mind described?
It is by way of emptiness that the equality of the mind is described."
Thus it is explained at length.
The intrinsic nature of the mind is the very dharmatā of the mind, which pervades the mental nature of all sentient beings; therefore, it is called the equality of the mind.

In order to clarify the nature of the mind as such a dharma, it is said that because they are truly inseparable, the fundamental nature of the mind of sentient beings is originally pure; thus, although it is pure by its very nature, because it is now newly freed from adventitious defilements and obscurations, the Tathāgata is established as having a pure mind.
Furthermore, the equality of the minds of all sentient beings is itself reality, as it is subsumed within the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
Because this equality of the minds of all sentient beings is their true characteristic, it signifies not abandoning the minds of all beings;
and because it is the true characteristic of the mind-nature, it signifies proceeding without abandoning the mind-nature of all sentient beings.
This means that because it functions universally, it is never separated from [the mind], yet it is not defiled by those faults because its intrinsic nature is pure.

"Defilements" refers to greed and so forth, because they cause the characteristics of the mind to become faulty and lead to impurity. Although they are driven by adventitious conceptual discriminations, they do not constitute its essence; therefore, while they cannot be entirely discarded, they can be purified.

Based on this underlying intention, it is said: "The nature of this mind is pure and luminous; the *dharmatā* of the mind is what is called 'mind,' and there is no other pure mind apart from the *dharmatā* of the mind."
How is it that the minds of sentient beings possess greed and so forth?

Because they are sustained by the power of their own conceptual discrimination, because the perversions of the mind have not been permanently severed, and because these arise through the power of ignorance.
The meaning of this passage is as follows: for example, although the intrinsic nature of space is pure, because it is impaired by cataracts, distorted appearances manifest that seem impure.

Although the intrinsic nature of this dharmadhātu is pure, due to the power of various causes and conditions arising from one's own conceptual discrimination—specifically, because the cataracts of ignorance impair the eye of wisdom—inverted appearances manifest as if it were impure.
If the eye of wisdom, pure in every respect, never perceives impurity;

and if the pure dharma-realm is undifferentiated and pure in every respect, it is called the dharma-body of all Tathāgatas, and is also called the true essence of the Tathāgata, because it is eternally unchanging at all times.

Because this dharmadhātu exists equally within the mental continuums of all sentient beings, it is said that "all sentient beings are the tathāgatagarbha" and "all sentient beings possess buddha-nature. This is stated in order to lead those of indeterminate lineage toward the Mahāyāna, causing their minds to become resolved in its pursuit.
Regarding those sentient beings who possess the lineage of the Tathāgata, it is said that all sentient beings shall become Buddhas.
This is like the statement that "all is impermanent" and "all is suffering"; such statements refer only to a partial "all," not to the entirety of all things.

If it were not so, it would contradict what has been taught regarding the fivefold lineages; for the merits of all Buddhas would then be subject to exhaustion, as there would be no one to be delivered, which would thus contradict the teaching.

The merits of the Tathāgata are eternally inexhaustible and should not be considered fruitless, for he dwells perpetually in the world with the original vow to deliver sentient beings and seek the fruit of Buddhahood.

Although this pure dharmadhātu is omnipresent and equally exists everywhere, because it is sustained by the power of one's own obscurations, it is like those born blind who do not see the sun or the moon.
As a verse says: "The faults of sentient beings prevent [the Dharma] from appearing, Like the moon in a broken vessel;
Yet it pervades all worlds, Through the light of the Dharma, like the sun."
By this reasoning, as previously stated, it is also associated with the stains of afflictions such as greed, just like other categories of contaminated mind and mental factors.
To claim that the pure *dharmadhātu* becomes impure would entail the fallacy of non-exclusive uncertainty (*anaikāntika*).
Although space is associated with the defilement of form, it is not itself impure.

Likewise, although the categories of mind and mental factors are associated with afflictions such as greed, they have the pure *dharmadhātu* as their intrinsic nature and are therefore not impure; thus, [the opponent's example] does not constitute a valid analogy.

As it is said, for one whose intention (*āśaya*) is impure, seeing that the mind is impure, they likewise perceive the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) as impure, because the aspect of purity does not manifest.

Regarding the purity of the mental disposition (*āśaya-viśuddhi*): because one perceives that the intrinsic nature of the mind associated with stains such as greed is fundamentally pure and free from defilement, the *dharmadhātu* is eternally pure.
Thus, the reason (*hetu*) established by them remains unestablished (*asiddha*), as previously stated.

Because this dharmadhātu pervades all things, it is like space; it is not defiled by the faults of sentient beings. This statement that the dharmadhātu pervades all things does not require further proof, as the emptiness of the grasped objects (dharmanairātmya) is universally present.
The Sūtra says:
"Furthermore, just as space contains all actions of body, speech, and mind, yet this space has no activity or agency;
so too, the Tathāgata’s pure dharmadhātu contains all the deeds manifested by omniscience for the benefit of sentient beings, yet the pure dharmadhātu has no activity or agency."
The Commentary says:
Furthermore, there is an objection:

"If the pure dharma-dhātu of all Tathāgatas has true suchness as its essence, then it is free from conceptual proliferation and devoid of activity; how, then, can the conditions for the arising of wisdom that accomplishes the welfare of sentient beings be accommodated?"
"If there were room for wisdom to arise, then there would be activity; how then could the Tathāgata have True Suchness as his characteristic?
To resolve this difficulty, the third simile of great empty space is taught.

Furthermore, as for how space contains all actions of body, speech, and mind: just as the great void, though devoid of volition, is able to accommodate the three types of karma of sentient beings—since the two karmas of body and speech possess physical obstruction, they require such accommodation.
What is mental action?

It is not without form or substance, for it possesses resistance; thus it requires the accommodation of others. This very requirement is termed "accommodation," meaning that when it arises, it does not act as an obstruction.
Just as obstructive material objects are said to be "contained" by space because they encounter no obstruction at the moment of their arising, so too is this phenomenon:
since it arises without obstruction at the moment of its arising, it may likewise be said that space contains it.

Furthermore, when an object that possesses resistance is not obstructing its space, it allows other objects to be accommodated so that they may pass through; based on this phenomenon, "space" is conventionally established.

Mental action (*manas-karman*) is likewise: when it is about to cease, it accommodates other phenomena, allowing them to arise. Why, then, could "space" not be conventionally established based on this phenomenon as well?
If it were otherwise, and space truly existed as a substantial entity pervading all places, how could it accommodate things?

If its essence truly exists and is called "accommodation" because other phenomena are able to arise therein due to its non-obstructive nature, then all formless phenomena that possess a truly existent essence would likewise be unobstructed and capable of accommodation; consequently, they too should be named "space."
As for the statement in other places that space is merely the absence of matter, this is said in reference to its coarse characteristics as commonly known in the world.
Therefore, there is no fault in asserting that space accommodates the three types of action.

Furthermore, this space has no creator or agent; it does not engage in such discrimination as "I shall accommodate this" or "I shall not accommodate that. Although it lacks volitional intent, it is nonetheless capable of accommodating all things.

The radiance of the sun, moon, lamps, and so forth is likewise; although they lack any volitional effort or discrimination between "this" and "that," by the very nature of things (*dharmatā*), when they arise, they are able to illuminate all forms.
The wish-fulfilling jewel is likewise; although it lacks intentional effort, it can satisfy the wishes and desires of sentient beings.
It is the same with all other things; for now, by citing the analogy of space, all are made manifest.

Regarding how the Tathāgata’s pure dharma-realm contains all activities for benefiting sentient beings manifested by omniscience: this means that the pure dharma-realm of all Tathāgatas abides in its own nature without deliberate effort, yet it establishes all activities for benefiting sentient beings.
"All-knowing wisdoms" refers to the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom and the others.
"All that is emanated" refers to the emanations of body, speech, and mind.

"All activities for the benefit of sentient beings" means being able to accomplish all matters conducive to the superior welfare and happiness of sentient beings; this is because the pure *dharmadhātu* can contain them all, as it serves as the auxiliary cause when those phenomena arise.

The pure dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) is without arising or agency. "Arising" refers to mental attention (manasikāra), because it causes the mind to abandon other objects and incline toward other conditions.
"Agency" refers to the movement of the mind, because the fluctuations of mental deliberation result in action.

This means that although the pure dharma-realm is devoid of mental application and the fluctuations of thought, it is nevertheless able to accommodate the transformative manifestations of various wisdoms for the sake of benefiting sentient beings.
Furthermore, it encompasses all that is manifested by omniscient wisdom.

Regarding the activity of benefiting sentient beings: this refers to the pure dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) which encompasses both the enjoyment body (saṃbhogakāya) and the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya). Because the causes for performing the benefit of sentient beings are inexhaustible, because they are utterly vast, and because they are without obstruction, although it is free from conceptual discrimination, its sovereign power is able to give rise to them.

The general meaning of this is as follows: when the capacity to contain form and the activity of arising and so forth function, such as in the case of space and other phenomena, although there is no self, nor the conceptual proliferation of "mine" or volitional engagement, the power of *dharmatā* spontaneously performs all various functions.

In this way, although the Tathāgata abides in the untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*) and is devoid of all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), mental engagement (*manasikāra*), and various discriminations such as "self" and "mine," yet by the power of the great vows previously cultivated, he is able to initiate all the activities manifested by omniscience for the benefit of sentient beings. Thus, the Tathāgata’s foremost, inconceivable, and securely established *dharmakāya*, being sustained by the power of his prior vows, remains adorned with the merit of all the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) throughout the duration of the kalpas until the end of saṃsāra; though free from discrimination, it performs all the activities manifested by omniscience for the benefit of sentient beings.

Although the Tathāgata has no such discrimination as "I shall perform or not perform such and such deeds," by the power of his original vow, he is able to accomplish everything exactly as he previously vowed.

Whether one enters sleep or the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), although there is no mental attention (*manasikāra*), one awakens and emerges from that absorption according to one's prior commitment. As stated in the *Sāgaramati-paripṛcchā-sūtra*: "For example, when bhikṣus commit themselves to entering the meditative absorption of cessation at the sound of a bell, even though they do not hear the bell and have no conceptualization, they emerge from the absorption at the appointed time by the power of their prior commitment."
Thus it is explained in detail.
*Buddhabhūmi-sūtra-śāstra*, Fascicle Three;
*Buddhabhūmi-sūtra-śāstra*, Fascicle Four.
Composed by Bodhisattva Bandhuprabha and others;
translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang, by imperial decree.
The Sūtra says:
Furthermore, just as various forms and appearances manifest their arising and ceasing within space, yet this space itself neither arises nor ceases;

so too, within the Tathāgata’s pure dharma-realm, the manifestations of various wisdom-transformations and activities for benefiting sentient beings appear to arise and cease, yet the pure dharma-realm neither arises nor ceases.
The treatise says:
Furthermore, there is an objection:

"If the pure dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) pervades all objects of knowledge (jñeya), being inseparable and invariably concomitant with them, then the dharma-realm itself must undergo arising and ceasing."
"If there were no arising and ceasing, it would not pervade all objects of knowledge, nor would it be inseparable and constantly following along.
To resolve this objection, the fourth analogy of great empty space is taught.

Furthermore, regarding the statement that "various forms and appearances manifest as arising and ceasing within space," the intended meaning is this: just as the great void pervades all forms and contains these appearances without ever being separated from them, following them in every instance—even though various forms manifest as arising and ceasing—the nature of space itself is neither born nor extinguished.

In this way, the Tathāgata’s pure dharma-realm pervades all objects and encompasses all activities for the benefit of sentient beings manifested by omniscience; these are never separated from it and invariably follow its movement. Although wisdom and so forth undergo appearance and disappearance, the pure dharma-realm itself is without arising or ceasing.
With this underlying intention, it is said in a sūtra:
"Mañjuśrī! Because he is neither born nor extinguished, he is called the Tathāgata."
...and so forth, as explained at length.

From the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), all phenomena such as form (*rūpa*) are without arising or cessation; from the perspective of conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*), arising and cessation are provisionally designated (*prajñapti*). Therefore, it is said that they "appear."

This means that, according to conventional characteristics, there is the appearance of arising and ceasing, but in terms of the ultimate essence, there is no actual arising or ceasing; the same applies to the activities of the various wisdom-transformations within the pure dharma-realm that benefit sentient beings.
The Sūtra says:

"Furthermore, just as various forms and appearances manifest in space as increasing or decreasing, yet this empty space neither increases nor decreases; so too, within the Tathāgata’s pure dharma-realm, the Tathāgata’s ambrosial holy teaching is displayed as increasing or decreasing, yet the pure dharma-realm neither increases nor decreases."
The Commentary states:
Furthermore, there is an objection:

"If the pure dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) pervades all things and is never separated from them, then since the holy teachings of the Tathāgata are seen to increase now and will later diminish, the dharma-realm—being identical to them—should likewise possess increase and decrease."
"If that were so, the dharma-realm would not be pure.
To resolve this objection, the fifth simile of great empty space is taught.

Furthermore, regarding the appearance and disappearance of various forms and characteristics within space: among all the false and inferior teachings of the non-Buddhists and the entire world, the holy teaching of the Tathāgata is the most true, supreme, and pure; it is like clarified butter (*sarpis*) and like nectar (*amṛta*), for it enables one to attain nirvāṇa and never die again.

Thus, by practicing in accordance with this holy teaching, one realizes the state of an Arya and attains the fruit of Arhatship; because such instances occurred in great numbers prior to the passing of a thousand years, it is said that the Buddha’s True Dharma lasts for only a thousand years, not that the Buddha’s teachings remain for only a thousand years.

Furthermore, although the Śrāvaka Piṭaka split into many schools even after a hundred years had passed since the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the Bodhisattva Piṭaka remained pure and of a single flavor for a thousand years without any discord; it was only after those thousand years that the two divergent doctrines of Emptiness and Existence arose.

Therefore, it is said that while the Tathāgata’s True Dharma lasts for only a thousand years, the pure dharma-dhātu neither increases nor decreases. This is because the Tathāgata’s holy teaching undergoes increase and decrease according to the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*); it does not do so with respect to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), for the dharma-dhātu, being its very nature, is devoid of increase and decrease.

The same applies to form and the other aggregates: the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) is their intrinsic nature (svabhāva), which neither increases nor decreases. From the perspective of ultimate truth (paramārtha), it is like space, devoid of any characteristics of increase or decrease.

Therefore, it is said that they "appear"; this means that from the perspective of conventional reality (saṃvṛti), consciousness and so forth manifest as if there were increase or decrease, but not from the perspective of the true nature within the pure dharma-realm, because all phenomena such as form are free from the characteristics of conceptual proliferation (prapañca) and discrimination.
The Sūtra says:

"Furthermore, just as the forms and appearances in the ten directions within space are boundless and inexhaustible because the realm of space itself is boundless and inexhaustible, yet this space neither goes nor comes, and neither moves nor turns."

Thus, within the Tathāgata’s pure dharma-realm, the establishment of benefit and happiness for all sentient beings throughout the ten directions consists of manifold activities that are boundless and inexhaustible, because the pure dharma-realm is itself boundless and inexhaustible; yet, this pure dharma-realm neither comes nor goes, and it is without movement or transformation.
The Commentary says:
Furthermore, there is an objection:
"If all Tathāgatas have the dharma-realm as their essence, and the Tathāgatas bestow benefit and happiness upon all sentient beings by either going or coming;..."
Because the dharma-realm is not separate from them, it would follow—just as with other phenomena—that it must have coming and going, and it must have arising and so forth.
If that were so, the dharma-realm would not be pure.
"If the Dharma-realm were devoid of activities such as coming and going, it would not be able to bestow benefit and happiness upon sentient beings throughout the ten directions.
To resolve this objection, the sixth analogy of great empty space is presented.

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "likewise, the forms and appearances in the ten directions within space are boundless and inexhaustible," it is because the realm of empty space is boundless and inexhaustible, and the worlds of the ten directions are likewise boundless and inexhaustible; therefore, the various forms and appearances therein are also boundless and inexhaustible.
It has no single direction as its limit, nor does it exhaust all directions; whether considered in terms of time or space, it is therefore called "boundless" and "inexhaustible.

Furthermore, this empty space neither goes nor comes, neither moves nor transforms, because the great void contains all things and pervades everywhere, and because it is devoid of functional activity.

Thus, regarding the establishment of all sentient beings throughout the ten directions within the Tathāgata’s pure dharma-realm, the activity of providing benefit and happiness is boundless and inexhaustible; the meaning is as explained previously.

Regarding the phrase "because the pure dharma-realm is boundless and inexhaustible": because the pure dharma-realm is boundless and inexhaustible, although it is devoid of movement, its sovereign power enables the turning of activities for the benefit and happiness of infinite sentient beings within infinite worlds throughout the ten directions.
Regarding the statement that the pure dharma-realm has neither going nor coming: to abandon this and resort to that is called "going," while to abandon that and resort to this is called "coming.
It is without movement and without transition; the former provides the thesis, which is subsequently explained.
The Dharma-realm is "non-existent" [in the sense of being unconditioned] because it is without boundaries and because it is without form or obstruction.

If there were dharmas with boundaries and form-obstructions, one could speak of their coming, going, moving, and shifting across different directions; however, this cannot be said of the boundless and non-obstructive Dharma-realm, which—like space and other such things—cannot be said to perform actions of coming, going, or moving.

The general meaning of this is as follows: The pure *dharmadhātu* is the ultimate essence (*paramārthasvabhāva*) of all Tathāgatas. This *dharmadhātu* is omnipresent within the mental continuums (*saṃtāna*) of all sentient beings. Due to the power of the maturation of their own virtuous seeds and through the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*) of the pure *dharmadhātu*, when those consciousnesses arise, they evolve through such functional manifestations; this is called the Tathāgata performing the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings.

Apart from this function, there is no further activity of the Tathāgata’s Dharmakāya as a sovereign condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) capable of performing deeds for the benefit and happiness of sentient beings.
As a sūtra says:
"O son of good family!..."
"The Tathāgata is entirely devoid of such matters as going and coming.
To speak, however, of the Tathāgata's going and coming refers to the *saṃbhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya*; thus, there is no contradiction.
The Sūtra says:
"Furthermore, just as within space the three-thousandfold world-system appears to disintegrate and appear to form, yet the realm of space neither disintegrates nor forms;

so too, within the Tathāgata’s pure dharma-realm, immeasurable signs appear—the manifestation of attaining equal and perfect enlightenment, or again, the demonstration of entering great parinirvāṇa—yet the pure dharma-realm neither attains equal enlightenment nor enters into cessation."
The treatise says:
Furthermore, there is an objection:
"If the pure dharma-realm is free from coming and going and so forth, how can it attain perfect enlightenment, parinirvāṇa, and so on, without having spatial locations or coming and going?"
"If there were coming and going, one would again incur the aforementioned fault.
To resolve this objection, the seventh analogy of great empty space is taught.

Furthermore, regarding the statement "as in space, the three thousandfold world-systems," this objection is not valid; for example, although the world-systems appear to disintegrate and appear to form, the realm of empty space itself has neither formation nor destruction.

Although within the pure dharma-realm there are Buddhas manifesting perfect enlightenment and entering parinirvāṇa, in truth the pure dharma-realm has no such events as the attainment of perfect enlightenment or nirvāṇa.
If such things were to exist, then for that reason there would be going, coming, and so forth.

Just as the destruction and formation of various worlds appear within empty space, these are according to conventional truth and not in an ultimate sense, for they are all empty by nature like the great void.

In this way, the Tathāgata’s pure dharma-realm manifests infinite marks—whether attaining equal and perfect enlightenment or entering parinirvāṇa—yet these also exist by way of conventional truth and not ultimate reality.

Since those who attain perfect enlightenment and those who enter nirvana both do not exist [independently], and because the dependently arisen aggregates lack the nature of a self, if the pure dharma-realm were considered in terms of ultimate reality, these two would not be truly real; for a truly real phenomenon does not abandon its own characteristic to assume another.

If one were to allow that the dharma-realm abandons what is not perfect awakening to achieve equal and perfect awakening, or abandons what is not nirvāṇa to attain parinirvāṇa, then it would not be ultimate reality.
If there is the notion that this very meaning constitutes ultimate reality, [it is not so].
The Truly and Fully Enlightened One has never at any time not been truly and fully enlightened;
the one who has entered Parinirvāṇa has never at any time not entered Parinirvāṇa; therefore, this is the reality.

If that were so, other matters would likewise have to be thus: the eon of destruction (saṃvarta-kalpa) would be constantly destroying and there would be no time when it did not destroy; the eon of formation (vivarta-kalpa) would be constantly forming and there would be no time when it did not form; and a jar, for instance, would never not be a jar. All such matters would consequently have to be real.
If that were so, practitioners of meditation would not be able to cross over worlds filled with blazing fires and the like to travel to other worlds, for they ought to be burned by the fires therein.

One who has attained the power of superior resolute conviction would lack the sovereign power to transform the earth and other elements; likewise, one who has not attained the sovereign power of supreme meditative concentration cannot manifest perfect enlightenment or parinirvāṇa, nor can they manifest as not being perfectly enlightened or not having entered parinirvāṇa.

Therefore, although there are the prior stage of perfect enlightenment and the present stage of nirvāṇa, pure *tathatā* does not abandon its own characteristic; thus, the pure *dharmadhātu* neither attains equal enlightenment nor enters nirvāṇa.
In this context, both of these two types are superimpositions taken as intrinsic characteristics, and thus do not exist in reality.
Since both the agent and the action are of the nature of the thoroughly imagined (parikalpita-svabhāva), neither exists at all.

As for the statement that awakening is called *bodhi* because it is the subsequent realization of all phenomena, this refers to the attainment of perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) through supramundane non-conceptual wisdom. Within this state, because the two kinds of conceptualization regarding the wisdom that takes suchness as its object do not manifest, it is neither [mere] perfect enlightenment nor parinirvāṇa.
It is precisely based on such an intentional meaning that it is said:
"O Son of Heaven, you should know that because all phenomena are without arising, the Buddhas manifest birth without attainment or realization."
...and so forth, as explained at length.

Because that which is imagined through pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*) does not exist, and because conceptual constructions such as "arising" (*utpāda*) likewise do not exist, the Tathāgata manifests these two matters—namely, the two [bodies]—by means of conventional designation (*saṃvṛti-naya*) and by way of manifesting the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), in order to accord with the inclinations of the sentient beings to be converted. These two matters are cited here as examples to illustrate all such cases.
The Sūtra says:

"Furthermore, just as various forms and appearances dependent upon space may be seen to undergo transformation—becoming decayed, rotten, burned, or withered—yet the realm of space is not transformed by them, nor does it suffer weariness or exhaustion."

Thus, based upon the Tathāgata’s pure realm, various forms of transgression may occur within the realm of sentient beings through the violation of precepts by means of the actions of body, speech, and mind;
yet the pure dharma-realm does not undergo alteration because of them, nor does it suffer any weariness or exhaustion.
The Commentary says:
Furthermore, there is an objection:
"If the pure dharma-realm pervades all classes of sentient beings, how can sentient beings commit transgressions?"

If there were no transgressions within the dharmadhātu, because its nature is pure, the establishment of training rules would also be in vain, as sentient beings would never commit any transgressions.
"If there were transgressions, there would necessarily be weariness and exhaustion, and one would be no different from the two vehicles, lacking ultimate purity.
To resolve this objection, the eighth analogy of the great empty space is taught.
Furthermore, regarding the argument that "various forms and characteristics depend upon space," this objection is not valid, because [the Tathāgata] is like space.

For example, although various transformations such as decay and change can be observed in grasses, trees, and other things depending upon space, pure space itself is not transformed by those objects; though they exist within it, space undergoes no transformation, nor does it suffer weariness, for it is not oppressed by the suffering of decay and the like.

Thus, although various transgressions may be observed within the realm of sentient beings based upon the Tathāgata’s pure realm (*dharmadhātu*), the pure *dharmadhātu* itself undergoes no alteration and experiences no weariness. Although within that pure realm one perceives sentient beings manifesting two kinds of transgressions of body, speech, and mind arising from their own conceptual constructions—namely, the various unwholesome transgressions such as those committed by householders who harm their parents and so forth—[the pure realm remains unchanged].

Among those who have gone forth, there are likewise various instances of transgressions according to their respective circumstances, and for the purpose of preventing these, various rules of training (śikṣāpada) have been established.

All these are worldly transgressions; yet the pure dharma-realm is not altered by such transgressions, because it lacks any distinct nature, nor is it subject to weariness or exhaustion, as it is free from oppression.
If one is oppressed by suffering and lacks the capacity for endurance, then there is weariness and exhaustion, as in the case of the śrāvakas and others;
however, the pure dharma-realm cannot be oppressed by any suffering and thus possesses no weariness or exhaustion, just like space.
Furthermore, just as in space, although phenomena such as form undergo destruction and so forth, these are merely conventional and not ultimate;
likewise, within the Tathāgata’s pure dharma-realm, although there is the violation of established precepts, these are merely provisional designations and do not exist in reality.

Why is this so? The unwholesome nature of the three types of action—body and so forth—is established through conventional designation based on the power of their association and origination, rather than by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). A clod of earth or a stone cannot be truly established as unwholesome and so forth through the power of origination.

The same applies to bodily action (*kāyakarman*), as it is of a nature constituted by the combination of the earth element and so forth; verbal action (*vākkarman*) is likewise like the sound of a bell or a drum. Furthermore, the various unmanifest actions (*avijñaptikarman*), such as those that are non-virtuous and so on, are not substantially existent, because their nature consists solely in non-action (*akriyā*).

Mental karma is also established as unwholesome and so forth by the power of association, just like other associated factors; since the cause is not substantially real, the effect should likewise be so.

Therefore, within the dharma-realm, whether it be karma or its fruit, everything arises from conceptual construction; it is produced through the transformations of conventional consciousness and so forth. These are established according to their manifested appearances, yet none of them are real.
The Sūtra says:

"Furthermore, just as the great earth, great mountains, light, water, fire, Śakra and his retinue, and even the sun and moon, are all found depending upon space, yet the realm of space does not possess those various characteristics."

Thus, based upon the Tathāgata’s pure realm (dharmadhātu), the aggregates of ethical discipline, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation can be found; yet the pure dharma-realm is not characterized by those [phenomenal] marks.
The treatise states:
Furthermore, there is an objection:

"If the pure dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) pervades all phenomena, then it should lack the characteristics of the untainted aggregates such as morality (*śīla*), because they are not separate from it; consequently, like the dharma-realm itself, it should not possess the nature of an aggregate."
To resolve this objection, the ninth simile of great empty space is taught.
Furthermore, as for the argument that [the Buddha] depends upon space, the great earth, great mountains, light, water, fire, and so forth—this objection is not valid, because he is like empty space.

For example, although emptiness can be apprehended in dependence upon space, earth, and so forth, it does not constitute the nature of an aggregate (skandha) because it is not concomitant with earth and the like.

Likewise, although the aggregates such as morality can be apprehended in dependence upon the Tathāgata’s pure realm (dharmadhātu), the pure dharmadhātu itself is not the aggregates of morality and so forth.

It should be understood that herein, untainted pure morality is called the aggregate of morality; untainted concentration and wisdom are called the aggregates of concentration and wisdom; the supreme resolve of one beyond training is called the aggregate of liberation; and the right view of one beyond training is called the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation.
The former three are the causes, and the latter two are the fruits.

One interpretation holds that all [these] are exclusively those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*); the wisdom that takes liberation as its object is called "knowledge and vision of liberation" (*vimukti-jñāna-darśana*), while the remaining wisdom is simply called "wisdom" (*prajñā*).

Another interpretation holds that all [of them] pertain to both those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training; they are partially attained during the stage of training and perfected in the stage beyond training, for Buddhas and Bodhisattvas possess all five.

In this way, although the five aggregates rely upon the dharma-realm, the pure dharma-realm does not share their characteristics, nor do they lose their own specific characteristics as aggregates; herein, one should also speak of the five aggregates of clinging, because the untainted [factors] such as ethical discipline are identical to the dharma-realm.

To speak briefly: although within the pure *dharmadhātu* there are no functional merits such as the precepts and so forth, there exists a dharma-gate of the merit of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). This serves as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for the growth of all conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) merits. Unlike space, the dharma-gate of the merit of the ultimate truth of the *dharmadhātu* is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and therefore is not subsumed under the aggregates (*skandha*).

Based upon it, all conditioned virtues arise and perish; being comprised within the aggregates (*skandha*), it is also called "permanent" because it is never severed or exhausted. Yet, this does not mean it is eternally indestructible, for it is definitively taught that whatever arises must inevitably return to cessation. Because it is comprised within the aggregates, it is not an unconditioned phenomenon (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*); furthermore, because it possesses functional meanings such as objective referents and mental engagement, and because it is preeminent, it is said that the five aggregates constitute the reality of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), which is the actual basis for the merits of all three vehicles.
The Sūtra says:

"Furthermore, just as within space various causes and conditions arise in succession, such that the revolving cycle of immeasurable worlds in the trichiliocosm can be perceived, yet the realm of space itself performs no act of arising."

Thus, within the Tathāgata’s pure dharma-realm, there are present immeasurable marks, and the circular assemblies of all Buddhas can be perceived; yet, the pure dharma-realm itself is devoid of any arising or activity.
The treatise says:
Furthermore, there is an objection:
"If all Buddha-dharmas have the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) as their essence, there should be no distinction between the enjoyment of this or that; how then can there be different assemblies?"
If there were distinctions in what is experienced and enjoyed, how could the *dharmadhātu* of all Buddhas be pure?
To resolve this difficulty, the tenth simile of the great empty space is taught.
Furthermore, as for the objection regarding the successive arising of various causes and conditions within space, this critique is not valid, because [the mind] is like space.

Just as within space, the arising of the three thousandfold world-systems and the surrounding wind-circles can be perceived, and although space lacks the conceptualization of "mine" or any discriminative thought, it is nonetheless able to contain all these various distinct worlds; so too is the case here.

Thus, within the Tathāgata’s pure dharma-realm, there may be found a single assembly-circle where various perfect signs arise through the sovereign power of their own karma, wherein bodhisattvas who have attained the empowerment of omniscience gather together; these arise from distinct causes and conditions, and are not like the causes and conditions for the assembly of a single Buddha—the same applies to the second and third [Buddhas].

Based on this, other sūtras state that the various pure lands of the Buddhas can be found, as well as the various assemblies of the Buddhas; yet within the pure dharma-realm, there are no distinctions in the enjoyment of self or what belongs to a self, nor can the conceptualizations of agent, subject, or object be found.

The general meaning of this is as follows: although the *dharmakāya* of the Tathāgata is devoid of any differentiated conceptual elaborations regarding form or image, the *saṃbhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya*—by the power of his original vows and the power of his own sublime conduct—give rise to various Buddha-fields of purity, complete with all manifold marks.

The various distinctions among the assemblies of the Buddhas can be perceived; these are all manifestations of pure consciousness (*viśuddha-vijñāna*), and their manifold differences do not exist as ultimate reality.

Just as a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*), by the power of his past vows and for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, performs sublime deeds and gives rise to various distinctions such as the "Woman-Jewel" (*strī-ratna*) and other exquisite articles of pleasure.

The Buddhas are likewise; for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, they perform sublime deeds, and through the sovereign power of their own karma, they give rise to various distinctions of pure lands, assemblies, and the requisites for enjoying the bliss of the Dharma. The only difference from what preceded is that these are entirely free from conceptual discrimination.
Furthermore, thus has been explained the profundity of the characteristics, the profundity of the functional activity, and the profundity of the locus of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
Regarding the profundity of characteristics: it refers to being free from ten kinds of impure faults; one should know that these are precisely the ten pure characteristics.
There are ten kinds of faults regarding impurity:
first, the fault of differentiation;
second, the fault of affliction.
3. the fault of having activity;
4. the fault of being conditioned;
5. the fault of increase and decrease;
Sixth, the fault of activity;
seventh, the fault of eternalism and nihilism;
eighth, the fault of exhaustion and weariness.
9. The fault of accumulation;
10. The fault of gathering a following.

As for the ten characteristics of purity, they are: the characteristic of non-differentiation, the characteristic of non-defilement, the characteristic of not being characterized by volitional activity, the characteristic of not being conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), the characteristic of neither increase nor decrease, the characteristic of lack of movement, the characteristic of being neither annihilation nor permanence, the characteristic of lack of exhaustion, the characteristic of not being an accumulation, and the characteristic of having no "mine" (*amama*); these correspond respectively to the [ten] points above.
The profundity of karmic activity should be understood as the activities of transformation and so forth.
The profundity of the locus should be understood as the assemblies in the pure lands of all Tathāgatas, which are devoid of movement yet perfect in all their characteristics.
The reason that space is used as a metaphor in all instances is to demonstrate that all coarse characteristics (*sthūla-lakṣaṇa*) of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) are identical to space.
As a sūtra states:

"Whatever metaphors or designations may be employed to illustrate the virtues of the Tathāgatas, such as their ethical discipline (*śīla*), they all constitute a slander of the Tathāgatas, with the sole exception of the single metaphor of space; for the immeasurable virtues of the Tathāgatas, such as their ethical discipline, are identical to space."
...and so on, as extensively explained.
The Sūtra says:
"Furthermore, Subhūti!"

Regarding the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom: just as various images and reflections appear based upon a round mirror, so too do the various images of the sense bases, objects, and consciousnesses appear based upon the Tathāgata’s wisdom-mirror.

As for using the circular mirror alone as an analogy, one should know that the circular mirror and the Tathāgata’s wisdom-mirror are equal and identical; therefore, the wisdom-mirror is called the Mirror-like Wisdom (ādarśajñāna).
The treatise says:
Having established the abandonment [of defilements], one should now establish wisdom; it is in reference to this that the following is said.

Furthermore, Subhūti, regarding the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom and so forth, it should be understood that here the metaphor is used to demonstrate that the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom is the equal causal condition capable of producing and manifesting the images of all phenomena. That is to say, the eighth pure consciousness of the Tathāgatas can manifest and produce the images of wisdom and so forth, just as a great perfect mirror can manifest all images of the world. Because it is associated with wisdom, it is metaphorically designated as "wisdom."
The "bases" (āyatana) refer to the six internal bases, namely the eye and so forth.
The "objects" (viṣaya) refer to the six external objects, namely form and so forth.
These six internal bases and six external objects constitute the twelve bases (*āyatana*).

Based upon these twelve, there arise the three categories of consciousness and their associated mental factors (*citta-caitta*). Because consciousness is predominant, they are collectively termed "all consciousnesses. These consciousnesses are called "images of various forms," for they manifest as the distinct characteristics of diverse modes of activity (*saṃskāra*).
A subsequent sutra states:
"The Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom, at all times, depending upon various conditions, gives rise to the appearances of various wisdom-images.
Such passages as these explain that it is called Mirror Wisdom because it serves as the cause for the arising of wisdom-images.

The Wisdom of Equality takes the dependently originated phenomena of the Mirror-like Wisdom and the others as its object; the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation takes the specific and general characteristics of all dharmas as its object; it should be known that the Wisdom of Accomplishing Action is likewise.

In this way, the mental states associated with these three types of knowledge manifest clearly as various images—resembling all particular and universal characteristics—upon all objects of cognition and grasping within the six internal bases and the six external spheres.
These images all arise due to the Tathāgata’s Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*) and appear with distinct clarity; therefore, they are called "manifest.

These are manifested solely by the Tathāgata’s wisdoms and so forth, for at the stage of Buddhahood, the Wisdom of Equality (*samatā-jñāna*) and the others constitute its very nature. When these wisdoms arise, they are able to realize and know the various specific characteristics of their own modes of activity; only the Tathāgata’s awakened intelligence can analyze and explain these characteristics, as no one else possesses such capacity.
The Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom is called "capable of manifesting," because it serves as the condition for the arising of those images, just as a clear mirror manifests all reflections.

Furthermore, the three factors—the locus, the object, and consciousness—are each distinct: the locus refers to the six sense organs; the object refers to the six sense fields; and consciousness refers to the six types of consciousness. Thus, the manifold images of the eighteen elements are manifested.

These various images and reflections appear according to their respective requirements within the category of the three wisdoms; because they can manifest the "exhaustive nature" (*yāvadbhāvikatā*) and the "nature as it is" (*yathāvadbhāvikatā*) through the wisdom of observation (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*) and the others, the pure consciousness associated with the Tathāgata’s mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) acts as the condition to produce these images of the three wisdoms, and thus they are said to "appear. Furthermore, they are manifested solely by the Tathāgata’s wisdom and so forth; to speak extensively, up to the point that only the Tathāgata’s awakened discernment analyzes and demonstrates their characteristics, the rest is as previously explained.

Furthermore, all eighteen realms manifest as images within the mental state associated with the Tathāgata’s Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom. Since the Mirror Wisdom of all Tathāgatas arises capable of illuminating all objects, the bases, objects, and consciousnesses appear clearly within this wisdom, just like reflections.

Because this mirror-like wisdom arises by apprehending those images, although it is devoid of the distinctions between grasped object and grasping subject, or of identity and difference, all objects of knowledge appear within it like a great round mirror.
When this wisdom arises, it possesses such a mode of activity because that is its very nature.

Although the Tathāgata is free from the conceptualization of grasped and grasper, or of identity and difference, he is nonetheless able to directly realize the images of all phenomena—both their specific and general characteristics—as they appear within his own mind.
Because of this realization, he is able to explain the specific and general characteristics of all phenomena without error.

By means of these images, the Tathāgata achieves the quality of non-forgetfulness; for at all times, the images of all objects of knowledge clearly manifest upon the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) and the others, as there is no forgetting.
If it were not so, how could the Tathāgata be called "Omniscient"?
For without the Mirror-like Wisdom and the others, he would be unable to directly realize and know at all times the specific and general characteristics of all phenomena.
If it is argued that [the Buddha] is called "Omniscient" because the continuum possesses such capacity, as a verse says:
"The continuum possesses capacity, Just as fire consumes everything."
To say, "All-knowledge is not the simultaneous knowing of all things," is merely empty talk;

for when the knowledge of others' minds and other such cognitions apprehend one object, they do not apprehend other objects, and because they do not know those others, they are not omniscient. Furthermore, even in terms of their continuity, they cannot apprehend and know the present.
In your school, a single moment of consciousness cognizes only one portion of the common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena.

If this were so, the Tathāgata would have to be designated by a conventional name as "Omniscient" (*sarvajña*); it is not possible to designate him as "not omniscient. For if he were [merely] omniscient in that conventional sense, he would not be a truly omniscient one.

Furthermore, with the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*) of the Tathāgata as its condition, the various images of the objects, bases, and consciousnesses of mundane and supramundane virtues within other continuums appear as reflections. This is because neither mundane nor supramundane virtues could arise if mirror-like wisdom were absent; when those phenomena arise, they do so through this power, and it is also capable of cognizing them.

The meaning of this statement is as follows: through the sovereign power of the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) of the Tathāgata, all worldly and supramundane wholesome objects, locations, and consciousnesses are able to arise, just as various images appear within a clear mirror.

Although all sentient beings each possess their own causal power, it is only through the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) acting as a dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*) that [their qualities] can arise. This is just as, although seeds exist, sprouts and the like will not grow without earth and other conditions; or as, although an object exists, its various reflections will not appear without a mirror and so forth.

If that were so, the Blessed One would be identical to those with false views who maintain that Īśvara and others are the cause of the world, because he would have established them as the equal cause for the arising of all worldly effects.

There is no such fault, because at the time of its arising, it can only act as a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*); it is not an agent, it is impermanent, and it arises from the accumulation of the two provisions of merit and wisdom over immeasurable eons; furthermore, the virtues and virtuous conditions of all sentient beings arise by means of this.
The false views of the non-Buddhists hold that Īśvara and others act as the creator of all worlds; because their nature is eternally abiding, they are not analogous [to the reflection].
If there were no real object, how could a reflection arise in a perfect mirror? How, then, could it serve as a metaphor?
When a physical object and a mirror come together as conditions, such an appearance manifests; therefore, it serves as an analogy.

That is to say, due to the power of the maturation of the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) for inverted attachment to images, one's own consciousness undergoes a transformation based on the surface of the mirror as a condition, manifesting what resembles the reflection of a face. Because of this, people in the world give rise to overweening pride (*abhimāna*), saying, "I see the reflection of my face in the mirror," for there is no separate reflection produced within the mirror.

The sūtra merely states that various images and reflections appear; it does not say they arise. In this way, one should understand that all objective phenomena are manifestations of the transformations of one's own consciousness and do not exist as separate realities. Because consciousness is predominant, it is said to be "consciousness-only" (vijñapti-mātra); this does not mean that mental factors are non-existent, nor does it mean that there is only a single consciousness.

Because all sentient beings each possess eight consciousnesses and mental factors, although all forms and other phenomena each have their own seeds, these are all transformations and habitual perfumings of one's own consciousness. Having as their nature the specific functional capacities upon consciousness, they do not depart from consciousness even when they manifest.

To speak according to conventional truth, there are distinct mental factors (*caitta-dharma*); however, this is not the ultimate meaning, because from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), all phenomena lack any fixed, distinct nature. Even *tathatā* (suchness), though not a transformation of consciousness, is nonetheless not separate from consciousness, for it is the true nature of consciousness and is revealed by the common characteristics of the two kinds of emptiness and selflessness within consciousness.

This term "consciousness-only" merely negates the false imaginings of the ignorant who recklessly conceive of all minds, mental factors, and external determinate entities such as matter as being grasped through universal imagination; it does not eliminate or separate the mind, mental factors, and all phenomena such as matter from their dependent nature and perfected nature, for these are not non-existent.
Because they are equal, these two are equal; therefore, it is said that they are "equal and equal.

The worldly round mirror and the Tathāgata’s wisdom-mirror are both free from discrimination, and both are able to manifest reflections without distinction. For this reason, it is called the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*).
The Sūtra says:

It is like a great round mirror that a person seeking merit and happiness hangs in a high and excellent place so that it remains unshaken; all the immeasurable sentient beings who come and go observe their own gains and losses therein, desiring to preserve what is gained and abandon what is lost.

In this way, because the Tathāgata’s Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom is suspended within the pure *dharmadhātu* without interruption, it remains unshakable; yet, desiring to cause immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings to contemplate both defilement and purity, so that they may grasp the pure and abandon all that is defiled, [the Buddha manifests].
The treatise states:
"A high and superior place refers to a lofty banner or other such superior locations.
The pure dharma-realm is stainless true thusness."
"Abiding" means dwelling securely; it refers to the fact that this wisdom either relies upon or takes as its object [the dharmadhātu] without interruption.

"Unwavering" means that because this mirror-like wisdom relies upon and takes the dharmadhātu as its object, continuing uninterruptedly throughout the limits of saṃsāra, it is constant and follows [its object] without cessation; therefore, it is unwavering.

The meaning of this passage is as follows: the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom is forever free from all conceptual movement and fluctuation; once attained, it continues uninterruptedly until the end of the future.

Although the remaining three knowledges lack false conceptualization, they still possess the mental discrimination of non-grasping attention; even after realization, one may practice them or not, and thus they are not unshakable.

There is another interpretation that the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*) also does not manifest in the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), because the treatises state that the seventh consciousness is absent in this absorption,
and further state that it also ceases a portion of the constantly active mind and mental factors.

If that were so, since the treatise states that the seventh [consciousness] is absent in all three stages, then when one practices the untainted direct realization (*anāsrava-abhisamaya*) from the first bhūmi upward, as well as in the stage of a Tathāgata, this wisdom would not exist; this would constitute a major error, as it contradicts both the sūtras and the śāstras.

However, the intention behind the statement that [it] does not exist is to say that there is no afflicted seventh consciousness, not that it is entirely non-existent; for until one attains the wisdom of the selflessness of dharmas (*dharma-nairātmya*), the habitual clinging to the conceptualization of dharmas constantly manifests as its support.

As long as one has not yet realized the wisdom of the emptiness and selflessness of the person (*pudgala-nairātmya-jñāna*), that grasping persists; because it relies upon this consciousness, the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* states that the ālayavijñāna necessarily functions simultaneously with the manas-vijñāna.
If the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) arises, it necessarily functions simultaneously with two consciousnesses at once;
if any one of the five sensory consciousnesses arises among them, it necessarily functions simultaneously with three consciousnesses at once.
Even when the five consciousnesses arise at a certain time, they necessarily function simultaneously with the seventh consciousness.

Therefore, one should know that within the Noble Path, the Cessation Attainment (*nirodhasamāpatti*), and the state of No-More-Learning (*aśaikṣa*), there also exists non-defiled conceptual grasping; because its modes of activity (*ākāra*)—such as those of the seventh consciousness associated with the Wisdom of Equality—are subtle, it does not contradict the Cessation Attainment.

Because this meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) is induced by the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*), its essence is untainted, and it is diametrically opposed to the ego-grasping of the afflicted mind (*kliṣṭa-manas*), it is a partial cessation rather than a cessation of everything. Therefore, although the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*) manifests constantly within the state of Buddhahood, after it has been realized during the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), when afflictions or tainted minds (*sāsrava-citta*) arise, this wisdom does not manifest; because it is thus intermittent, it is not "immovable."
Furthermore, because the other two wisdoms do not function constantly within the state of Buddhahood, they are not immovable.
For what reason is the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom established in the Pure Dharma Realm?
It is for the sake of causing immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings to contemplate defilement and purity.
Why do they contemplate them?
It is because they desire to adopt purity and abandon all defilements.
"Defilement" refers to the characteristics of afflictions, karma, and birth; "abandonment" refers to their suppression and eradication.
This is because they are temporarily suppressed and ultimately eradicated by means of both the mundane path and the supramundane path.
"Purity" refers to all that is wholesome, for it can cause the minds of sentient beings to become pure.
"Grasping" refers to sustaining, establishing, nurturing, and maturing the seeds, so that one may realize liberation according to one's aspirations and requests.

The meaning here is as follows: when all Tathāgatas were formerly in the stage of bodhisattvas, desiring to accomplish the welfare and happiness of all sentient beings in every possible way, they constantly maintained an intention for the benefit and peace of all beings based upon the pure *dharmadhātu*. They continuously directed their accumulated stores of merit and wisdom toward this goal, and through the diligent cultivation of skillful means and the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*), they realized this wisdom which, taking the *dharmadhātu* as its objective support, remains continuous and unshakable.

Although it is free from volitional attention, conceptual discrimination, and discursive proliferation, its continuous flow serves as a dominant condition that causes sentient beings to establish, nurture, and mature immeasurable seeds of wholesome roots according to their aspirations, thereby attaining worldly happiness and supramundane liberation.

This arises from the Tathāgata’s Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (ādarśajñāna), which initiates the activity of emanation to proclaim the essential points of the Dharma for all sentient beings, enabling them to recognize defilement and purity, and to adopt the pure while abandoning the defiled; this is the very foundation for bringing benefit and happiness to sentient beings.
The Sūtra says:

Furthermore, just as a perfectly polished and refined round mirror is clear and stainless, its radiance shining everywhere, so too is the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*) of the Tathāgata.

Because it has forever transcended all stains of the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) within the Buddha-wisdom, it is perfectly polished and refined. Because it is sustained by the meditative concentration that serves as its support, it is clear and stainless. And because it performs the work of bringing benefit and happiness to all sentient beings, its radiance shines everywhere.
The treatise states:

"Mirror-like" refers to the fact that its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is utterly pure; "pure" refers to the fact that its specific qualities (*viśeṣa*) are free from adventitious defilements (*āgantuka-mala*).
As for the term "stainless," it summarizes the preceding two types, signifying that they are perfectly complete, free from impurity, and supremely pure.
"Luminosity" arises from reflection; "clarity" arises from purity; and what is called "universal illumination" arises from being stainless. Regarding the phrase "in the Buddha’s wisdom," etc.:

both the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) are termed "stains. Because they have been ultimately severed, it is called "perpetual transcendence.
