Since it possesses the sense of having eternally transcended all obstructive stains, the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) is said to be perfectly polished.

Furthermore, regarding "afflictions" (*kleśa*): this refers to all afflictions such as greed, hatred, and so forth, whether they exist in the state of active outbursts (*paryavasthāna*), latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), or both; because they possess the power—whether manifest or dormant—to obstruct the arising of the Noble Path and the attainment of *nirvāṇa*, and because they disturb the body and mind, they are called the "affliction-obstruction" (*kleśāvaraṇa*).

Regarding the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*): they consist of non-afflicted ignorance regarding the objects of knowledge that obstructs omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), yet they do not obstruct *nirvāṇa*. Although these obscurations exist, one still perceives that Śrāvakas and others attain *nirvāṇa*. Furthermore, these two types of obscurations are also termed "stains" (*mala*), because they hinder pure wisdom from arising and defile pure wisdom.
Because the adventitious stains of the obscurations never arise again once their antidotes have been attained, it is called "ultimate transcendence.
Because it is eternally free from these obscurations, the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom is perpetually and utterly pure; therefore, it is said to be "thoroughly polished and refined."

Regarding the phrase "because it is sustained by the meditative concentration that serves as its support": it is called the "support" (āśraya) because it is that upon which [the wisdom] relies; since the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (ādarśajñāna) arises based upon this, the support itself is the concentration, and thus it is termed "concentration-as-support."
Alternatively, when wisdom relies upon meditative concentration, it is called "relying on concentration.
Immediately following this, the path of liberation arises because it is utterly pure.

This supporting concentration is precisely the sublime diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*), for by the power of that concentration, hindrances are permanently severed. Since this wisdom is sustained by the power of that supporting concentration, it is termed "sustained" (*parigṛhīta*).
Because this wisdom arises immediately after that meditative concentration.
Due to the power of that concentration being supremely pure, it is free from all conceptualization and devoid of discrimination, as the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) arises.
Since this wisdom is sustained by the meditative concentration that serves as its basis, it is clear, pure, and stainless, with a naturally pure essence; therefore, it is called "clear" (*ādarśa*).
Because it is free from the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), it is called "pure" (*viśuddha*).
It is called "stainless" because it is free from the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

Regarding its being "all-pervasively radiant" due to performing acts for the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings: because this wisdom is sustained by meditative concentration (*samādhi*), it is also able to initiate all manner of beneficial and happy deeds for all sentient beings; it is by virtue of performing these that it is all-pervasively radiant.
Because its intrinsic nature is pure and reflective, it is called "light" (*āloka*).

Being free from the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), it is called "luminous universal illumination" (*prabhāsvara-vyāpi*) in their respective order.

The intended meaning here is as follows: just as a great round mirror, having been thoroughly polished and refined, is clear, pure, and stainless, and is called "luminous universal illumination" for the sake of benefiting others by enabling them to see their own facial features and defects; so too is this [the Buddha-nature].

The Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom is pure by its very nature; being far removed from the two obscurations, it is clear, pure, and stainless. Although it cannot be seen, it gives rise to the Enjoyment Body and the Transformation Bodies, capable of generating all forms of wisdom to accomplish every beneficial matter for sentient beings; therefore, it is called "Universal Illumination."
The Sūtra says:
"Furthermore, just as various images and appearances arise in dependence upon a round mirror and its objective essence,
so too the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom of the Tathāgata gives rise to various images and appearances of wisdom at all times, in dependence upon various conditions."
The treatise says:

If the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*) is the cause for the arising of all images, such as the various forms of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) for all sentient beings, why is it that these images have distinctions in their characteristics?
And why is it that the essence of this wisdom itself has no distinctions?
Furthermore, since it can always act as a cause at all times, why does it not constantly and simultaneously produce the images of all sentient beings, its own cognition, and so forth?

To resolve this difficulty, it is said: "Moreover, just as various images and appearances arise based on the essential substance (bimba) and conditions upon a round mirror, the nature of the mirror does not differ because the images are different; nor do the images arise constantly and simultaneously, for they depend upon various conditions."

In this way, the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*), at all times, gives rise to various distinctions such as the reflections of wisdom and so forth by depending upon manifold conditions. It is not because those [reflections] are different that the wisdom itself becomes various distinct entities such as blue and so on; nor does it constantly and simultaneously produce the reflections of all sentient beings as well as its own noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*) and so forth, for it is only by depending upon time and conditions that it is able to produce them.
The meaning intended here is that the pure consciousness associated with the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom has two kinds of functions:

first, the causal function, which means that within this pure consciousness there exist all the seeds capable of manifesting and generating the pure phenomena of bodies, lands, objects, and cognitions.

First, the function of the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*): when encountering external conditions, it immediately manifests various images of physical bodies, lands, and realms, as well as the distinctions in the characteristics and modes of mental activities associated with the arising of the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*) and so forth;

second, the function of the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), which refers to its being produced by the power of the roots of goodness and vows of the Buddha’s pure consciousness (*viśuddha-vijñāna*).

If sentient beings possess their own requisite causes and conditions, at that time the pure consciousness immediately provides assistance, enabling them to grow, develop, and reach fulfillment without obstruction.

Therefore, although the essence of the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) is one, it can manifest and produce the images of all phenomena; yet because it depends upon external conditions, these do not arise instantaneously.
The Sūtra says:
"Just as upon a round mirror, many diverse images arise, yet there are no images upon the round mirror, and this round mirror is without movement or activity."

In this way, upon the Tathāgata’s mirror-like wisdom (ādarśajñāna), the reflections of many diverse cognitions arise; yet, within the mirror-like wisdom, there are no such reflections, and this wisdom-mirror is without movement or activity.
The treatise says:
If the images of the various wisdoms already possessed substantial existence upon the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*), how could they arise with that mirror-like wisdom acting as their condition?
If they did not previously possess substantial existence, how could it produce the images of the various wisdoms without undergoing any activity?
One does not see a potter performing any action, yet he is able to produce jars and other objects that previously did not exist.

To explain this difficulty: it is like the many images upon a round mirror. Just as a great round mirror can give rise to various reflections—called "not one" because they are numerous of the same kind, and called "many" because they are countless of different kinds—it is said to be "not one" when considering the exclusion of a single instance among those of the same kind, and "many" when considering the manifestation of countless instances among those of different kinds.
In this way, although no images existed on the mirror beforehand, many images arise; yet the mirror lacks thought, discrimination, or movement.
Mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) is likewise: although no images such as wisdom previously existed, it is able to give rise to various images of dharmas, such as wisdom and so forth.
In relation to its own kind, it is said to be not one; in relation to other kinds, it is said to be manifold.
Although it gives rise to such images as cognition and so forth, it is devoid of volition, conceptualization, or activity.

The meaning here is as follows: just as a great round mirror, though devoid of conceptual discrimination, is able to give rise to various reflected images, so too is the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*);

although it is free from the grasping at a self and what belongs to a self, as well as the conceptualization of the mental attention toward the apprehended and the apprehender, it is nonetheless able to give rise to the reflected images of various dharmas, such as the [other] wisdoms.
The Sūtra says: Furthermore,
just as a round mirror and its various reflected images are neither joined nor separated— because they do not aggregate, yet because those conditions appear—
so too the Tathāgata’s Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom and the reflections of various wisdoms are neither joined nor separated— because they do not aggregate, yet because they are not lost.
The treatise says:
If the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom is conjoined with the images of the various wisdoms and so forth, how is it that this [Mirror Wisdom] does not become differentiated by virtue of their differences?
If it is not conjoined, how can it serve as their cause?

One does not see seeds and the like acting as causes for sprouts and the like without being in conjunction with their effects; nor do sunlight and the like illuminate lime and the like without being in mutual conjunction.

To explain this objection: it is like a round mirror and its various reflections, which are neither conjoined nor separated. For example, although a worldly round mirror can act as a cause for the arising of various reflections, it does not become conjoined with those reflections.

Since that [reflection] does not exist prior to its arising and thus lacks a substantial entity to aggregate, it cannot be said that this [mirror] and that [reflection] are either simultaneous or non-simultaneous in a manner that constitutes conjunction.

Furthermore, the round mirror and the reflection are not separate; because the conditions for the latter appear, they are not non-conjoined by virtue of this very principle, since the existence of the former is required for the existence of the latter.
Although it serves as the manifesting cause for images, the mirror does not become differentiated because the images possess differentiation.

Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom is likewise: although it can act as the cause that produces images such as wisdom, it is neither conjoined with nor separate from them, because they do not aggregate and are not lost.
Regarding the statement that they are not conjoined: before they have arisen, because their substance does not yet exist, they do not aggregate.

Regarding the statement that they are not separate: there must be the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) for reflections such as wisdom and so forth to arise; if it were absent, they would not arise, for [the mirror-like wisdom] is never lost.

That which is devoid of destruction and non-existence is called "non-disappearance"; that which is the opposite of this is called "non-non-disappearance. Alternatively, because it gathers and produces that [state], or because it does not forget the characteristics of the focal object (*ālambana*), it is called "non-disappearance."

Because all aspects of the objects of knowledge appear within the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*), if one does not universally know the wisdoms of the three times and so forth, as well as all sentient beings, this wisdom will not arise; it arises only when everything is known. Therefore, this wisdom does not forget the aspects of any object of focus and is thus called "non-dispersal."

Because it is not lost or scattered, it is not "separated" [from its objects]; although it can act as a cause to give rise to reflections such as cognition, it does not become differentiated based on the differences of those [objects], just as a great round mirror functions without differentiation.

The meaning intended here is as follows: Just as a worldly circular mirror, though it can act as the cause for the arising of various reflections, is not touched by the distinctions of conjunction or separation;

so too is the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*), which, though it can act as the cause for the arising of reflections such as [other] wisdoms, is not touched by the distinctions of conjunction or separation. Furthermore, although seeds and the like can act as causes for sprouts and the like, they likewise cannot be said to be either conjoined with or separated from them.

The subtle divisions of light are likewise not identical with form and the other [sensory objects], yet because they coexist in mutual conjunction, they cause the consciousness to arise as if it were conjoined with form and the others. Since we observe in the world that all causes and effects can function as causes despite being neither joined nor separated, there is no definitive conjunction between the two characteristics of cause and effect.
*The Treatise on the Buddha-bhūmi Sūtra*, Scroll Four;
*The Treatise on the Buddha-bhūmi Sūtra*, Scroll Five.
Composed by Bodhisattva Bandhuprabha and others.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang, by Imperial Decree,
the Sūtra says:
Furthermore, it is like a perfectly polished round mirror, which serves as the universal basis and condition for the arising of all reflected images in every place.

In this way, the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom of the Tathāgata is ceaselessly polished by the infinite accumulation of various practices, serving as the pervasive basis and condition for the arising of all images of wisdom—namely, the images of wisdom of the Śrāvaka Vehicle, the images of wisdom of the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle, and the images of wisdom of the Unsurpassed Mahāyāna. This is for the purpose of enabling those of the Śrāvaka Vehicle to attain liberation by relying on the Śrāvaka Vehicle, those of the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle to attain liberation by relying on the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle, and those of the Mahāyāna to attain liberation by relying on the Unsurpassed Vehicle.
The treatise says:
How can a single wisdom, at all times, produce the images of all dharmas such as the various types of omniscience of the three vehicles?
To explain this difficulty, it is said: "Furthermore, it is like a perfectly polished round mirror."

Just as a worldly circular mirror manifests all images, such as a face, throughout its entire surface, so too, when its front and back surfaces are polished through various applications, it can universally serve as a condition to manifest all reflections in every location.

The mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) is likewise. Although all Tathāgatas possessed the spiritual lineage (*gotra*) while they were bodhisattvas, it was obscured by hindrances and had not yet manifested. Because they diligently cultivated and continuously refined immeasurable multitudes of practices to produce reflections of all dharmas, such as the various forms of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) of the three vehicles (*triyāna*), at the moment the diamond-like concentration (*vajropamasamādhi*) becomes manifest, it becomes pure and perfect, free from all hindrances, and is able to universally produce all reflections, including the wisdoms of the three vehicles.
In terms of space, it is immeasurable because it is uninterrupted and without limits; in terms of time, it is immeasurable because it extends through infinite time.

This means that during the stage of the cause, one pervades all places and diligently cultivates various practices over immeasurable periods of time, thereby removing hindrances and skillfully polishing the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom, which is able to produce images such as the wisdoms of the three vehicles.

Furthermore, because the mirror-like wisdom (ādarśa-jñāna) is at all times free from all defilements and is perfectly pure due to being adorned with the fullness of various qualities and virtues, it is able to manifest all reflections in all places and at all times.

As it is said: by means of the supreme Vajropama-samādhi, one eliminates all obscurations and realizes the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*) of the Tathāgata; adorned with the perfection of various meritorious qualities, it is able to manifest all images of the three vehicles at all places and throughout immeasurable time.

The meaning here is as follows: when the various distinct ripenings of the roots of goodness arise as the superior path, the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom acts as a powerful condition—either proximately or distantly, as appropriate—to ensure that those of determinate lineage attain liberation by relying on their respective vehicles, while those of indeterminate lineage may attain liberation by relying either on the Mahāyāna or another vehicle.
What is called "transcendence" (nairyāṇika) is precisely nirvāṇa.

The practitioners of the three vehicles take their own spiritual lineage as the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), and the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) of the Tathāgata as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*). Through diligent application of skillful means, they cultivate and accumulate the provisions that induce the noble path; thereby eliminating the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), each realizes nirvāṇa according to their respective capacity.

Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas of the determined lineage who abide in the stage of no-more-learning, because they delight in quiescence, initiate karma that moistens rebirth; yet, because their afflictive obstructions have been eternally extinguished, the body and mind induced by prior karma and afflictions cease spontaneously and they do not undergo further birth, as they lack any basis for such existence.

All seeds of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), whether with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*), are completely severed and extinguished; there remains only the body of liberation—the pure *dharmadhātu*, the stainless *tathatā* characterized by the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*) and free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*). This is called the realm of *nirvāṇa* without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇadhātu*), which is eternally abiding, blissful, ultimately quiescent, beyond all numerical categories, and inconceivable.

They are identical to all Tathāgatas, except that because they lack the adornment of conditioned, untainted merit, they no longer have the capacity to further bring about the welfare and happiness of sentient beings.

Unlike the Tathāgatas, śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas of indeterminate lineage who abide in the stage of no-more-learning, although they are free from afflictions and delight in bodhi, by the power of their concentration and vows they maintain the continuity of their physical existence to cultivate Mahāyāna practices, until they attain the diamond-like samādhi (*vajropama-samādhi*), whereby all obstacles are extinguished and they realize the three bodies of a Buddha.
Although they possess conditioned, untainted merits, because no tainted body or mind remains, they realize the realm of great *nirvāṇa* without remainder.
"Remainder" refers to the tainted body and mind within the three realms.
When Bodhisattvas have completely severed the two obstacles and attained the state of Buddhahood, they are then said to have realized the realm of *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (Nirvana without remainder).
For this reason, those of the Two Vehicles first enter the realm of *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (Nirvana with remainder) and subsequently enter the realm of *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.

When a bodhisattva first realizes the stage of the Tathāgata, they suddenly realize two kinds of great nirvāṇa realms; because all contaminated body and mind have been exhausted, it is called "nirvana without remainder."
Because there still remain transformations of body and mind that resemble the characteristics of outflows (*āsrava*), it is called "with remainder" (*sopadhiśeṣa*).
Because it is realized through uninterrupted compassion and wisdom, it is also called the "Great Nirvāṇa Realm of Non-abiding."

Nirvāṇa is the meaning of the permanent cessation of obscurations upon the essence of suchness (tathatā), because it is realized by severing all defilements through the discernment of the principles of truth by means of untainted wisdom (anāsrava-prajñā).

It is also called "cessation through discernment" (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). Such cessation through discernment is provisionally designated upon *tathatā* (suchness) and has no separate, substantial entity.

When it reaches the ultimate stage, it is called *nirvāṇa*. It is named *nirvāṇa* because there is nowhere further to go, because it is free from foul odors, because it is free from weaving, and because it is free from the dense forest [of afflictions].
Since Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas have not yet extinguished the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), how can they realize ultimate nirvāṇa?

Because these habitual tendencies of the cognitive obstructions are a form of non-cognition and are not afflictive, they obstruct the fruit of bodhi but do not obstruct nirvāṇa; because they are not afflictions, they cannot moisten rebirth.

If, through the power of aspiration, one turns the mind toward the Great Vehicle and reaches the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), one will surely attain eternal quiescence at the end of one’s lifespan.
As the Sūtra says:

"Just as great reflections can be perceived in a perfect mirror—namely, the reflections of the great earth, great mountains, great trees, and great palaces—yet the perfect mirror is not equal in size to those objects."

In this way, upon the Tathāgata’s mirror-like wisdom (ādarśajñāna), the cognitive images of the wisdoms from the Stage of Extreme Joy up to the Buddha Stage can be perceived, as well as the cognitive images of all mundane and supramundane phenomena; yet the mirror-like wisdom itself is not limited by those proportions.
The treatise says:
If the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*) can give rise to cognitive images (*jñāna-bimba*), then it should be possible to perceive distinctions corresponding to their respective magnitudes.
To explain this objection: just as large images, such as the great earth and so forth, can be perceived within a round mirror.

Just as a worldly circular mirror, though it can serve as a condition for the arising of reflections such as mountains and the like, is not equal in size to those objects: within a single small mirror, large reflections of many mountains and so forth may be perceived, while within a single large mirror, small reflections of many stones and so forth may be perceived; thus, although they possess physical obstruction, they do not correspond to the size or quantity of the shadows.

The mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) is likewise; although it gives rise to the images of all mundane and supramundane cognitions of the various stages, it is without form or obstruction. Nevertheless, it does not share the same magnitude or numerical quantity as those images of all-knowledge. For this reason, the mirror-like wisdom of the Buddhas is called the "Treasury of Great Wisdom" (*mahājñānagarbha*), because it is the root of all mundane and supramundane cognitions. As it is said: "The World-Honored One has become the Treasury of Great Wisdom, the Mirror-like Wisdom, for it is able to give birth to all-knowledge."

It should be understood that here, all virtues are designated by the term "wisdom. Because the pure consciousness associated with the mirror-like wisdom (ādarśa-jñāna) is fully endowed with the seeds of all virtues for one’s own benefit and the benefit of others, it can serve as the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) for producing images such as wisdom within one’s own continuum, and as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for producing images such as wisdom within the continua of others.

Because this mirror-like wisdom can manifest bodies that produce wisdom and preach the Dharma, thereby successively generating reflections such as the wisdom of others; or because it is accomplished through the cultivation of the power of compassion and vows, acting as a spontaneous dominant condition for the wholesome dharmas such as the wisdom of others, thereby enabling the wisdom and other wholesome dharmas within the bodies of others to easily arise and grow.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"All wholesome dharmas and sublime fruits possessed by all sentient beings arise through the predominant power of the Tathāgata’s compassion and vows."
The Sūtra says:

"Furthermore, just as a round mirror is not the condition for the arising of reflections from objects that are obstructed, so too the Great Mirror-like Wisdom of the Tathāgata is not the condition for the arising of the cognitive images of sentient beings who are obstructed by being influenced by evil friends and hearing incorrect teachings; for they are not suitable vessels."
The treatise says:

If the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom produces various mental images of wisdom in order to enable those of the three vehicles to attain liberation, and if these images—produced as superior conditions through the cultivation of the power of compassion and vows—give rise to both mundane and supramundane wisdom-images, why is it that correct wisdom does not arise in the various non-Buddhist outsiders of the world?
Because the causes and conditions that produce [cognition] are always in harmony, non-Buddhists and others should not possess inverted views.

To resolve this objection, it is said: furthermore, just as a round mirror is not the locus for the obstructing substance or its reflected image and conditions, so too, although a worldly round mirror can serve as a condition to manifest various images, it is not the locus where the reflected images of substances obstructed by walls and such arise.

The mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*) of the Tathāgata is likewise: although it can serve as a condition for the arising of the images of wisdom, it does not reside within the sphere of those influenced by evil associates (*pāpa-mitra*), nor is it a condition for the arising of the images of wisdom in those who obstruct themselves by delighting in hearing false teachings (*mithyā-dharma*). This is because such persons are not vessels capable of receiving empowerment, nor are they vessels fit to hear the true Dharma (*saddharma*).

Therefore, because the seeds of wholesome dharmas have been damaged and suppressed while the seeds of unwholesome dharmas encounter the conditions for their arising, the non-Buddhists do not give rise to the noble path and constantly harbor inverted views.

Since beginningless time, all sentient beings have practiced virtue for a short duration while committing evil for a long duration; therefore, although wholesome dharmas encounter powerful conditions, they are difficult to grow, whereas unwholesome dharmas flare up even when encountering slight external conditions.
The Sūtra says:
"Furthermore, just as a round mirror is not a condition for the arising of reflections from objects situated in darkness,

so too the Tathāgata’s Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom is not a condition for the arising of the reflection of wisdom in sentient beings who delight in evil and are ignorant, for they are not suitable vessels."
The Treatise says:

Just as external conditions obstruct the reflection of wisdom so that it does not arise, so too do internal conditions—namely, the habitual tendency toward evil and the darkness of ignorance—obstruct the reflection of wisdom so that it does not manifest.

Although those who delight in evil may have all afflictions such as greed and hatred blazing intensely, delusion (*moha*) is particularly predominant, because they fail to understand the superior and inferior nature of the causes and effects of good and evil.

In this world, there currently exist the true Dharma of the Buddhas, which benefits and brings peace and happiness to all sentient beings; and the excellent field of the Triple Gem, from which grow immeasurable masses of merit, both mundane and supramundane. Yet, you do not wish to hear or accept it, nor do you delight in taking refuge in it; instead, you listen to and accept the profitless and joyless false teachings of non-Buddhist paths, and take refuge in various malevolent spirits that produce immeasurable evil karma and induce manifold sufferings—is this not the power of the obscuration of ignorance and delusion?
Therefore, ignorance that obstructs the wholesome is the most grave; one should diligently cultivate the light of wisdom, for those whose ignorance is heavy are not vessels for the wholesome.
As the Sūtra says:
"Furthermore, it is like a round mirror: it is not a condition for the arising of images when the objects are at a great distance."

In this way, the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom of the Tathāgata does not serve as the condition for the arising of the reflection of wisdom for sentient beings who are impure, who have accumulated karma that results in the deprivation of the Dharma, and who lack faith, because they are not suitable vessels.
The treatise states:
Thus, due to the obstructive power of these two conditions—internal and external—the reflection of wisdom does not arise.

First, because of karma accumulated in previous lives that results in a deficiency of the Dharma, one does not hear the true Dharma for a long period of time; that is, having reviled the true Dharma in a prior birth, one undergoes this karmic obstruction and does not hear the Buddha’s teachings for immeasurable kalpas. This very failure to hear the true Dharma of the Buddhas constitutes the karmic fruit that obstructs the reflection of wisdom, preventing it from arising and resulting in not hearing the true Dharma.
Since its essence is non-existent, how can it be called the fruit of slandering the true Dharma?
How can it obstruct the reflection of wisdom that is capable of arising?

It is not said that the failure to hear the true Dharma is itself the fruit or the obstruction; rather, it is said that because of that [slander], one incurs karma that results in the deprivation of the Dharma, and the resulting dullness of body and mind—characterized by an inability to listen to or receive the true Dharma and the lack of [healthy] faculties—is what constitutes the fruit and the obstruction.

Second, due to lack of faith: this refers to those who lack the spiritual lineage (*agotra*) and possess no nature for *nirvāṇa*; they do not delight in *nirvāṇa* and lack the seeds of the supramundane noble path. They possess absolute obstacles to realizing *tathatā*, and upon hearing the supramundane teachings, they do not believe or accept them at all; thus, they will ultimately never attain the *nirvāṇa* of the three vehicles.

Because the continuity of such bodies and minds is impure, they are not vessels for the noble Dharma; consequently, the reflections of supramundane merit and wisdom will never arise within them, either temporarily or ultimately, just as turbid and filthy water cannot produce reflections of the moon and other celestial bodies.
Mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) is likewise; it cannot produce images of cognition therein.

Thus, in brief, mirror-like wisdom has nine characteristics by which it excels all other wisdoms: namely, the characteristic of etymological definition, the characteristic of non-conceptuality, the characteristic of purification from obstructions, the characteristic of producing images of cognition through the causal conditions of its support, the characteristic of being without "mine-ness" and without grasping, the characteristic of not forgetting any object of knowledge, the characteristic of constantly and universally producing images of cognition, the characteristic of being the root that can give rise to all forms of wisdom, and the characteristic of being unable to produce [images] in those who are not vessels for the Dharma.
There are three kinds of those who are not vessels for the noble Dharma:
first, those who associate with unwholesome friends and hear incorrect teachings, possessing temporary obstacles and thus being non-vessels for the noble Dharma;
second, those who are obstructed by the hindrances of afflictions and delusion, and are thus non-vessels for the noble Dharma.

Third, those obstructed by extremely heavy karmic hindrances, as well as those who lack the seeds of the supramundane noble path and will ultimately never become vessels for the noble ones over a long period of time—
these three types are collectively termed the ninth characteristic of being unable to produce [the qualities] in one who is not a vessel for the Dharma.
The Sūtra says:
Furthermore, Subhūti,
the wisdom of equality is perfectly accomplished through ten aspects.
The Commentary states:

The Wisdom of Equality is fully accomplished through ten aspects; it should be understood that this is the fruit of cultivation in the ten stages (*bhūmi*). Briefly stated, one realizes a specific aspect of equality in each stage, and through the perfection of such cultivation, one accomplishes the Wisdom of Equality of the Buddha-stage. Therefore, it is said that the Wisdom of Equality is fully accomplished through ten aspects.

If explained in detail, within each and every stage (bhūmi), one realizes the immeasurable equality of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) and, through the perfection of cultivation, accomplishes the wisdom of equality (samatājñāna) of the Buddha-stage.
The Sūtra says:
"Because one realizes the supreme joy of all marks through the perfect accomplishment of the equality of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
The Commentary says:

Regarding "all marks" (*lakṣaṇa*): this refers to the marks of a Great Being (*mahāpuruṣa*) and the secondary signs (*anuvyañjana*). Because they are distinctions among marks, they are all termed "marks.
Such marks, being devoid of the nature of imagined construction (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), are said to be "equality."
Therefore, a sutra states: "The marks of a Great Being (mahāpuruṣa), the Tathāgata declares them to be non-marks; for this reason, they are called the marks of a Great Being.

Regarding "supremacy" (ādhipatya): it refers to wealth, nobility, and sovereignty. Neither the individual aggregates (skandhas), such as form and the rest, possess wealth, nobility, or sovereignty, nor does their collection possess them, because they remain distinct in nature. When phenomena combine, they do not abandon their own inherent natures (svabhāva); apart from these, there is no real person (pudgala).
Therefore, all wealth, nobility, and sovereignty, being free from the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), are said to be equal.
Thus, a sutra states:
"O Bhagavan!..."
"I now understand that because all things are without self, there is neither poverty nor wealth.
"Affection" refers to all forms of affection.
By the power of conceptual construction (*parikalpa*), one gives rise to joy toward phenomena that accord with that [affection] and gives rise to sorrow and distress toward phenomena that oppose it.

Because all phenomena that are conceptually constructed (*parikalpita*) do not exist, the attachment and delight toward all those conceptually constructed things also do not exist; this is called "equality.
To realize and understand the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*)—which is the equality of the aforementioned signs, superior attachment, and delight—is therefore termed "attainment" (*pratilambha*).

A bodhisattva first realizes this at the first stage (*bhūmi*); thereafter, through gradual skillful means, they cultivate it until it increases, reaching full perfection at the final Buddha-stage. From that point onward, there is no further increase.
Because it is realized through this perfect accomplishment, the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*) is fully perfected.

One should know that herein, because of this perfect accomplishment, the fifth transformation is spoken of in the third location; all [transformations] should be understood as being due to perfect accomplishment, yet such an expression is used for the sake of linguistic convenience based on the similarity of their categories.
The Sūtra says:
"Because one has realized all dependent origination as it is experienced, and because the equality of the dharmatā is perfectly accomplished.
The Commentary says:
Dependent origination is twofold:
namely, internal and external.
Internal dependent origination refers to the twelve links of existence, beginning with ignorance.
Regarding external dependent origination, this refers to all external things such as seeds, sprouts, and so forth.
Internal [dependent origination] should be observed through the modes of both defilement and purification, in both forward and reverse order;

external [dependent origination] should be observed through the modes of "because this exists, that exists" and "because this arises, that arises," meaning that because seeds and so forth exist, and because seeds and so forth arise, sprouts and so forth come to exist and sprouts and so forth come to arise.
In these two types of dependent origination, everything exists because the cause exists, and the effect arises because the cause arises.
The meaning of dependent origination is the absence of functional agency; the meaning of dependent origination is emptiness and selflessness, and the absence of a *pudgala*.
The self-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) in such meanings is that which is experienced; therefore, it is called "experience" (*vedanā*).
Alternatively, because a sentient being—whether real or nominal—is able to experience it, it is named "experience."

The dependently originated phenomena are that which is experienced; in this way, all such experiences of dependent origination are called "equality" because they are devoid of functional activity, empty and selfless, and lack a *pudgala*, being thus free from the nature of imagined construction (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
Because one thoroughly understands and accepts all such explained dharmas of the equality of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), it is called "attainment" (*adhigama*).
Through this attainment, because the prior cultivation has been brought to perfection, the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*) is fully accomplished.
Thus, the dharmatā of the equality of dependent origination is itself the dharmatā of the equality of all phenomena.
As it is said: "O Brahmin, the dharmatā of all phenomena is precisely the dharmatā of dependent arising and dependent origination. To realize and understand this is called bodhi.
As the Buddha perceives it, the nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*) is thus: it is precisely the nature of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
Furthermore, a sūtra states:

"Not even the slightest phenomenon is seen apart from the nature of dependent origination. Herein, the equal nature of phenomena within dependent origination is termed the "nature of dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpādatā*).

Based on this underlying intention, it is said: "If one sees dependent origination, one sees the nature of phenomena (dharmatā); if one sees the nature of phenomena, one sees all Buddhas; for the true nature of dependent origination is the ultimate dharma and the ultimate Buddha."
The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is equal and without distinction in all places; therefore, this statement is made.
The Sūtra says:
"Because one realizes the equality of the nature of phenomena, which is free from both distinct characteristics and the absence of characteristics, it is perfectly accomplished."
The treatise states:
Because the characteristics of transformation and decay in phenomena such as form (*rūpa*) are dissimilar, they are termed "distinctive characteristics" (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*).
To be free from such individual distinctive characteristics is precisely the "universal characteristic" (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*).
What constitutes the characteristic of such common characteristics?
It is characterized by being non-characteristic. As the Sūtra says:
“The nature of all phenomena has but a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of non-characteristic.
This characteristic of non-characteristic is the equal nature of phenomena (*samatā-dharmatā*).
To thoroughly understand that the nature of all phenomena, which is conceptually constructed (*parikalpita*), is ultimately and eternally without such an equal nature of phenomena.
Therefore, it is called "attainment.
Because this attainment is fully perfected through the aforementioned cultivation, the Wisdom of Equality (*samatājñāna*) is completely accomplished.

Furthermore, there is another meaning: being free from distinct characteristics (*nimitta*) is the absence of characteristics; being free from non-characteristics is the absence of non-characteristics. This state of neither existence nor non-existence is termed "equality" (*samatā*). The rest is as previously explained.
The Sūtra says:
"Because the great compassion that extensively rescues [beings] is fully perfected through the nature of equality.
The Commentary says:
There are three kinds of loving-kindness (*maitrī*):
first, that which has sentient beings as its object; second, that which has phenomena as its object; and third, that which has no object.
Third is the objectless [compassion].

Bodhisattvas and others at the stage of the initial resolve mostly cultivate compassion directed toward sentient beings; this is predominantly with outflows (*sāsrava*), because its objects are conventional and conditioned phenomena.

Bodhisattvas on the stages of application (*prayogamārga*) mostly cultivate compassion that takes phenomena as its object (*dharmālambana-maitrī*); this is also largely with outflows (*sāsrava*), because the teachings of the Mahāyāna serve as its objective sphere.

Bodhisattvas who have attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*) mostly cultivate objectless compassion (*anālambana-maitrī*); although it has an object, its object is the *dharmadhātu*.

Just as the various resultant phenomena (*vipākadharmas*) such as the eyes lack conceptual discrimination and function spontaneously without applied effort (*prayoga*), this is called the great compassion associated with the wisdom of equality that is objectless.

According to another interpretation, it is called "objectless compassion" because it takes only the dharma-realm as its object; since conceptualization regarding objects of perception is forever absent, and because it does not take sentient beings or various phenomena as its objects, it is termed objectless compassion.
Furthermore, there is another interpretation according to which it also takes all phenomena as its object.

According to the ultimate meaning, however, it takes sentient beings as its object but without conceptual differentiation. It is called "Equalizing Wisdom" because it understands with an equalizing mode of activity that the nature of all conventionally designated sentient beings is equal, that the nature of dependently originated phenomena is equal, and that the nature of true thusness devoid of self is equal.

This wisdom, when associated with its objective referents, possesses all three types of loving-kindness (*maitrī*); however, because it functions with equanimity and without conceptual differentiation, it is termed "objectless" (*anālambana*).

Within the stage of a Tathāgata, the great loving-kindness associated with the Wisdom of Equality (*samatājñāna*) is constantly manifested as all characteristics are fully perfected. Since the Tathāgata already possesses this objectless great loving-kindness, the other two types are naturally accomplished without being explicitly mentioned.

Because the Tathāgata, by means of these three kinds of loving-kindness, impartially rescues and protects all sentient beings—not merely bestowing a small measure of happiness upon them, but universally turning toward the equality of the suchness of the selflessness of all phenomena in all sentient beings—he constantly manifests this practice to deliver all; therefore, it is called "Great Loving-Kindness" (mahāmaitrī).
It is not like that of the śrāvakas and ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), who practice for a brief duration and only partially, and are unable to rescue all sentient beings.

Because it surpasses all śrāvakas and others, because it rescues all sentient beings, and because it is perfected through the long-term accumulation of the provisions of merit and wisdom, it is called "vast salvation" (*mahānugraha*).

The great compassion that provides vast salvation as thus described operates without distinction throughout all places; therefore, it is called "equality. This very equality is designated as the "nature of phenomena" (*dharmatā*).

Alternatively, because it takes as its object the very same great compassion that provides universal relief—the equal nature of phenomena (dharmatā) as previously described—it is termed "equal nature of phenomena" with respect to its objective referent.
Through this great compassion, as it is cultivated and brought to perfection as before, the wisdom of equality (samatājñāna) is fully accomplished.
The Sūtra says:
"Great compassion is without dependence, because it is perfectly accomplished through the equality of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
The Commentary says:
The compassion of the śrāvakas and others is unable to deliver all sentient beings; it functions only for a brief duration, directed toward limited aspects within the desire realm alone.
The great compassion of the Tathāgata is universally capable of delivering all sentient beings; it functions at all times, directed toward the pervasive aspects throughout all three realms.

To speak of being "without dependence" means that one never ceases to rescue others regardless of external conditions; that is, being without reliance on anything else, one delivers sentient beings from the three types of suffering according to their needs, constantly turning toward them without ever abandoning them, just as an elder cherishes his only son.
It operates with impartiality toward all sentient beings, because the realm of sentient beings is without limit.

In maturing sentient beings, there is never a moment of neglect, nor does it ever miss the proper time for maturing them; for the Tathāgata is constantly endowed with great compassion, such that it cannot be said that he only occasionally arouses or applies it.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"O son of good family!
One should not say that the great compassion of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, arises and turns toward sentient beings only momentarily."
Why is this? Because it revolves perpetually.
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, do not finally realize unsurpassed bodhi as long as their great compassion has not yet established its root.
Having realized great enlightenment, the Tathāgata constantly reflects:
"I shall establish all sentient beings in the roots of all that is wholesome.
If there are those who have not yet awakened to all phenomena, I shall bring them to awakening."
"In this way, the Tathāgata constantly gives rise to great compassion for all sentient beings," and so on,
as explained at length.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"The Tathāgata constantly observes the world during the six periods of day and night.
How, then, can it be said that "great compassion constantly functions"?
This statement refers to the continuity of its activity throughout the six periods, being ever-present and uninterrupted; therefore, there is no contradiction.

Great loving-kindness and great compassion have as their intrinsic nature the roots of goodness consisting of non-anger, non-harming, and non-delusion; they differ in their modes of activity—bestowing happiness and extracting suffering—yet both possess three types of objects, such as sentient beings and so forth.

Loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is non-aversion, and compassion (*karuṇā*) is non-harming. Loving-kindness takes as its object those who lack happiness and desires to grant them happiness; compassion takes as its object those who possess suffering and desires to extract their suffering. Because great compassion functions without dependence or distinction, it is called "equanimity" (*samatā*); this is either the very nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) or it takes that equal *dharmatā* as its objective support.
Because this great compassion has been cultivated to perfection as previously described, the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*) is fully accomplished.
The Sūtra says:
"It manifests according to the inclinations of sentient beings, because the nature of equality (*samatādharman*) is fully accomplished."
The treatise states:
In accordance with the various inclinations of sentient beings to behold the distinct forms of the Tathāgata’s rūpakāya, the Tathāgata manifests such rūpakāyas.

Although the Tathāgata abides in a state free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*), by the sovereign power of his wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*), the pure consciousness associated with the great perfect mirror wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) manifests subtle and wondrous rūpakāyas, such as those of lapis lazuli. This causes the roots of goodness of sentient beings to ripen; their own minds undergo transformations that appear as these sense organs, whereby they perceive the body of the Tathāgata as if it were external to their own minds.
As stated in a sutra:

"By the power of the roots of goodness of the Tathāgatas' benevolence and compassion, they manifest appearances that cause gods, humans, and others to perceive the body of the Tathāgata as transformed within their own minds, appearing as golden in color and so forth."
Furthermore, as a sūtra says:

"If there are immeasurable sentient beings who are to be transformed and who should see the color of lapis lazuli and mani-jewels, the Tathāgata is able to manifest various colors of lapis lazuli and mani-jewels without obstruction, causing their own minds to likewise undergo such a transformation."
Thus it is extensively explained.
In this way, the manifestation of the equal form of all Tathāgatas is itself the *dharmatā*; therefore, it is called the "equal *dharmatā*."

This means that the Tathāgatas, in accordance with the inclinations of the sentient beings to be converted who wish to see their physical forms, each manifest a form identical in location, time, and kind, causing those beings' own minds to thus perceive them, thereby performing acts of benefit and happiness.

Just as the *ālaya-vijñāna* of all sentient beings matures through common seeds, each manifests the appearance of a world and so forth; though they occupy the same location, these similar appearances do not obstruct one another.
This is also like this.
Just as it is with the marks of the physical body, so it is with other matters.
By means of this manifestation, because the prior cultivation has been perfected, the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*) is fully accomplished.
The Sūtra says:
"All sentient beings respectfully receive what is taught, because the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is perfectly fulfilled in its equality.
The Commentary says:

If there is such a kind of vocal action that can cause the roots of goodness of sentient beings to mature, such that upon hearing it they give rise to joy and attain pure faith and delight, the Tathāgata then manifests such vocal action so that they may hear it.

Although the Tathāgata is free from conceptual proliferation and discrimination, he manifests in this way through the power of his compassion and vows; and the sentient beings to be converted, by the power of their own resolute belief, undergo such a transformation that they perceive the Buddha’s voice as existing outside of their own minds.

Because all the speech uttered by the Tathāgata accords with the capacities and needs of beings, no humans, devas, or others find it contrary to themselves; therefore, it is called "reverently received.
If it did not accord with their capacities, he would not manifest it; thus, it is said that the words of the Buddhas are never in vain.

Although there may be sentient beings who do not comply with the Buddha’s words, these are either emanations or individuals who will certainly find benefit and eventually come to believe and accept them.

Speaking in general terms, it is said that "all [beings] respectfully receive what is taught"; such speech is called "equal" because, according to the principles mentioned above, all Buddhas manifest it identically.
Such equality is precisely what is called the *dharmatā*.
Because it is manifested through this [equality], and because it has been perfected through prior cultivation, the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*) is fully accomplished.
The Sūtra says:
"The tranquility of the world is of a single flavor, for the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is perfectly fulfilled in equality.
The Commentary says:

The five aggregates with outflows (*sāsrava-skandha*) are called the "world" (*loka*); because they are moment-to-moment countered by two kinds of destruction, their cessation is termed "tranquility" (*śānti*).

Because one attains tranquility therein, this refers to the noble path (*āryamārga*), nirvāṇa, and the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*). Since the world and tranquility both converge in suchness (*tathatā*), which is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), they are said to be of a single flavor (*ekarasa*).

Furthermore, that which is "the world" is the thoroughly imagined nature; its inherent non-existence is termed "quiescence. Because the suchness revealed by such quiescence is undifferentiated, it is called "of one taste," and this is precisely what is termed the "equal dharma-nature."
Because this single flavor is fully perfected through cultivation as previously described, the Wisdom of Equality (samatājñāna) is fully accomplished.
The Sūtra says:
"All worldly phenomena, whether suffering or pleasure, are of a single flavor, because the nature of equality (samatā-dharmatā) is fully accomplished."
The Treatise says:
There are briefly eight kinds of phenomena in the world:
first, gain; [and so forth].
2. Decline; 3. Disparagement; 4. Praise;
5. Praise; 6. Blame; 7. Suffering.

8. Pleasure (*sukha*). The acquisition of agreeable things is called gain (*lābha*); the loss of agreeable things is called decline (*alābha*). To be slandered behind one's back is called defamation (*nindā*); to be praised behind one's back is called praise (*praśaṃsā*). To be praised in one's presence is called fame (*yaśas*); to be slandered in one's presence is called censure (*ayaśas*). That which afflicts the body and mind is called suffering (*duḥkha*); that which brings gratification to the body and mind is called pleasure (*sukha*).
These eight kinds are comprised of two categories:
four that are contrary [to the noble ones] and termed "suffering," and four that are favorable and termed "pleasure," because they give rise to joy and grief respectively.

Alternatively, within this context, the final pair of suffering and pleasure is explained in brief; the Noble One dwells in the middle with constant uniformity—neither elated when gaining profit nor dejected when encountering decline—and thus remains without craving for pleasure and without resentment toward suffering.
As a sūtra says: "The noble ones dwell in the world with a single, equal flavor, just like space; it is only the foolish who, while in the world, conceive of distinctions.
Because they have distanced themselves from that which is conceptually imputed, the eight worldly dharmas are of one and the same flavor in all circumstances."
This is precisely what is called the "equality of dharmatā.
Because this single flavor is cultivated to perfection as previously described, the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*) is fully accomplished.
The Sūtra says:
"Because one has cultivated and perfected immeasurable merit, and because the equal nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is fully accomplished.
The Commentary says:
Merit refers to the various dharmas of merit such as the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*).
To infuse seeds, nurture them, and bring them to maturity for liberation is termed "cultivation and planting.

Although the Wisdom of Equality (*samatā-jñāna*) is free from conceptual discrimination, through the sovereign power of the Buddhas' and Bodhisattvas' wisdom—like a wish-fulfilling jewel—it causes the merits within other bodies to grow, mature, and lead to liberation.
Regarding "ultimate," it means that one is able to attain parinirvāṇa through the three vehicles.
Since this brings about liberation, the attainment of worldly happiness is not mentioned as being explicitly stated [as a primary goal], yet it is naturally accomplished.
Such wisdom is called the "equal dharma-nature" (samatā-dharmatā), because it is far removed from the nature of pervasive conceptual construction (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).

Alternatively, when various bodhisattvas cultivate and plant immeasurable, sublime merits such as the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma) until they reach their ultimate consummation, this very state is termed the "equal dharma-nature" (samatā-dharmatā).
By virtue of these merits, as they have been cultivated and brought to perfection as previously described, the Wisdom of Equality (samatājñāna) is fully accomplished.
The Sūtra says:
"Furthermore, Subhūti!"
Regarding the wisdom of wondrous observation (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*),
the treatise states:
One should know that the wisdom of wondrous observation is to be distinguished based on ten kinds of causes.
The ten kinds of causes are:
first, the establishing cause;
second, the originating cause;
Third, the cause of joy;
fourth, the cause of discrimination;
fifth, the cause of enjoyment;
Sixth, the cause for the differentiation of destinies;
seventh, the cause for the differentiation of realms;
eighth, the cause for raining down the great rain of Dharma;
9. The cause for subduing enemies;
10. The cause for severing all doubts.
The Sūtra says:
Just as the world-system sustains the realm of sentient beings,
so too does the Tathāgata’s wisdom of wondrous observation sustain all doors of dhāraṇī and samādhi, and unimpededly expound the sublime Dharma of all Buddhas.
The Commentary states:
This section demonstrates the establishment of the characteristics of causes.

For example, regarding how the world-system supports the realm of sentient beings: just as the various world-systems—such as the lower wind-circle and so forth—which are transformations of the minds of sentient beings themselves, are able to support the realms of sentient beings, such as the eyes and other faculties, which are likewise transformations of their own minds.

In this way, the Tathāgata’s wisdom of wondrous observation can sustain all dharanī-doors, extensively including even the sublime Dharma of all Buddhas, because it is associated with them and capable of inducing them.

As for *dhāraṇī*, it is the superior mindfulness and wisdom that is able to universally sustain immeasurable Buddha-dharmas so that they are not forgotten or lost. Within a single dharma it sustains all dharmas; within a single phrase it sustains all phrases; within a single meaning it sustains all meanings. Because it gathers and stores immeasurable merits, it is called the "Inexhaustible Treasury."
This dhāraṇī is briefly of four kinds:
first, the dhāraṇī of phenomena (dharma-dhāraṇī);
second, the dhāraṇī of meaning (artha-dhāraṇī).
Third, the dhāraṇī of mantras;
fourth, the dhāraṇī for attaining the bodhisattva’s patience.
Their characteristics are explained in detail in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
How is it that within a single phenomenon (dharma), one can universally sustain all phenomena?

It is said that through the inconceivable power of the superior mindfulness and wisdom of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, all phenomena appear within the appearance of a single phenomenon as a mental object-part (*svacitta-nimitta-bhāga*); the same applies to their words and meanings.

Furthermore, it can manifest immeasurable and inexhaustible dharma-gates of merit; because its own essence as a constituent part also possesses boundless superior efficacy, it sustains all things so that they are not forgotten. Such inconceivable power of mindfulness and wisdom is called *dhāraṇī*.

Samādhi refers to superior concentration (*adhipati-samādhi*), namely the *sudurjayā* and other such samādhis. Because it can surpass all mundane and supramundane samādhis, while others cannot surpass it, it is called "Invincible" (*sudurjayā*).
Furthermore, it is called "Heroic Progress" (*vīryāpāramitā*) because it is the practice of Buddhas and Bodhisattva heroes;
for only Bodhisattvas of the tenth stage and Buddhas attain this samādhi,
whereas other samādhis do not.
One should explain their names according to what is stated in the sūtras.

That is to say, both *dhāraṇī* and *samādhi* are collectively termed "gates" (*mukha*), just as the three gates of emptiness, wishlessness, and signlessness; for they are able to universally produce immeasurable qualities, both of the same kind and of different kinds.
Unimpeded eloquence consists of the four kinds of analytical knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*):

of phenomena (*dharma*), meaning (*artha*), expression (*nirukti*), and eloquence (*pratibhāna*). Because one is able to expound the sublime Dharma for sentient beings by means of these four, it is called "eloquence."

The sublime Dharma of all Buddhas consists of the Tathāgata’s powers, fearlessnesses, and other immeasurable Buddha-qualities; every single term therein should be explained accordingly. Because the wisdom of wondrous observation transforms the mental consciousness, its functioning becomes vast and expansive, and it is thus able to sustain all meritorious virtues.
This sixth mental consciousness associated with this wisdom is universally associated with all merits and is capable of eliciting all merits; therefore, it is said to be able to sustain them.
The Sūtra says:
"Furthermore, just as this world serves as the causal condition for all sentient beings to suddenly give rise to various and immeasurable consciousnesses of signs,

so too does the Tathāgata’s wondrously discerning wisdom (pratyavekṣaṇājñāna) serve as the causal condition for the sudden arising of various and immeasurable consciousnesses of signs— the unimpeded, wondrous wisdom regarding all that is knowable."
The Commentary states:

This section reveals the characteristics of the cause of arising, because the wisdom of wondrous observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*) can act as the cause for the simultaneous arising of all consciousnesses that take the aspects of the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*).
"World" refers here to the various receptacle worlds (*bhājana-loka*).
Just as the vessel-world serves as the cause for the arising of the various perceptions of forms upon the earth and within the immeasurable reaches of space for sentient beings,

so too does the Tathāgata’s wondrously discerning wisdom (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*)— simultaneously and instantaneously regarding all objects of experience— like space itself, perceive them without obstruction and serve as the cause for the arising of the various perceptions of forms within all kinds of mundane worlds and the immeasurable supramundane realms.

The meaning of this passage is as follows: the *pratyavekṣaṇajñāna* (wonderfully discerning wisdom) of all Tathāgatas can instantaneously cognize all objects of knowledge. These appear as manifold aspects, just as the colors in a painting possess various characteristics; the essence of the wisdom, as the seeing-division (*darśanabhāga*), serves as the cause for the arising of such consciousnesses characterized by these aspects.
This [condition] is said to be the cause of arising because it can manifest that [result], though it is not a direct cause of arising, since [the result] arises from the seed.

This very [condition] is called the "causal condition" (*hetu-pratyaya*) as a supporting condition; for although there is no difference in essence, it may still function as a cause because they are not identical, given that the characteristic arises from seeing or the function arises from the substance.
Just as the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) and so forth arise from the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*), this case is also like that.
The Sūtra says:
"Furthermore, it is like a world adorned with various delightful gardens, groves, ponds, and so forth, which is exceedingly lovely and pleasing."

In this way, the Tathāgata’s wisdom of wondrous observation is adorned with various delightful perfections, factors of enlightenment, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and the unique buddha-qualities; it is exceedingly worthy of affection and joy.
The treatise says:
This passage demonstrates the characteristics of the causes for joy.
Just as the various delightful gardens, ponds, and so forth of the vessel-world (bhājana-loka), arranged in exquisite patterns with blazing majesty, cause all sentient beings to feel joy and delight.

In this way, the Tathāgata’s wisdom of wondrous observation—adorned with various delightful perfections (*pāramitā*), factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*), and so forth, arranged in a variegated display—blazes with majestic splendor, causing all bodhisattvas to feel joy and delight.
The pāramitās are briefly of six kinds, namely giving and so forth.
Alternatively, they may be expanded into ten by adding the four of skillful means, expediency, and so on.
Or again, they may be expanded into eighty-four thousand, as explained at length in the sūtras.
If categorized individually, their number is immeasurable.
The factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) are briefly thirty-seven, yet in detail they are also immeasurable.

As for the "ten powers" (*daśabala*), these refer to the power of knowing what is possible and impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñānabala*) and so forth; they are subsumed within the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*) in the body of a Tathāgata, as well as the faculty of one who has already attained full knowledge (*ājñātāvīndriya*).

Regarding "fearlessness," this refers to the four fearlessnesses, which are subsumed under the five faculties, as well as the faculty of one who has already known—all of which consist of the five beginning with faith.
There are eighteen kinds of unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*).

As explained at length in the sūtras, such qualities as these are for the most part subsumed within, associated with, and brought forth by this wisdom; therefore, all adornments are centered upon this wisdom.
The Sūtra says:

"Furthermore, it is like the world, with its continents, islands, sun and moon, the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, the Heaven of the Thirty-three, as well as the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, and the Brahmakāyika Heavens, all exquisitely adorned and arranged in succession."

In this way, the Tathāgata’s wisdom of wondrous observation—regarding the causes and effects of worldly and supramundane decline and prosperity—is perfectly realized without remainder by Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas, and is exquisitely arrayed as a wondrous ornament of observation.
The Commentary states:
This section demonstrates the characteristics of the causes of conceptual differentiation (*vikalpa*).
For example, within the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*), the infinite continents and so forth are exquisitely adorned and arranged in succession without being confused with one another.
"Continents" refers to the four great continents, namely Jambudvīpa and the others.
"Islands" refers to the eight small islands, namely Camara and the others.
By briefly mentioning the sun and moon, all the lunar mansions are included.
The Heaven of the Four Great Kings refers to the fourth tier of Mount Sumeru, where they each reside on one of its four sides.

The Heaven of the Thirty-three refers to the summit of this mountain, which has eight great heavenly kings on each of its four sides, with Śakra residing in the center; thus, it consists of this number.
As for the Yāma Heaven, it is so called because the gods therein experience pleasure according to the seasons; thus, it is named "Seasonal" (Kāmadhātu).
As for the Tuṣita Heaven, Bodhisattvas in their final birth teach and transform within it, and because they cultivate contentment and joy there, it is named "Contentment" (Tuṣita).
The gods of the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations (Nirmāṇarati) delight in their own emanations, creating various instruments of pleasure to amuse themselves.
The gods of the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Emanations (Paranirmita-vaśavartin) delight in causing others to emanate various instruments of pleasure, thereby manifesting their own mastery.

Regarding the Brahmakāyika devas: they are called "Brahma" because they have departed from desire and are tranquil; "kāya" means a multitude; and "equal" (samāna) refers to including all the heavens above them.

In this same way, the Tathāgata’s *pratyavekṣaṇājñāna* (wonderful investigative wisdom) is universally able to observe the causes and effects of decline and prosperity in both the mundane and supramundane realms, as well as the perfect realization of the three vehicles, which are exquisitely adorned and arranged in orderly succession without confusion.
The causes and effects of the miserable realms (durgati) are called the decline of the world, while the causes and effects of the happy realms (sugati) are called the prosperity of the world.
Furthermore, the destruction of the world and the formation of the world are respectively termed decline and prosperity.
Furthermore, diminution is called decline (*śīta*), and increase is called prosperity (*utsāha*).
The causes and fruits of the Two Vehicles are called worldly decline, while the causes and fruits of the Mahāyāna are called worldly prosperity.
Moreover, regression is called decline, and progress is called prosperity.
What is called "perfect realization" refers to the stage of fruition (*phala-avasthā*), whereas the names of the three preceding vehicles indicate their causal stages (*hetu-avasthā*).
Furthermore, "perfect realization" refers exclusively to the fruit of Buddhahood.

Because the wondrous discerning wisdom (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*) perceives that the characteristics (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*) of these various phenomena are distinct, the wisdom manifests clearly with its aspects (*ākāra*) unmixed, exactly as they are in the object; therefore, it is called "wondrously adorned and arrayed."
The Commentary on the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra*, Fascicle Five;
The Commentary on the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra*, Fascicle Six.
Composed by Bodhisattva Bandhuprabha and others.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang, by Imperial Decree.
The Sūtra says:
Furthermore, it is like the world, which serves as a vast resource for the enjoyment of all sentient beings.

In this way, the Tathāgata’s wisdom of wondrous observation manifests the assemblies of all Buddhas and rains down the great Dharma rain, in order to cause sentient beings to experience the great joy of the Dharma.
The Commentary states:
This passage demonstrates the characteristics of the causes for enjoyment.

Just as the physical world (bhājana-loka) arises through the predominant power of the karma of sentient beings, so too does the ālayavijñāna, by means of its seeds of common characteristics, transform and produce various common material requisites in order to enable sentient beings to experience them extensively.

In this way, the Tathāgata’s wisdom of wondrous observation acts as a dominant condition for the wisdom of equality, striking and activating the pure consciousness associated with the mirror-like wisdom. It manifests the various assemblies of the Enjoyment Body (*saṃbhogakāya*), whose majestic power is blazingly intense as it rains down the great Dharma rain, so that the great Bodhisattvas on the stages may experience the great joy of the Dharma; furthermore, it acts as a dominant condition for the Tathāgata’s wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done.

It activates the pure consciousness associated with the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*), manifesting various assemblies of transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) of blazing majesty that rain down the rain of the True Dharma, so that sentient beings to be converted prior to the stages may enjoy the bliss of the Dharma.
The Sūtra says: "Just as the five destinies are found within the world— namely, the realms of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, and devas— so too,
upon the Tathāgata’s wisdom of observation, the distinctions of the five destinies, with their boundless causes and effects, are fully manifested."
The Commentary states:
This passage demonstrates the characteristics of the causes for the differentiation of the realms of existence (*gati*).

Just as within the world, by the predominant power of the karma of sentient beings, the non-common seeds of the *ālayavijñāna* transform and give rise to the various differentiations of cause and effect within the five realms of existence, which are thus perceived.

In this way, the Tathāgata’s wisdom of wondrous observation takes the causes and effects of the five destinies as its object; therefore, it manifests appearing as the two distinct aspects of those causes and effects of the five destinies, yet it does not actually give rise to the five destinies.
The various classes of asuras are not fixed; they may be gods, ghosts, or even animals, and therefore they are not mentioned separately.
As for the cause of the five destinies, it refers to the intermediate state (antarābhava), because it serves as the means for entering those five destinies.
A "destination" (gati) is that which is to be reached; since the intermediate state (antarābhava) is that which reaches it, it is not subsumed under the destinations themselves.
However, when the four modes of birth (yoni) are established according to the classification of rebirth, the intermediate state is also included within the category of birth.
According to one interpretation, because there is the means (*upāya*) for proceeding toward a realm of existence (*gati*) within the state of becoming (*bhava*), it is said to be "within the realms.
The term "causes" here refers to karma, afflictions (*kleśa*), and so forth; the "fruits" are the five realms of existence.
As the Sūtra says:
Just as the realms of desire, form, and formlessness can be found within the world,
so too, upon the Tathāgata’s wisdom of observation, the infinite distinctions of the three realms, together with their causes and effects, are fully manifested.
The Commentary states:
This section demonstrates the characteristics of the causes for the differentiation of the realms (*dhātu*).

Just as within a world-system, by the predominant power of the karma of sentient beings, the seeds of both common and uncommon characteristics within the *ālayavijñāna* transform and give rise to the obtainable differentiations of cause and effect across the three realms.
In this context, "world" encompasses both the sentient and the insentient, namely the world of sentient beings (*sattvaloka*) and the physical receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*).

Were it otherwise, the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) would not be included therein; for that realm possesses only matter produced by meditative concentration (*samādhi*), lacking matter produced by karma and lacking spatial location.

Within the world-system, the three realms are established according to their respective natures: that is to say, within the container-world (*bhājana-loka*), there exists only the realm of desire-form (*kāmarūpa-dhātu*) consisting of both sentient and insentient entities.

Within the realm of sentient beings (*sattva-dhātu*), all three realms are present; however, it is only the realm of sentient beings that, by means of the container-world, sustains both the sentient and insentient realms, whereas the world of sentient beings itself can only sustain the realm of sentient beings.

In this way, the Tathāgata’s wisdom of wondrous observation takes the causes and effects of the three realms as its object; therefore, it manifests as the distinct characteristics of these two aspects—the causes and effects of the three realms—but it does not actually produce the causes and effects of the three realms, being similar to the two types of discrimination mentioned previously.

The meaning intended here is that because the wisdom of wondrous observation is universally able to observe all objects, it manifests everywhere as the various realms, destinies, and births, appearing as the causal and resultant characteristics of the mind, mental factors, and so forth, which are comprised within the maturation of the formations induced by afflictions and karma.

This refers to the *pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna* (the wisdom of profound discernment) that arises through the sovereign power of the *ādarśa-mahājñāna* (the great mirror-like wisdom) of all Tathāgatas. Although it is devoid of any grasping at subject or object, because it is far removed from the two obscurations of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the cognizable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), it discerns all matters such as causes and effects and is capable of teaching them. Just as a pure, circular mirror manifests a multitude of images, all objective phenomena appear within it; yet, there is no fault of non-differentiation in the mirror-wisdom.
Because the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom is not ignorant regarding anything, it manifests all images and functions spontaneously, yet remains free from conceptual discrimination.

This wisdom is able to manifest the appearances of all objects and also possesses discrimination; if it were without discrimination, it would be unable to contemplate matters such as cause and effect, nor could it preach the Dharma to assemblies to sever their doubts.
