Since these factors such as attachment, aversion, and ignorance are subsumed under the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*), the analytical investigation of the two types of grasping occurs solely within the sixth and seventh consciousnesses.

If attachment, aversion, and so forth are not subsumed under views, they also exist within the five sensory consciousnesses when they do not involve investigative inquiry; furthermore, the essential nature of the afflictive hindrances, such as the various forms of self-grasping, exists only within the two types of mind that are either unwholesome or obscured-neutral.

If the essence of the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), such as the attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*), also exists within the mind that is non-obscured and indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta-citta*), this is because they still manifest even in the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) of the two vehicles.
Within the stage of no-more-learning, there are no unwholesome states or obscured-indeterminate states; therefore, from the perspective of the two vehicles, these are termed "non-obscured."
If one regards the bodhisattva [obscuration] as being defiled, it is also called "obstructed" (nivṛta).

Therefore, the cognitive obscuration (jñeyāvaraṇa) is both called "unobstructed" (anivṛta) and "obstructed"; these two names refer to a single entity, distinguished only by the perspective from which they are viewed.

Within the afflictive obscuration (kleśāvaraṇa) there exists the cognitive obscuration (jñeyāvaraṇa), because it serves as its basis; for one must necessarily grasp at phenomena and conceive of a self.

Although their essence is not two, their functions are distinct. Just as a single consciousness-essence has multiple functions in apprehending objects, so too the essence of a single seed produced by this perfuming has multiple functions.
Although they arise simultaneously, they are abandoned sequentially because the power of the noble path has specific limits.

If the cognitive obstacles (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) are said, with respect to the two vehicles, to be non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*), among the four types of neutral states, under which category are they subsumed?
It is comprised within that which is born of maturation (*vipākaja*), because it arises from the maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*). If so, what is not born of maturation?

Like the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*), all that is not included elsewhere is included herein; furthermore, because minds such as those of deportment (*airyāpathika*) lack firm attachment, are not universal (*sarvatraga*), and do not possess the nature of the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*).
If there were no grasping at phenomena within virtuous or non-obscured neutral states of mind, how could one fail to realize the emptiness of phenomena?
Likewise, if there were no grasping at a self, how could one fail to realize the emptiness of persons?
Since this [ignorance] does not realize the emptiness of persons because it coexists with the grasping at a self within the seventh consciousness,
it should likewise not realize the emptiness of phenomena because it coexists with the grasping at phenomena within the seventh consciousness.
If one does not realize the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), [consciousness] arises as if consisting of the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) and the subjective aspect (*darśana-bhāga*).
Why, then, is this not termed being subsumed under the grasping to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*)?
Furthermore, the untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas also possesses these two aspects; why is it not considered grasping?
Therefore, the object-aspect (*nimittabhāga*) and the subject-aspect (*darśanabhāga*) of dependently arisen phenomena are subsumed under the dependent nature (*paratantrasvabhāva*).
If one falsely imagines that these exist externally to the mind or as having a fixed intrinsic nature, it is only then termed "clinging" (*abhiniveśa*).

Therefore, as for the cognitive hindrance (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) residing in the seventh consciousness, it is universally associated with the minds of the three natures across the six consciousnesses; it is not of the nature of a mental concomitant (*saṃprayukta*).
Let us cease this extensive debate and proceed to explain the main text.

Regarding the characteristic of purity: it means that this true suchness (tathatā) is pure by nature, yet it is obscured by the two hindrances; thus, it is impure in a manner similar to how the pure sky is obscured by smoke, clouds, and the like.

Having attained the supramundane path that realizes *tathatā*, one gradually eliminates all seeds of the two obstacles, just as a great wind disperses smoke and clouds. When the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) manifests, all seeds of the obstacles are extinguished and abandoned, and one attains the ultimate transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) within the pure *dharmadhātu*; this is termed the "characteristic of purity."
Thus, the pure dharma-realm among the aforementioned five dharmas has been revealed.

According to one interpretation, this reveals the aspect of purity of the self-nature portion of the dharma-realm; that is, it is the self-nature portion among the six aspects, the text of which is explained as before.
The Sūtra says:
"Dharma-knowledge has that as its object; it is characterized by mastery and inexhaustibility.
The Commentary says:

There is an interpretation that this reveals the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom as the "Dharma-wisdom" because it takes the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature) as its object; thus, the Mirror Wisdom is called "Dharma-wisdom.
Furthermore, the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom also takes conventional *paratantra-svabhāva* as its object, because it manifests its images and is not deluded regarding them.

Regarding the phrase "that which has it as its object" (*tad-ālambana*): "that" refers to *tathatā* (suchness), not to the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*). Although there is a separation of phrases, the logical force of the meaning remains consistent; therefore, there is no fault.

Because the knowledge of phenomena takes that [suchness] as its object, it is called "having that as its object"; it does not mean that the knowledge of phenomena itself is the object of that [suchness].

The Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) also takes the ultimate perfected nature (*pariniṣpannasvabhāva*) as its object, because it internally realizes that [nature] until the very limit of saṃsāra.

This teaching states that mirror wisdom takes all phenomena—both their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*)—as its objects, since both the dependent nature (*paratantrasvabhāva*) and the perfected nature serve as its objective spheres. As for the imagined nature (*parikalpitasvabhāva*), it is merely what is reckoned by the deluded minds of ordinary beings; it is not the sphere of noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*), and therefore it is not said to be taken as an object.

As stated in the treatise: the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is the object only of ordinary cognition; the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is the object only of noble cognition; and the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is the object of both ordinary and noble cognition. Because the thoroughly imagined nature lacks any intrinsic substance, it is not realized by the noble ones.
If that were so, noble wisdom would not know all things; since it would then be non-cognition, what could it possibly know?
If it were to know them as existing, it would constitute a cognitive inversion.

If it were to know them as non-existent, then they would not be manifestations of the mind as the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*); they would not be subsumed under the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), and the principle of suchness (*tathatā*) would not be subsumed under the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).

Therefore, although noble wisdom knows both existence and non-existence, it does not take them as its object; that is, it does not take the nature of the thoroughly imagined (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) as its objective sphere.

As for "sovereignty," because it is accomplished through the cultivation of the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom and the six *pāramitās*, it possesses the ten sovereignties with unimpeded and wondrous function.
The characteristic of inexhaustibility means that it reaches the limit of birth and death, being a continuous succession without interval or interruption.
"Characteristic" refers either to the characterized or to the characterizer, as it manifests its own essence.
Thus, this collectively reveals the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) among the aforementioned five dharmas.

According to one interpretation, this reveals a portion of its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); that is, the four wisdoms of the Buddha-fruit constitute a portion of the intrinsic nature within the six aspects (*ṣaḍlakṣaṇa*).

The conditioned meritorious dharmas are precisely the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*). By the power of its antidote, it transforms and eliminates the *ālayavijñāna*, which is the basis of all coarse heaviness (*dausthulya*), and instead attains the purified dependent nature (*paratantrasvabhāva*). It is utterly free from all mental deliberation and discrimination; the equality between the object of cognition and the cognizing subject is perfectly uniform and ineffable.

The nature of dependently arisen phenomena neither increases nor decreases; the mode of internal realization can manifest the images of all phenomena, for it universally illuminates and understands all objects without conceptual discrimination.

That which is collectively termed "Dharma-knowledge" (dharma-jñāna) is precisely the Wisdom of Equality (samatā-jñāna). By the power of its antidote, it transforms and eliminates the seventh manas-consciousness that clings to sentient beings and phenomena; it subsequently attains the pure dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva), which serves as the basis for the Mirror-like Wisdom (ādarśa-jñāna) and the others, and is equal and identical with the Pure Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu). Because its mode of internal realization is such, it is called "wisdom."

That which is the object of focus consists of the other two types of wisdom; through the power of their antidotes, they eliminate the worldly conceptualization of the six consciousnesses and transform into the purified dependent nature, whether supramundane or both mundane and supramundane.

That subsequently attained [knowledge] takes the suchness of the higher realms and the dharma-knowledge as its object; it has the dependent nature as its sphere of activity, and while non-conceptual, it appears as if it were an object of cognition, distinguishing within itself between the realized and the realizer.
Because it takes as its object the aforementioned true suchness (*tathatā*) and the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), it is called "that which has that as its object.
Thus, because these four knowledges function with wondrous and unimpeded efficacy, they are termed "sovereign" (*vaśitā*).
Because it functions incessantly until the very limit of birth and death, it is called "inexhaustible.
Because the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom and the Wisdom of Equality are constantly uninterrupted, they are called "inexhaustible."

Although the wisdom of wondrous observation and the wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done are subject to interruption, they can manifest as soon as one briefly directs the attention toward them; because they arise repeatedly without end, they are also called inexhaustible.

The "characteristics" refer to the essential natures (lakṣaṇa), all of which arise from conditions; these are termed the pure *paratantra-svabhāva*. Because they are entirely free from inversion, they are termed "pure.
All [aspects of] the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* are internally realized; its function of illuminating objects manifests as if it were the object itself, and this is termed "wisdom" (*jñāna*).
Such meanings as these can manifest its own essence; therefore, they are called "characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*).
The Sūtra says:
"The wisdom of universal *tathatā*, through cultivation, is realized in perfection."
The Commentary states:

According to one interpretation, this reveals the wisdom of equality (*samatā-jñāna*). That is to say, at the time of the first clear realization (*abhisamaya*) within the first stage (*bhūmi*), one attains this non-conceptual wisdom of equality and contemplates the equality of all things, such as *tathatā* (suchness).

Thereafter, through gradual cultivation across the successive stages (*bhūmi*), it becomes increasingly superior and increasingly pure, until at the stage of Buddhahood one realizes perfect and ultimate purity. One realizes that all phenomena and principles, such as the *dharmadhātu*, are entirely equal. In this way, the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*) among the five preceding dharmas is revealed.

There is an interpretation that this reveals the characteristic of the cause among the six [characteristics]. That is to say, within the first stage (*bhūmi*), non-conceptual wisdom contemplates the first *dharmadhātu* during the three moments of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*). It abandons the one hundred and twelve root afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) to be abandoned by the path of seeing, as well as extinguishing the coarsest portion of the non-afflicted ignorance (*akliṣṭājñāna*) and the conceptual grasping at phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) to be abandoned by the path of seeing; thereby, it manifests the increase of the seeds of wisdom regarding the first *dharmadhātu*.

From this point onward, throughout all stages during the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), non-conceptual wisdom contemplates the suchness (*tathatā*) of the remaining dharma-realm. Through the stages of application—such as the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation, as well as skillful means—one gradually practices these in succession. In this manner, according to what is appropriate, one gradually subdues the sixteen afflictions and secondary afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation, and accordingly, one gradually eliminates the innate grasping at phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) associated with non-afflicted ignorance (*akliṣṭājñāna*) that is to be abandoned through cultivation.

The remaining portions manifest the growth of the seeds of wisdom regarding the other dharmadhātus; with this as the cause, one attains the perfection of the four wisdoms of the dharmadhātu up to the stage of Buddhahood.
The Sūtra says:
"It establishes two kinds of sentient beings, with inexhaustible results for all their various seeds.
The Commentary says:

There is an interpretation that this reveals the wisdom of wondrous observation (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*); that is to say, because this wondrous wisdom can preach the sublime Dharma and so forth for sentient beings, establishing them in benefit and happiness, it is called "the two."
These two types consist of many varieties; therefore, they are called "various kinds.
Since these two matters persist until the very limit of saṃsāra and function constantly without interruption, they are said to be "inexhaustible."
This is precisely what is called "fruit," because it is the fruit of wisdom.
In this way, the *pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna* (wisdom of wondrous observation) among the first five dharmas is revealed.

According to another interpretation, this reveals the characteristic of the fruit within the [six]fold set—namely, that both the *dharmadhātu* (pure dharma-realm) and the four wondrous wisdoms are all capable of establishing all sentient beings in benefit and peace.
Causing one to cultivate wholesome causes is called "benefit"; causing one to obtain pleasant fruits is called "peace and happiness.
Furthermore, causing one to abandon evil is called "benefit"; causing one to embrace what is wholesome is called "peace and happiness."
Furthermore, extracting their suffering is called "benefit" (*hitā*), and bestowing happiness upon them is called "well-being" (*sukha*).

This should be understood to apply likewise to this world and other worlds, as well as to worldly and transcendent matters. Because these categories are manifold, they are termed "various kinds" (*nānāvidha*); because they extend to the limits of the future, they are termed "inexhaustible" (*akṣaya*).
These two matters consist of inexhaustible seeds, for they arise from the pure dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) and the fruits of the four wisdoms (*caturjñāna*).
As the Sūtra says:
"The emanations of body, speech, and mind are the activities of skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*)."

The Commentary states: According to one interpretation, this reveals the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is to Be Done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*). That is to say, this wisdom is able to manifest transformations of body, speech, and mind; because it accords with the capacities and needs of sentient beings, it is called "skillful" (*kauśalya*); because its preparatory application (*prayoga*) is uninterrupted, it is called "expedient means" (*upāya*); and this is precisely what is termed "activity" (*karman*).

Alternatively, this wisdom, through its skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), is able to give rise to the three types of transformative activity of body, speech, and mind; in this way, it demonstrates the wisdom of accomplishment (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*) among the aforementioned five dharmas.

There is an interpretation that this reveals the functional characteristics (*karmalakṣaṇa*) among the six [qualities]: namely, that the pure dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) and the four sublime wisdoms (*prajñā*) are able to give rise to the three types of transformative activity (*nirmāṇakarma*) of body, speech, and mind, as well as the activities of skillful means (*kauśalya*) and expedient methods (*upāya*).
The Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is to Be Done gives rise to the three types of transformative activities of body, speech, and mind;
the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation gives rise to skillful activities, because it observes the capacities and requirements of beings with extreme dexterity;
and the remaining two wisdoms, along with the Pure Dharma Realm, give rise to expedient activities, because they spontaneously serve as the means for all activities.
The transformation of the body is of three kinds:

first, correspondence with one's own body, which refers to transforming one's own body into various forms such as a universal monarch (cakravartin), as well as manifesting various past-life stories (jātaka);

second, correspondence with the bodies of others, which refers to transforming the Māra king into the body of a Buddha, or changing Śāriputra into a celestial maiden (*devakanyā*), manifesting various transformed forms by means of the bodies of others.

Third, non-embodied manifestation: this refers to manifesting the great earth as the seven precious jewels and so forth, or manifesting immeasurable transformation bodies of Buddhas and so forth, or emitting light that illuminates boundless realms.

Such categories as these—manifesting emanations distinct from one's own or another's body in various forms of sentient and insentient matter, shaking the earth, emitting light, and producing wind and fragrance—are all for the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness to sentient beings; thus, they are all termed the Buddha’s activity of emanation-body (nirmāṇakāya-karman).
Thus, emanated speech also has three types:

first, that which corresponds to one's own body, meaning the Buddha’s own body manifests the Brahma-voice to universally proclaim throughout boundless worlds and so forth—this constitutes various vocal activities;

second, that which corresponds to another's body, meaning causing the great disciples among the śrāvakas and others to proclaim the profound Dharma of the Mahāyāna using the Buddha’s Brahma-voice; therefore, when śrāvakas and bodhisattvas preach the profound and wondrous Dharma that is not within their own domain, it is entirely the work of the Tathāgata’s transformations and is not produced by their own power.

Third, those not associated with the body: this refers to the transformation of mountains, seas, grasses, trees, and other such things, even up to empty space, which also produce sounds to preach the Great Dharma and so forth; all such instances are termed the vocal karma of transformation.

The transformation of the mind consists of only two types: first, that which is associated with one’s own body, meaning the manifestation upon one's own mind of various distinct images of minds and mental factors; second, that which is associated with the bodies of others, meaning causing the minds of others to likewise manifest various distinct images of minds and mental factors. Both of these are aspects of the perceived (nimitta-bhāga) appearing as if they were the aspect of the perceiver (darśana-bhāga).
There is an interpretation that the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) can cause one's own mind to understand phenomena that are not its natural domain;

this is called "transforming one's own mind. To empower sentient beings such that those who are ignorant understand profound and subtle teachings, and those who have lost mindfulness attain right recollection—this is called "transforming the minds of others."
However, the mind itself cannot be transformed, because it lacks form and substance.
As the treatise states: "Because the mind has no form, it cannot be transformed.

Furthermore, it is said that the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) is devoid of mind and mental factors; this is spoken with reference to the meditative power of the two vehicles and ordinary beings, for their meditative power is inferior and cannot manifest phenomena that lack form and substance.
The inconceivable samādhis of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are capable of manifesting transformations.
If this were not so, how could the Tathāgata manifest greed, anger, and the like?
And how could śrāvakas, animals, and others perceive the mind of the Tathāgata?
How is it that the sūtras state that the emanated beings of immeasurable kinds are all endowed with minds?
How is it that the aforementioned [passage] speaks of the mental karma (*manas-karman*) of these emanations?
And how is it that the sūtras state that there is reliance upon the mind of another?

However, while all manifested forms (nirmāṇa-rūpa) function identically to real forms, the manifested sense organs (indriya) and mind merely manifest their appearances and do not function as actual entities; furthermore, this statement is made from the perspective of the lower classes [of beings].
If that is so, why does one not transform insentient things to cause mental images to appear?
Since insentient things are already the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) of the mind and its associates, how could one further cause mental images to appear within them?

If the mental aspect manifests, it is termed a sentient being and is not subsumed under the category of non-sentient things; therefore, the transformative mind (*nirmāṇacitta*) is said to be of only two kinds.

As previously stated, the *pratyavekṣaṇājñāna* (wisdom of profound observation) is able to observe the *dhāraṇī*-gates and *samādhis* of self-realization, and is able to observe the faculties, inclinations, and dispositions of sentient beings; its skillful activity in preaching the medicine of the sublime Dharma is called "skillful activity" (*kauśalyakarma*). The other two wisdoms and the pure *dharmadhātu* serve as the basis for all virtuous qualities and are able to initiate various activities that benefit sentient beings; this is called "expedient activity" (*upāyakarma*).
The Sūtra says:
"Samādhi and the gateways of dhāraṇī constitute the two boundless accomplishments.
The Commentary says:
One interpretation holds that this reveals the qualities of the retinue subsumed within the four wisdoms (*jñāna*).

Another interpretation holds that this reveals the aspect of association (*samprayukta-lakṣaṇa*) among the six aspects; the "gateways of meditative concentration" (*samādhi-mukha*) refers specifically to the eighty-four thousand gateways of *samādhi*.
The gateways of dhāraṇī refer to the eighty-four thousand dhāraṇī gateways.

These two types [of gateways] universally give rise to all conditioned merits, universally manifest all unconditioned merits, and universally induce all supernatural powers and activities to benefit sentient beings; therefore, they are called "gateways."

Regarding the "two kinds of boundlessness": these are the two types of adornment, merit and wisdom. Within them, there are immeasurable varieties of distinction; because they consist of eighty-four thousand [types of] merit and wisdom, or are accomplished through cultivation over immeasurable eons, they are called "boundless."

The first five pāramitās are termed merit (puṇya), while the latter five pāramitās are termed wisdom (prajñā); alternatively, each one, whether by its essential nature or its retinue, may possess both as appropriate.

Thus, these two gates and two kinds of adornment are each fully present within the four categories of wisdom; they are constantly in mutual association and likewise rely upon the pure *dharmadhātu*, never being separated from it. Therefore, they are called "accomplished."
The Sūtra says:
"The self-nature, the enjoyment, and the transformation [bodies] function through their distinctions.
The Commentary says:
One interpretation holds that this reveals the distinctions among the three bodies as they are constituted by five factors.

Another interpretation holds that this reveals the specific characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) among the six kinds of characteristics; for although there is no difference in the essential nature of the purified *dharmadhātu* upon which all Tathāgatas rely, there are various differences in the characteristics of the three bodies and different modes of transformation, and thus they are called "distinctions."
As for the *svabhāva-dharma*, it refers to the Tathāgata’s original *svabhāva-kāya*, which is eternal and unchanging; therefore, it is called "self-nature" (*svabhāva*).
Because it is the basis upon which all meritorious qualities such as the powers (*bala*) and fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*) rely, it is also called the "Dharmakāya."
Enjoyment refers to the second, the Enjoyment Body (*saṃbhogakāya*), because it enables both oneself and others to enjoy the manifold great joy of the Dharma.

Transformation refers to the third, the Transformation Body (*nirmāṇakāya*), because, for the sake of benefiting and bringing peace and happiness to sentient beings, it manifests various kinds of transformative deeds.
The meanings of essence (*tattva*), basis (*āśraya*), and the accumulation of manifold virtues (*guṇa-saṃcaya*) are collectively termed "body" (*kāya*).
This is a brief explanation of the names and meanings of the three bodies (*trikāya*).

Furthermore, the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) has ultimate transformation-basis (*parāvṛtti-āśraya*) and suchness (*tathatā*) as its characteristic; it is the equal basis of all Buddha-dharmas, capable of giving rise to all sovereign activities, and is manifested through the predominance of all pure dharmas (*śukla-dharma*). It is the equal nature of all Tathāgatas, subtle and difficult to fathom, wherein all conceptualization is extinguished and all discursive proliferation (*prapañca*) is cut off.

Therefore, the Sūtra says: "The Dharma-body of all Buddhas should not be sought through discursive thought; it is not an object of discursive thought, transcending all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) of thought. As for the Enjoyment Body (*saṃbhogakāya*), its characteristic is the perfection of all merits.

It is collectively integrated by all Buddha-dharmas, capable of initiating all sovereign activities, and arises through the predominance of all pure dharmas (*śukladharma*). The individual essence of each Tathāgata is subtle and difficult to fathom; dwelling in the purely pure lands, it is spontaneously and serenely present until the end of the future, enjoying the bliss of the Dharma for itself. It manifests various forms and preaches various teachings, causing the great Bodhisattvas likewise to enjoy the bliss of the Dharma.

The transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is characterized by the perfection of all miraculous transformations; it is the collective integration of all transformative functions, manifesting all sovereign activities. It is induced by the predominance of all pure qualities (*śukladharma*), and its individual transformative functions of all Tathāgatas are subtle and difficult to fathom. Dwelling in both pure and impure lands, it manifests in various forms and teaches various dharmas to mature bodhisattvas of lower stages, followers of the two vehicles, and ordinary beings, causing them to enter the great stages (*mahābhūmi*), transcend the three realms, and escape all evil destinies. This is a brief explanation of the characteristics and functions of the three bodies.

Furthermore, regarding how the first five dharmas subsume the three bodies (*trikāya*), there is an interpretation that the first two subsume the *svābhāvikakāya* (self-nature body), the middle two types subsume the *sambhogakāya* (enjoyment body), and the *kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna* (wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done) subsumes the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body); this is because the sūtras state that suchness (*tathatā*) is the *dharmakāya*.

The treatise states that the transformation of the *ālaya-vijñāna* results in the attainment of the *svābhāvika-kāya* (self-nature body), and that the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*) is attained through the transformation of the eighth consciousness; therefore, it is known that the first two [wisdoms] subsume the self-nature body.

This sutra states that the wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done (kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna) initiates various transformative activities (*nirmāṇa-karma*). The *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra* states that the wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done initiates all manner of diverse, immeasurable, and inconceivable transformative deeds within all realms. Therefore, it is known that the latter [wisdom] subsumes the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
The Wisdom of Equality is as described in other treatises: it is able to manifest various Buddha-bodies in pure lands according to the inclinations of the bodhisattvas.
The Wisdom of Wondrous Observation is also as described in the treatises: within great assemblies, it can manifest all sovereign activities, preaching the Dharma and severing doubts.

Furthermore, it is said that by transforming and eliminating the various evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*), one attains the Enjoyment Body (*saṃbhogakāya*); thus, we know that the middle two [of the three bodies] subsume the Enjoyment Body.
Moreover, since all three bodies of the Buddha are subsumed within the excellence of wisdom among the ten meanings, we know that all three bodies possess wisdom.

There is another interpretation: the first [of the four bodies] comprises the *svābhāvika-kāya* (self-nature body), which is the common basis associated with the nature of the four wisdoms; that which manifests as a subtle aspect for Bodhisattvas on the stages (*bhūmi*) comprises the *saṃbhoga-kāya* (enjoyment body);
and that which manifests as a coarse aspect for Bodhisattvas prior to the stages and others comprises the *nirmāṇa-kāya* (emanation body).
This is because all sutras state that pure *tathatā* (suchness) constitutes the *dharmakāya*;
the *Buddhastotra-śāstra* states that the Tathāgata’s *dharmakāya* is without arising or cessation;
and the *Mahāyāna-sūtrālaṃkāra-śāstra* states that the Buddha’s essential body (*svabhāvakāya*) is eternal by nature.
The *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-śāstra* explains the merit of upholding and expounding that sūtra:
it serves as the cause for realizing the Buddha-dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), and as the cause for generating the other two bodies (*rūpakāya*).

Various sūtras and śāstras state that ultimate transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) constitutes the dharmakāya; since this transformation of the basis is pure suchness (viśuddha-tathatā) rather than the path of antidotes, it is known that the dharmakāya has only the pure dharma-dhātu and suchness as its nature.
The *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra* states that the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom is the Enjoyment Buddha (*saṃbhogakāya*).
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states that by transforming the various evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*), one attains the Enjoyment Body.

However, regarding the statement that by transforming and eliminating the *ālayavijñāna* one attains the *dharmakāya*, this refers to the transformation and elimination of the seeds of the two obstacles within the eighth consciousness, thereby manifesting the pure *dharmakāya* as the basis for reliance; it does not refer to the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*), because the mirror-like wisdom is said to be the *saṃbhogakāya*.
Furthermore, the enjoyment body (saṃbhogakāya) is briefly of two kinds:
first, the self-enjoyment [body], which is produced through cultivation over three incalculable eons;
second, the other-enjoyment [body], which exists for the sake of enabling all bodhisattvas to experience the joy of the Dharma.
Therefore, the four wisdoms, together with their associated mental factors and a portion of their transformations, constitute the Enjoyment Body (*saṃbhogakāya*).

The sūtras and śāstras all state that the Transformation Body (*nirmāṇakāya*) manifests various forms for the sake of transforming sentient beings who have not yet reached the stages prior to the first bhūmi.
Since this is the realm of sentient beings prior to the stages [of the bodhisattva], it is known that these are not true merits, but rather merely transformative functions (*nirmāṇa-karma*).

The sūtras and śāstras state only that the *kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna* (all-accomplishing wisdom) can initiate transformative activities, but is not itself the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*). Although the three bodies are subsumed under the excellence of wisdom—since the *dharmakāya* is the basis upon which wisdom relies for realization, and the *nirmāṇakāya* is the function initiated by wisdom—it is metaphorically called "wisdom" because it appears as if it were wisdom; there is no fault in this.
Since the bodies of enjoyment and transformation of these three types of bodies are subject to arising and ceasing, why do the sūtras state that the bodies of all Buddhas are eternal?
It is because the *dharmakāya*, which is the basis upon which those two depend, is eternal.

Furthermore, although the Enjoyment Body (*saṃbhogakāya*) and the Transformation Body (*nirmāṇakāya*) undergo arising and ceasing, they are said to be "constant" because they perpetually enjoy various dharma-pleasures without cessation or interruption, and because they repeatedly manifest transformations throughout the worlds of the ten directions without end—just as one constantly enjoys pleasure or constantly bestows food. Thus, they are designated as "constant."
The *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra* states that there are three kinds of permanence:
first, natural permanence, which refers to the *svabhāvakāya*, because this body is eternally abiding by its very nature;
second, uninterrupted permanence, which refers to the *saṃbhogakāya*, because it constantly experiences the joy of the Dharma without interruption.
Third, permanence of continuity refers to the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body), because after it has vanished, it manifests again, and its emanations are inexhaustible.
Thus, although the *dharmakāya* is free from all conceptual proliferation and discursive thought (*prapañca*) and is without arising or ceasing, it is therefore said to be permanent.

Although the two bodies undergo moment-to-moment arising and ceasing, they are called "permanent" because they rely upon the eternal body without interruption and because they are perpetually continuous.

The sūtras state that all dharmas of the Tathāgata, such as form (*rūpa*) and sensation (*vedanā*), are eternally abiding; this is based on the following principles: [the two bodies] are not devoid of arising and ceasing, because they are produced from the cultivation and growth of untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*); because it is categorically taught that "whatever arises must cease"; because both form and mind are seen to be impermanent; and because a permanently abiding form or mind has never been perceived.
Regarding these three bodies, what are their dimensions?

The Dharma-body has pure *tathatā* (suchness) as its essence; since *tathatā* is the true nature of all phenomena (*dharmas*), and phenomena are without limit, the Dharma-body is likewise so—it pervades all phenomena, existing nowhere it is not present.
It is like space, for which one cannot describe its shape or magnitude; yet, in terms of its characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), it pervades all places.

As for the Enjoyment Body (*saṃbhogakāya*), it consists of both form and non-form. Because non-form phenomena lack physical substance, their shape and magnitude likewise cannot be described; however, in terms of its supporting body and its objects of knowledge, it may be said to pervade all places.
Form is of two kinds:
first, substantial form;
second, transformed form.

Regarding "actual form" (bhūta-rūpa): through the cultivation and realization of karma pertaining to the physical body, its marks, and signs over three incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), one transforms the impure physical body consisting of the five sense faculties and so forth, and attains the Buddha’s pure form consisting of the five sense faculties and so forth, which are untainted (*anāsrava*). Adorned with immeasurable marks and signs, that body pervades the entire Dharma-realm and is called the truly pure land.
Within the cycle of birth and death, the extent of karma is limited; however, the size of the physical body manifested by the ālayavijñāna is not fixed.
For instance, in this world, the people of Jambudvīpa possess the least superior wholesome karma, and their physical bodies reach a maximum length of four cubits (*hasta*).
Those of Pūrvavideha possess the next most superior wholesome karma, and their bodies are eight cubits long.

As these wholesome karmas gradually increase and become more excellent, the dimensions of the resulting physical body gradually grow larger, reaching even the Akaniṣṭha Heaven of the Form Realm; because it is the most preeminent among karmas that induce form, the resulting physical body measures sixteen thousand *yojanas*.
Because they are nourished and perfumed by the untainted roots of goodness of a Bodhisattva on the tenth stage, their physical forms become increasingly vast, as explained in detail in the sutras.

When the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) manifests, all hindrances are extinguished; because the power and capacity of these roots of goodness are boundless, the attained form-body fills the Dharma-realm and pervades the truly pure lands.

Because the bodies and lands manifested by the pure consciousness associated with the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) are limitless, the manifestations of the consciousnesses of all Buddhas occur in the same place and at the same time;

their characteristics are similar and do not obstruct one another, continuing without interval or interruption until the end of the future. Based on this, it enables all Buddhas to experience vast great joy and bliss; therefore, it is called the "Enjoyment Body and Land" (*saṃbhogakāya-bhūmi*).

Such bodies and lands are known only by the Buddhas; they are not realized by the five sense faculties of bodhisattvas, because each individual material faculty can realize all perceived objects without obstruction. Therefore, the Buddhas possess the mark of the invisible crown of the head and boundless Dharma-sounds, for the functions of all their material faculties are infinite due to their pervasive nature.

Regarding "transformed form" (*nairmāṇika-rūpa*): by the power of compassion and vows, for the sake of entering the stages of the great bodhisattvas, various bodies, various marks and signs, and various voices are manifested, depending on various lands with indefinite dimensions and proportions.

Regarding the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*): it is likewise through the power of compassion and vows that, for the sake of transforming sentient beings prior to the stages [of the bodhisattva path], the transformation body is manifested. It encompasses both the material and the non-material; the non-material refers to the mental karma of the transformation, as well as the characteristics of various merits such as the powers (*bala*) and fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), which, being devoid of physical substance, have no spatial dimensions. The material refers to the bodily and vocal karma of the transformation body, which—according to the time, place, and what is appropriate for the assembly—manifests in bodily forms of indefinite size, as explained at length in the sūtras.
Regarding these three bodies, are all Tathāgatas distinct or non-distinct?

Since the true nature of the Dharma-body is common to all Tathāgatas, there is no distinction; however, because there are distinctions in the causes by which they are realized, one speaks of distinctions as a conventional designation.

The remaining two bodies each have distinct causes for their arising and distinct intrinsic natures; while they truly possess differences, there is no attachment to them as being separate. Because they occupy the same location, share similar intentions for the benefit and happiness of others, and are equal in their activities, they are said to be without distinction.

Therefore, it is said that all Buddhas are without distinction in their three bodies according to their respective order, by virtue of their basis, their intention, and their activity: because the *dharmadhātu* which is their basis is without distinction, because their intention for the benefit and happiness [of beings] is without distinction, and because their shared performance of activities is without distinction.
Do these three bodies each possess distinct qualities?

The *dharmakāya* of the Tathāgata has the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*) of pure *tathatā* as its characteristic. It is a truly existent good, intrinsically pure, and because it is free from all defiled phenomena, because it is the support for all qualities, and because it is the true nature of all qualities, it is said to be "endowed with all qualities. However, there are no qualities characterized by the distinctions of form or mind.

The Buddha’s Enjoyment Body (*saṃbhogakāya*) is fully endowed with the true merits of all phenomena, such as form and mind, as well as the merit of manifesting transformational appearances for the sake of others.
The Buddha’s Transformation Body (*nirmāṇakāya*) possesses only the merit of manifesting all transformational appearances of form, mind, and so forth.
Therefore, it is said that all three bodies possess merits numbering more than the sands of the Ganges.
Are the sentient beings transformed by all Tathāgatas common [to one another] or uncommon?

There is an interpretation that they are all shared, because each and every Buddha is capable of transforming and delivering all sentient beings; their merit and wisdom are entirely equal, as they have diligently practiced and cultivated vows for three incalculable eons, seeking bodhi equally for the sake of rescuing all sentient beings. As it is said: "The sentient beings transformed by one Buddha are those transformed by all Buddhas."

There is an interpretation that [this power] is not shared [with others], because the various sentient beings transformed by the Buddha are fundamentally interconnected. For this reason, during the time of Tiṣya Buddha, the Tathāgata and Maitreya were once fellow disciples. The Buddha perceived that the roots of goodness among the beings to be transformed by Śākya would ripen first, while those to be transformed by Maitreya would ripen later; furthermore, he perceived that Maitreya’s causal practices would be fulfilled first, while Śākya’s would be fulfilled later. Consequently, at one location, he entered the fire-light samādhi and allowed Śākya to behold him. For seven days and seven nights, without setting down a single foot, Śākya offered praise in a single verse, thereby enabling him to surpass Maitreya and attain Buddhahood first.
Furthermore, when the Buddha was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he spoke these words:
"Those whom I was to deliver have all been delivered.
Moreover, a sūtra states:

"When the Buddha was about to enter nirvana, he observed a disciple who was currently in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana) and was destined to be born in this world to receive the Buddha's transformation. He therefore left behind a transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) to dwell secretly within this realm, while his previously received body manifested entry into nirvana."

Having passed away from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and been reborn here, he was taught the sublime Dharma by a transformation body left behind by the Buddha and attained arhatship; at that moment, the transformation body then vanished and became invisible.
Furthermore, it is taught throughout various sūtras that the relationship between the transformer and the transformed is fixed; therefore, the transformations performed by the Buddhas are unique.
According to the true meaning, however, there are both common and uncommon [transformations].

Since beginningless time, the spiritual lineages (*gotra*) have been naturally and mutually interconnected; that is, many may belong to one, or one may belong to many. Furthermore, when Bodhisattvas bring sentient beings to maturity during their causal stage, this is not fixed—it may be common or uncommon. Therefore, once they have attained Buddhahood, they may transform and deliver beings either collectively or individually.
If those beings to be converted were exclusively common [to all Buddhas], what need would there be for many Buddhas?

Since a single Buddha could convert all beings, only one Buddha should remain eternally in the world to teach and transform sentient beings, while all other Buddhas should enter eternal quiescence. Furthermore, a Buddha should not convert other sentient beings to lead them toward the Mahāyāna, as that would be useless; instead, he should only convert them to attain the three vehicles and enter eternal quiescence, as that is easier to achieve.
What wise person would abandon what is easy to pursue what is difficult, or light a lamp to assist the sun?
Therefore, those who are to be converted are not exclusively common [to all Buddhas].

If those to be converted were exclusively uncommon [to other Buddhas], Bodhisattvas would not have generated great vows to serve various Buddhas and study the Mahāyāna; Sudhana and others likewise would not have served many spiritual friends; and Buddhas would not have entrusted their own disciples to subsequent Buddhas. Since such matters would all be contradictory, it cannot be that they are exclusively uncommon.

Although each and every Buddha possesses the capacity to transform all sentient beings, sentient beings do not willingly accept transformation from Buddhas with whom they have no karmic connection, nor do they see or hear them.

Although each and every Buddha remains in the world until the end of the future, constantly teaching and transforming immeasurable classes of sentient beings, they manifest various transformations according to what is appropriate—whether appearing as perfect enlightenment or appearing as parinirvāṇa, or bearing names such as Śākyamuni or Maitreya—and from the perspective of any single transformative manifestation, it is said that all the sentient beings to be saved have already been saved.
Those born in the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana) are suitable to attain liberation by beholding the transformation-body (nirmāṇakāya) of Śākyamuni;

therefore, it is not contradictory that he leaves behind a transformation-body to await them. If all Tathāgatas transform the same beings, which Buddha would appear before them to effect their conversion?

Because all Buddhas possess the power of compassionate vows, it is not the case that when one manifests a transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*), the others must cease; rather, whenever there are sentient beings with the requisite conditions, the Buddhas appear in the same place and at the same time. Upon their subsequent attainment wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), each manifests a transformation-body, which is similar in form yet does not obstruct one another. These bodies intermingle and act as mutual dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*), causing the consciousnesses of those to be transformed to undergo such a transformation: namely, they perceive a single Buddha manifesting supernatural powers and preaching the True Dharma. Such matters are inconceivable; they cannot be understood through the mere principle of Consciousness-Only (*vijñapti-mātra*).

Furthermore, the svabhāvakāya is quiescent and blissful; it is primarily subsumed under the qualities of self-benefit. However, because it acts as a dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*) to benefit sentient beings, it also pertains to the benefit of others. Moreover, since it serves as the basis for the qualities of both benefits associated with the [other] two bodies, it is subsumed under both types of benefit.
The Enjoyment Body (*saṃbhogakāya*) possesses two aspects:

first, the aspect of enjoying the Dharma for oneself, which refers to having cultivated practices for one's own benefit throughout three incalculable eons; it fulfills the realization of the actual body of form and so forth, enabling one to personally enjoy subtle and wondrous joy.

Second, the aspect of enjoying the Dharma for others, which refers to having cultivated practices for the benefit of others throughout three incalculable eons; it fulfills the realization of the transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) of form and so forth, manifesting various forms and preaching various teachings for the sake of the assembly of bodhisattvas who have entered the great stages, thereby enabling those bodhisattvas to experience the great joy of the Dharma.

Based on these two aspects, some say this body is comprised solely of self-benefit, some say it is comprised solely of benefit for others, and some say it comprises both; none of these views are mutually contradictory.
The transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) manifests various transformed appearances solely for the benefit of others; therefore, it is subsumed under the category of benefiting others.
Since these three bodies consist of four aspects, they can be arranged into four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*):
first, the enjoyment body that is not a transformation body, which refers to the actual enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*) as the aspect of self-benefit.

2. Transformation body, not enjoyment body: This refers to the transformation body manifested for various classes of beings prior to the stages (bhūmi), which may be coarse or sublime, and may cause them joy or fear; because it changes and is unstable, it is called only a "transformation" body and not an "enjoyment" body, as it does not necessarily cause them to experience the bliss of the present dharma.

3. Both enjoyment and transformation: This refers to the various transformation bodies manifested for Bodhisattvas on the stages, which cause those Bodhisattvas to experience the bliss of the Dharma; because they change according to the occasion and are not fixed, they are both enjoyment and transformation.
4. Neither enjoyment nor transformation: This refers to the self-nature body (*svābhāvikakāya*).
In some places it is taught that the Buddha has two kinds of bodies:
first, the birth-body (janmakāya);
second, the dharma-body (dharmakāya).

Whether it be the *svābhāvika-kāya* (essential body) or the actual *sambhogakāya* (enjoyment body), both are termed the *dharmakāya* (dharma body), because it is the basis upon which all qualities of the Dharma depend and because it is that which is fully integrated by all qualities of the Dharma.

Whether it be the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) or the body of enjoyment for others (*saṃbhogakāya*), both are termed "birth-bodies" (*janmakāya*), because they manifest repeatedly according to what is appropriate for sentient beings.
Furthermore, another sutra states that there are ten kinds of Buddhas:
first, the Buddha of Manifest Complete Enlightenment; [and so forth].
2. Buddhas of Great Vows;
3. Buddhas of Karmic Maturation;
4. Buddhas of Sustenance;
5. The Transformation Buddha;
6. The Dharma-realm Buddha; 7. The Mind Buddha;
8. The Buddha of Concentration;
9. The Buddha of Original Nature;
10. The Buddha of Accordance with Wishes.

The first five [perfections] belong to the conventional truth, while the latter five belong to the ultimate truth; they are subsumed within the three bodies (trikāya) as appropriate. Such categories should be understood accordingly.
The Sūtra says:
"Such is the pure dharma-dhātu, as taught by all Buddhas."
The treatise states:

Thus, the Tathāgatas’ pure dharma-realm is spoken of in common by all Buddhas as being fully endowed with the five kinds of merit of the Buddha-ground and the distinctions of the three bodies, or alternatively, the characteristics of the six categories of meaning such as the self-nature and so forth.

By means of these four verses, all the qualities of the Buddha-ground are briefly explained; together with what was previously explained at length, one should know that this is collectively termed "that which is taught in the Holy Scripture.
The Sūtra says:

When the Bhagavat had finished speaking this sūtra, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Subhūti and others, along with the great śrāvakas, the world’s devas, humans, asuras, and the entire great assembly, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, were all greatly delighted and, with faith and acceptance, practiced accordingly.
The Commentary states:
This section demonstrates how the assembly that hears the Dharma practices in accordance with the teaching.

Drawn forth by the compassionate vows of the Buddha’s pure consciousness, through the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) of the transformation appearing as the Sūtra, the roots of goodness within the minds of the assembly ripen, and appearances resembling those [teachings] manifest; that is to say, upon hearing the Buddha’s discourse, they all give rise to joy, accept it with faith, and practice accordingly.

Whether they be emanations or actual beings, the various śrāvakas and others enjoy both the transformation land and the enjoyment land in the same location. Although the teachings heard by the assembly of listeners are identical, what each sees differs; these differences do not obstruct one another. Those above see those below, yet those below do not see those above, and thus each accomplishes the work of benefiting and bringing peace and happiness to others.
I have now briefly explained, according to my capacity, the profound meanings of the various phrases regarding the Buddha-ground;
may the merit thereof be universally bestowed upon all living beings, so that they may swiftly and equally attain the unsurpassed fruit.
May the merit born from all those who transcribe [this text], and the successive, increasingly superior fruits of its virtuous outflow,
continue in succession until the end of the future, bringing benefit and happiness to all sentient beings.
